items.titleOriginal: Why Are Indians Still Afraid of Going to Therapy?
items.description: Το να πάτε σε θεραπεία ΔΕΝ σημαίνει ότι είστε τρελοί. Ωστόσο, σε πολλές ινδικές οικογένειες, η αναζήτηση υποστήριξης ψυχικής υγείας εξακολουθεί να παρεξηγείται, να κρίνεται ή να απορρίπτεται. Η ηθοποιός Shefali Shah αμφισβητεί αυτή τη νοοτροπία μέσα από τα απομνημονεύματά της, The Audacity of Being, όπου ανοίγει για την ψυχική υγεία, την κατάθλιψη και τη σημασία της επαγγελματικής βοήθειας. Το μήνυμά της είναι ένα λημέρι…
items.descriptionOriginal: Going to therapy does NOT mean you're mad. Yet, in many Indian families, seeking mental health support is still misunderstood, judged or dismissed. Actor Shefali Shah is challenging this mindset through her memoir, The Audacity of Being, where she opens up about mental health, depression and the importance of professional help. Her message is a reminder that sadness should never be dismissed and asking for help should never be a source of shame. It's time we stopped treating therapy as a taboo and started treating emotional health with the same importance as physical health. Seeking help is not a weakness. It's a step towards healing. ❤️ #ShefaliShah #MentalHealth #MentalHealthAwareness #TherapyIsOkay #BreakTheStigma #MentalHealthMatters #DepressionAwareness #IndianFamilies #TherapyNotTaboo #TheAudacityOfBeing #MentalWellness #EndTheStigma #thebetterindia Subscribe Us Now : https://www.youtube.com/thebetterindia Follow us for more: Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/thebetterindia Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thebetterindia/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/thebetterindia LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/thebetterindia/ Website: https://www.thebetterindia.com/

items.title: Ένας πρόωρος τοκετός, 35 Lakh σε ιατρικούς λογαριασμούς και μήνες φροντίδας: Πώς τα κατάφερε αυτό το μωρό της Bengaluru
items.titleOriginal: A Premature Birth, 35 Lakh in Medical Bills & Months of Care: How This Bengaluru Baby Pulled Through
items.description: Υπήρξε μια εποχή που ο Gouthami Ravi και η Sharan Kulkarni θα έδιναν τα πάντα για να ακούσουν την κόρη τους να κλαίει. Σήμερα, στο σπίτι τους στη Μπανγκαλούρ, η ενός έτους Chikoo γεμίζει τις μέρες τους με μικρούς ήχους, παιχνιδιάρικες κινήσεις και την περιέργεια ενός παιδιού που ανακαλύπτει τον κόσμο γύρω της. Παίζει στο κρεβάτι, κάνει αισθητή την παρουσία της και χαρίζει στους γονείς της…
items.descriptionOriginal: There was a time when Gouthami Ravi and Sharan Kulkarni would have given anything to hear their daughter cry. Today, in their Bengaluru home, one-year-old Chikoo fills their days with little sounds, playful movements and the curiosity of a child discovering the world around her. She plays on the bed, makes her presence felt and gives her parents the kind of ordinary moments they once could only hope for. For months, they had watched over her breathing, learnt to manage medical equipment, and prepared for emergencies. A tracheostomy tube in her throat meant they could no longer hear her cry. Their home had become a medical care unit, and every day revolved around keeping their little girl safe. On 10 March 2026, after months of treatment, Chikoo's tracheostomy was finally removed. Sharan remembers that even before the procedure, he had held on to a belief that his daughter would survive. "We were not in a dilemma that it was 50-50 always. It was always 100%. She's going to survive," he says. That conviction carried the couple through a premature birth, frightening medical emergencies and months of round-the-clock care. But their experience also left them with a desire to help other families facing a similar journey. Born seven weeks premature, Chikoo weighed just 2.05 kg and needed breathing support soon after birth. When Chikoo needed a tracheostomy at barely a month old, they searched online for Indian parents who had been through the same experience. They found very little that could prepare them for what lay ahead. "I am so alone in this journey," Sharan remembers feeling. Today, Gouthami and Sharan want to make sure other parents facing a similar situation do not have to navigate it without guidance. They are open to speaking directly with families whose children may need a tracheostomy, sharing what they learnt through Chikoo's treatment and helping them understand what to expect. This includes practical guidance on questions to ask doctors, preparing a home for a child with a tracheostomy, learning tube changes and understanding how to respond to emergencies. They also want to be open about the medical, emotional and financial demands of long-term care, so families have a clearer picture of what lies ahead. While every child's medical needs are different and decisions must be made with the treating doctors, Gouthami and Sharan hope that sharing their experience can help another family feel less alone and better prepared. A premature birth, followed by an unexpected crisis Chikoo was born on 2 September 2025, seven weeks before her expected due date. Weighing just 2.05 kg, she needed breathing support and was moved to a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) soon after birth. A stomach infection added to her early medical challenges. After around 15 days of treatment, she was discharged. Her parents brought her home, believing that the difficult beginning was behind them. "We thought it was the same way," Gouthami recalls, explaining how they assumed their daughter had recovered as many babies do after a NICU stay. They began settling into the routines of caring for a newborn: feeding, bathing, and looking after their little girl. Then, about a month into her life, something frightening happened. During a feed, Chikoo began choking. Her skin turned blue, and she became unresponsive. Gouthami, who knew CPR, tried to help her while the family rushed to the hospital. Chikoo eventually began breathing again, and her oxygen levels appeared normal when they arrived. The family was sent home, with the episode attributed to a feeding issue. But when the same thing happened again about a week later, Gouthami and Sharan knew something was wrong. This time, Chikoo's oxygen levels began falling, and she needed sustained respiratory support. Chikoo's parents learnt to manage her tracheostomy care at home, from handling medical equipment to preparing for emergencies. Further investigations revealed a combination of airway conditions, including laryngomalacia, a laryngeal cleft and tongue-base obstruction. Together, these were affecting her ability to coordinate feeding and breathing safely. The couple had entered a world of medical terminology, hospital admissions and decisions they had never imagined making for their newborn. The decision that changed everything As they began navigating unfamiliar diagnoses and difficult treatment decisions, the family relied on the guidance of their medical team. Gouthami and Sharan are grateful to Dr Sudheer K A, Dr Srikanta J T, Dr Antony George and Dr Priyanka Potti, Dr Vikas Satwik and Dr Sneha Lingappa, and Dr Shwetha Anand Baratikke from the pulmonary, paediatric, and gynaecology departments. The family credits the doctors involved in Chikoo's care for helping them navigate a period filled with uncertainty and decisions they had never expected to make. Gouthami and Sharan spent months learning the practical aspects of tracheostomy care so they could look after their daughter safely at home. As Chikoo continued to need breathing support, doctors recommended a tracheostomy, a procedure in which an opening is made in the neck to provide an airway through a tube. For a baby barely a month old, it was an overwhelming prospect. The first attempt was unsuccessful. The family had already been through the fear of watching their daughter struggle to breathe and the weight of agreeing to a major procedure. Now, they had to find the strength to try again. The second tracheostomy, performed in October 2025, was successful. But the procedure was only the beginning of another demanding phase. Chikoo needed time to recover and gradually come off the ventilator and oxygen support. Her parents spent weeks waiting outside the NICU, looking for updates and hoping that each day would bring progress. "Emotionally, we were too down," Gouthami says, describing what the family went through. With a suction machine, pulse oximeter and feeding pump at home, the family adapted their everyday routines to meet Chikoo's medical needs. They were also thinking about Chikoo's future. Gouthami wanted to understand whether her daughter would be able to develop and live as other children did. The family sought medical assessments, including checks on her neurological responses, and held on to the reassurance that these results offered. For Sharan, the answer was to keep believing in his daughter , even when the outcome was uncertain. "I never asked God for anything else," he says, describing how he imagined a future in which Chikoo would grow up and experience life beyond the hospital. That belief did not make the difficult days disappear. It gave them something to hold on to as they navigated one decision at a time. When home became a medical care unit After months of hospital care, Chikoo was eventually able to return home with her tracheostomy in place. But bringing her home did not mean returning to normal life. The family had to prepare their house for her medical needs, arranging equipment such as a suction machine, a pulse oximeter and a feeding pump. They also changed their daily routines to reduce potential irritants in the air. With nurses working in shifts, Gouthami and Sharan ensured Chikoo received the care and attention she needed at home. For months, they avoided lighting incense and made special arrangements for cooking. Nurses cared for Chikoo in shifts, with a dedicated space arranged for them at home. Yet Gouthami and Sharan knew that professional help could not always be immediately available. They therefore underwent practical training to learn how to care for the tracheostomy and respond to emergencies. "We had a booklet given. We had to read through that, do the Google research and go back the next day and explain what it is about," Gouthami recalls. The training lasted around 20 days. They learnt the procedures, familiarised themselves with the equipment and prepared themselves to manage situations that could arise at home. Learning to care for Chikoo at home also meant learning to trust their own hands while knowing when to seek medical help. The couple remains grateful to the medical team for guiding them through the practical aspects of her care and helping them prepare for emergencies. Their home nurses, Amina Ajusha and Aditya Sivadas, were also part of the support system that helped the family manage Chikoo's daily needs. Every 15 days, the family travelled back to the hospital for a tracheostomy tube change, carrying the equipment Chikoo depended on. They also had to learn how to perform the change themselves under medical supervision, knowing that they might need to act in an emergency. From monitoring her breathing to managing medical equipment, Chikoo's home-care routine required constant attention and coordination. Work had to find its place around these responsibilities. Gouthami was able to draw on maternity leave, while Sharan reorganised his business so that much of his work could be managed from home. His team supported him, allowing him to attend to his daughter while keeping the business running. The couple also leaned heavily on their families. "The need for having parents at home is extremely important," Sharan says. "Even today, without them, we cannot stay at home even one day." Gouthami credits her employer, SAP, for supporting her through this period. "SAP stood by me like family. The medical insurance and mental-health support gave me the confidence to make financial decisions for my daughter's care. I am endlessly thankful to my company for being there for me when I needed that support the most," she says. The financial demands of Chikoo's treatment were considerable. From her hospital care and medical procedures to the home-care arrangements she needed until her tracheostomy was removed, the family spent approximately Rs 35 lakh. Insurance covered only a part of the total expense, leaving them to manage the remaining costs alongside the demands of her care. The day they heard her voice again For months, Chikoo's parents had been unable to hear her cry with the tracheostomy in place. Before the tube could be removed, she underwent a series of carefully monitored steps, including a speech-valve trial and a capping trial to assess her ability to breathe through her nose and mouth. For Gouthami and Sharan, hearing Chikoo cry again was an emotional moment after months of being unable to hear her voice because of the tracheostomy tube. The process required patience. Chikoo did not immediately tolerate every step, and there were moments when the family had to wait longer than expected. Rather than rushing, they followed the medical team's guidance and gave her the time she needed. Then came a moment they had been waiting for. "When we were cleaning the tracheostomy, she started crying, and we could hear her voice," Sharan recalls. It was a sound that meant far more than words could express. The family and the nurses who had cared for Chikoo were moved to tears. After the trials and necessary medical assessments, her tracheostomy was permanently removed on 10 March 2026. Sharan remembers that no words could describe the moment. They went to the doctor and thanked the medical team. Looking back, he says, "It is not about being right here. It is about taking the next step." Today, Chikoo attends daycare, plays with toys and spends her days exploring new experiences as her parents watch her grow. Today, watching Chikoo play, vocalise, and grow, they can see how far she has come. She now goes to daycare, where she spends her days surrounded by bright toys, new little friends and plenty of activity. While a few developmental milestones are still catching up, her parents describe her as curious, energetic, and full of life. The medical equipment and routines that once dominated their lives no longer define every moment of their daughter's day. If you are a parent looking to connect with Gouthami and Sharan, you can reach out to The Better India team for their contact details or connect with them directly through their Instagram accounts. All images courtesy of Gouthami and Sharan.

items.title: Άνδρας πηγαίνει με τα πόδια στο σπίτι στη μαμά του από την άκρη της Νότιας Αμερικής. Του πήρε 28 χρόνια.
items.titleOriginal: Man walks home to his mom from the tip of South America. It took him 28 years.
items.description: Ο Karl Bushby άφησε το σπίτι της μητέρας του στο Hull της Αγγλίας το 1998 με ένα σχέδιο να επιστρέψει σε αυτό, ξεκινώντας από το κάτω μέρος της Νότιας Αμερικής. Την περασμένη εβδομάδα, 28 χρόνια και 31.000 μίλια αργότερα, τελικά τα κατάφερε. Το πανό έξω από το σπίτι της Angela Bushby έγραφε «Welcome Home Son». Όταν ο γιος της ανέβηκε στην πόρτα, σπρώχνοντας το καρότσι που κουβαλούσε τον εαυτό του…
items.descriptionOriginal: Karl Bushby left his mother’s house in Hull, England, in 1998 with a plan to walk back to it, starting from the bottom of South America. Last week, 28 years and 31,000 miles later, he finally did . The banner outside Angela Bushby’s terraced house said “Welcome Home Son.” When her son walked up to the door , pushing the cart that had carried his belongings across four continents, she hugged him and asked the obvious question. “Where have you been?” The answer would take quite a while. Bushby, a 57-year-old former British paratrooper, set out from Punta Arenas, at the southern tip of Chile, on Nov. 1, 1998, with two rules: no transportation of any kind to move forward, and no going home until he had walked there. He was 29, and his marriage had just ended. His wife had moved to Northern Ireland with their young son. View this post on Instagram He walked north through the Andes and hacked through the Darién Gap between Colombia and Panama. He crossed the frozen Bering Strait from Alaska into Russia. Years later, he swam roughly 184 miles across the Caspian Sea . When authorities would not let him walk through the Channel Tunnel, he swam the English Channel instead, about 20 hours in the water over three days, coming ashore near Dover on Oct. 5. It was not 28 straight years of walking. Bushby told the BBC he spent about 15 of those years on foot, regularly heading back to Mexico to deal with visas, logistics, and sponsors. The 2008 financial crisis left him broke, and the pandemic stalled him too. He had not seen his mother since 2015. On Monday, Nov. 2, 28 years and one day after he left, he crossed into Hull to a civic welcome and a crowd of hundreds. “For 28 years, 10,229 days, Hull has been waiting for your return,” Lord Mayor Maria Coward told him. Then he walked the last stretch to his childhood home, where his mother was waiting, along with his son Adam, now 36, and his 12-year-old granddaughter, whom he had never met. “They say it takes a village, but literally it took a world to get me here,” Bushby said. “I didn’t do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth.” Werner Herzog ( @wernerherzogofficial ) is making a documentary about the journey called Walk of Life , and Bushby plans to write a book and give talks. First, though, he has to relearn the place he started from. View this post on Instagram “It’s almost like arriving in a foreign country,” he told CBS News . “I’ve worked with dollars for 28 years. I don’t know the brands in the stores.” The post Man walks home to his mom from the tip of South America. It took him 28 years. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι άνθρωποι περίμεναν να απολαμβάνουν περισσότερο τις άγνωστες ιστορίες. Ένα πείραμα βρήκε το αντίθετο.
items.titleOriginal: People expected to enjoy unfamiliar stories more. An experiment found the opposite.
items.description: Μερικοί άνθρωποι είναι θεαματικοί αφηγητές. Μπορούν να κρατήσουν ένα δωμάτιο —και προσοχή— φαινομενικά αβίαστα, και να κάνουν τους ανθρώπους να βασίζονται στα λόγια τους και να θέλουν ακόμα περισσότερα. Είναι πραγματικά μια αξιοζήλευτη επικοινωνιακή ικανότητα. Το σπουδαίο πράγμα του να είσαι σπουδαίος αφηγητής είναι ότι χρησιμοποιεί ένα φυσικό μέρος του να είσαι άνθρωπος: το να μοιράζεσαι ιστορίες είναι μια βασική δεξιότητα των ανθρώπων…
items.descriptionOriginal: Some people are spectacular storytellers. They can hold a room—and attention—seemingly effortlessly, and get people to hang on their words and still want more. It is truly an enviable communication skill. The great thing about being a great storyteller is that it taps into a natural part of being human: sharing stories is an essential people skill that connects us. For those who want to foster deeper connections and become skilled storytellers, a team of Harvard researchers has identified the secret sauce. Social psychological researchers Gus Cooney, Daniel Gilbert, and Timothy D. Wilson published a paper in the journal Association for Psychological Science titled “ The Novelty Penalty: Why Do People Like Talking About New Experiences but Hearing About Old Ones? “ Their findings were surprising: the stories that captivated listeners weren’t new, exciting, or enthralling—they were ones people could relate to. Successful storytelling Successful storytelling centers on shared context for listeners. In a series of experiments, 90 Harvard undergrads were recruited to be either a listener or a speaker. The listeners were instructed to watch one specific video, while the speakers were instructed to watch the same video as well as a novel (new) one. Afterward, the speakers were told to tell the listeners about both videos. “In our study, when both parties had viewed the same video, if the speaker made a mistake about something in their story, the listener could just fill in the information since they had seen the same video,” lead author and former Ph.D. student at Harvard’s Graduate School of Arts and Sciences Gus Cooney, Ph.D., told The Harvard Gazette . “But when the listener hadn’t watched the same video and didn’t have that necessary background knowledge, it was very easy for them to get confused.” The story that appealed most to the listeners was not the new video—it was the one they had already watched and were familiar with. “The speakers thought listeners would enjoy hearing about a novel story,” said Cooney. “In fact, listeners enjoyed the familiar story much more.” Researcher Daniel Gilbert shared with NPR , “Most of us, when we tell stories, leave all sorts of things out. As a result, if our listeners aren’t already familiar with the topic we’re talking about, they get lost really, really quickly.” The “novelty penalty” The phenomenon is something researchers referred to as the “novelty penalty.” In the study, researchers explained that storytellers often miss the mark because “they worry too much about boring their listeners and not enough about confusing them, and that they therefore tell novel stories to listeners who would have enjoyed hearing familiar stories a great deal more.” Cooney added, “It struck me that we always try to add these novel stories to conversations, and then it doesn’t go over as well as we think and then conversations kind of naturally drift back towards talking about familiar things or things that we have in common with other people.” Researchers also coined the term “novelty bonus,” which is essentially the opposite of the “novelty penalty.” In the “novelty bonus,” storytellers expect that by telling new, exciting stories, they will be rewarded. But the opposite happened. “I think our imaginations can often fail us if we’ve never [experienced something] ourselves. Imagination is great, but it also has its limits,” Cooney explained. How to be a good storyteller With this information, becoming a good storyteller centers on keeping our tales simple, relatable, and focused on the familiar. In the study, the researchers pointed out four specific reasons familiar stories were more powerful than novel ones. Familiar stories: “contain significant amounts of novel information, evoke rich personal memories, allow speakers and listeners to bond over common experiences, and allow listeners to gain information about themselves via social comparison.” To do this, Cooney explained, “Basically we should err more on the side of not trying to confuse our listeners rather than always trying to delight them and interest them with novel information.” Gilbert also told the Association for Psychological Science , “People are fairly awful storytellers who leave out a lot of important information. Our friends probably would enjoy hearing us tell them about a painting they’ve never seen or a book they’ve never read if we could describe those things well. But most of us can’t. As a result, our friends are actually a whole lot happier when we tell them what they already know because at least they understand what we’re talking about. We worry too much about thrilling our listeners and not enough about confusing them.” The post People expected to enjoy unfamiliar stories more. An experiment found the opposite. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι Millennials μοιράζονται τον τρόπο με τον οποίο επέστρεφαν στο σπίτι πριν από την Uber, και αυτό ταράζει τα μυαλά των νέων
items.titleOriginal: Millennials are sharing how they used to get home before Uber, and it’s blowing young minds
items.description: Κάποια στιγμή στις αρχές της δεκαετίας του 2010, μια μικρή εφαρμογή που ονομάζεται Uber κατέστρεψε τον κόσμο. Με ένα πάτημα σε μια εφαρμογή στο τηλέφωνό σας, μπορείτε να καλέσετε ένα αυτοκίνητο και έναν οδηγό για να σας μεταφέρουν οπουδήποτε θέλετε. Ούτε τηλεφωνήματα σε περίεργους αριθμούς, ούτε να βγάζεις το χέρι σου στο δρόμο και να φωνάζεις, «Τάξι!» Η Uber, η Lyft και άλλες εφαρμογές κοινής ωφέλειας άλλαξαν εντελώς τον τρόπο με τον οποίο εμείς…
items.descriptionOriginal: Sometime in the early 2010s, a little app called Uber took the world by storm. With a tap on an app on your phone, you could summon a car and driver to take you anywhere you wanted to go. No phone calls to weird numbers, no sticking your arm out in the street and yelling, “ Taxi !” Uber, Lyft, and other rideshare apps completely changed the way we get around. They’ve become so popular for getting home from places like concerts, bars, and even the airport that cities have to design dedicated pick-up spots for the large crowds who rely on these services. But it all begs the question: what did Millennials and Gen Xers do before rideshare? How did they get home when they couldn’t drive? Lucky for us, they’ve got stories. Millennials and Gen X share their most chaotic getting home stories Professional dancer, choreographer, and actor Blake McGrath recently took to Instagram with a funny observation: “So Gen Z is asking Millennials how we got home from a night out in the 2000s. And, to be honest, I have no idea,” he quipped in a recent Reel. “I do not remember anything. I do not remember whose car I got into … All I remember is waking up the next morning and being like ‘Oh, I made it.'” McGrath was curious whether he was the only Millennial who felt this way, and asked his viewers to chime in with their own stories about how they got home before Uber existed. The post went viral, reaching five million views, and the 30- and 40-somethings had a lot to say. View this post on Instagram Designated driver mayhem Most of the older generation were smart enough to utilize a designated driver when going out on the town. But the process was rarely organized or smooth: “I was DD a ton of the time, so I hauled all my drunk friends and whoever they made friends with in the club to Denny’s and then home … and we did work after yes. (Lots of those people didn’t remember how they got home, and I’m just glad it was safely with me)” “There was also a lot of ‘here are my car keys, there’s my car, but I can’t drive.’ And someone would just drive us.” “Someone’s boyfriends cousins brothers friends coworkers boyfriends car.” “For every 9 people drinking, there was 1 sober friend driving them home all in one shot. People in the trunk, laying across laps, whatever it took to get home” View this post on Instagram Impromptu sleepovers Before you could pull up an app and get a ride home anytime, anywhere, sometimes you never made it home at all. And that was perfectly alright. “You slept at a random house on a couch until you woke up sober enough to drive home.” One commenter dropped an incredible philosophical conundrum: “Maybe we are all still out somewhere and never got home” Walking home, no matter the distance Most Gen Zers would be mortified at the thought of walking a long distance home at night, potentially in the freezing cold. But that was just how Millennials and Gen X got by. “walked an hour in heels and somehow never got lost” “As a GenX woman we knew it was safer to stay out dancing till dawn when the streets were safer to walk home” View this post on Instagram What about taxis? Many Millennials and Gen Xers took taxi cabs home from a night out. But if you didn’t live through it, it’s hard to overstate how chaotic it was to get a cab. For one thing, you never knew up front how much it would cost, and many of them didn’t take credit cards. “Yellow cabs in nyc! But you’d have to ask them to stop at an atm to get cash out” “We pulled up to my apartment and asked the cab driver how much we owed him. He said ‘I’m not a taxi you ran in front of my car on the street and asked me for a ride home'” The mystery method A frequent theme among Millennial commenters is that they simply don’t remember how they got home most of the time. Probably because (aside from having a few drinks) the patchwork methods all blended together after a while. “We don’t know … and straight to work” “just assumed home came to me” “I know there was pizza involved too but how, I can’t tell you” One person summed up the Millennial bar-hopping experience beautifully: “Phase 1: leave the bar … Phase 2: … Phase 3: in bed” No matter how you wound up getting home, one thing almost all Millennials and Gen X can agree on is that you had to stop for greasy food on the way. When Uber and Lyft hit the mainstream, they eliminated a major source of friction in the daily lives of many people. Finally, there was a relatively safe, convenient, and affordable way to get home when you couldn’t drive. Studies even show that the rise of rideshare apps played a big role in reducing drunk-driving rates . But like many friction-reducing modern conveniences, rideshare also partially eliminated the sense of whimsy, the adventure of not knowing, the resourcefulness of finding a ride or a safe place to sleep. Do we want those days back? Probably not. But for Millennials and Gen X, those chaotic late nights helped shape who we are, and we’re still nostalgic for the memories after all these years. The post Millennials are sharing how they used to get home before Uber, and it’s blowing young minds appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ένας φωτογράφος ζήτησε από αγνώστους να χαμογελάσουν. Τα πορτρέτα πριν και μετά είναι εκπληκτικά.
items.titleOriginal: A photographer asked strangers to smile. The before-and-after portraits are stunning.
items.description: Μια εικόνα αξίζει όσο χίλιες λέξεις, ή έτσι λέει η παροιμία. Αλλά μερικές φορές αυτές οι χίλιες λέξεις αποκαλύπτουν περισσότερα για το άτομο που κοιτάζει την εικόνα παρά για το άτομο σε αυτήν. Το 2013, ο Αυστραλός φωτογράφος Jay Weinstein εξερεύνησε αυτή την ιδέα στο έργο του, γι' αυτό τους ζήτησα να χαμογελάσουν. Όπως υπονοούσε ο τίτλος, η σειρά συνδύαζε πορτρέτα αγνώστων ta…
items.descriptionOriginal: A picture is worth a thousand words, or so the saying goes. But sometimes those thousand words reveal more about the person looking at the picture than the person in it. Back in 2013 , Australian photographer Jay Weinstein explored that idea in his project, so i asked them to smile . As the title implied, the series paired portraits of strangers taken before and after he asked them to smile . The idea came to Weinstein while wandering the streets of Bikaner, India, his longtime home. He noticed an interesting-looking man standing near some motorcycles and wanted to photograph him, but felt hesitant to ask. Just then, the man shouted, “Take my picture too!” and, instinctively, Weinstein responded, “Smile,” before snapping a photo. View this post on Instagram Weinstein then had two images: one of the man smiling and one of him with a straight face. Seeing the images side by side, he couldn’t help but notice how vastly different they were. In essence, it felt like he had photos of two entirely different people. The same face can tell an entirely different story He began exploring this idea by photographing strangers around the world, from China to Singapore, Australia, Kenya, Nepal, and beyond. Each time, he would snap a photo before and after asking these strangers to smile. View this post on Instagram View this post on Instagram View this post on Instagram The collection of side-by-side portraits became an intriguing thought experiment about first impressions. They show how quickly we fill in the blanks when looking at an image. Research from the University of Glasgow suggests that we naturally look for meaning in faces, even when a neutral expression gives us relatively little information. Add a smile, and the same face can suddenly seem more open and approachable, even though the person hasn’t told us anything new about themselves. That’s what makes this series so effective. The second photograph doesn’t necessarily tell us more about the person. Instead, it gives us a chance to notice how quickly we change our interpretation when we’re given one additional piece of visual information. Over the course of the project, Weinstein would also notice differences in how different cultures respond to smiling for the camera In Fort Kochi, India , for example, people would sometimes smile while talking with Weinstein, then lose their smiles when he raised the camera. Once he lowered it, the smiles returned. View this post on Instagram Meanwhile, in Beijing, young people were often completely comfortable being photographed and would happily offer a grin and a playful pose. View this post on Instagram In rural Chinese villages, older people often wanted to check a mirror before agreeing to be photographed. People in rural Indian villages, however, often posed immediately. In Bengal, he noticed people sometimes smiled and then covered their teeth with a hand while being photographed. The project has taken a few unexpected and delightful (even profound) pivots since it started Weinstein eventually turned the project into a traveling photography exhibition, bringing his portraits to audiences around the world. Then the COVID-19 pandemic made travel difficult and put masks over the smiles that had become central to his work. In a 2021 interview , Weinstein said the collective experience made the project “even more relevant,” because “the common smile we took for granted” was suddenly hidden from view. Then, while photographing strangers in Kenya, one man turned the camera on Weinstein and asked to take his photograph . He even asked Weinstein to give him the same smile he had requested from strangers for years. A fitting twist, to say the least. In the end, Weinstein’s photographs don’t give us the answers to who these strangers are. But they do give us a chance to acknowledge how quickly our minds try to find those answers, and how easily one small change can make us reconsider the story we’ve already started telling ourselves. Be sure to follow the ongoing so i asked them to smile project on Instagram for even more thought-provoking images. The post A photographer asked strangers to smile. The before-and-after portraits are stunning. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Every geological epoch leaves signatures. One of the Anthropocene’s may be a noise. Oceans echo with the drone of ship engines and blasts of sonar. Cities and suburbs roar with speeding cars and revving motorcycles. Even remote wilderness hums with passing airplanes and strolling hikers. Humanity has turned up the volume on the whole planet. That soundtrack is far reaching. New research in Science finds that noise pollution more than doubles death rates among wild animals. It is also rewriting the rules of who eats whom. In noisy places, prey grow jumpy and predators go hungry. Sometimes an animal fleeing the din runs straight into danger. Noise, the authors write, “reshapes the acoustic arms race” between species, and it creates winners and losers. The researchers argue that protecting wildlife in the Anthropocene means protecting quiet. “This work shows that noise pollution is an underrated threat to wildlife worldwide,” said Hansjoerg Kunc , an ecologist at Queen’s University Belfast and the paper’s lead author. Soundscapes, he said, should be safeguarded with the same seriousness as forests, wetlands and other physical habitats. Scientists have long known that noise harms living things. The World Health Organization calls it a serious health hazard for people: it shortens lives, impairs children’s brain development and disrupts sleep. In wildlife, noise has been shown to spike stress hormones in freshwater fish, alter feeding behavior , and cause forest dwellers to flee in panic . .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby What was missing was the big picture. Kunc and Queen’s colleague Rouven Schmidt gathered 214 studies examining noise effects on 177 species across six continents, from tiny beetles to hulking whales. They focused on controlled experiments, which can more reliably pin effects on noise itself. The effects were widespread. Noise was tied to fetal deformities, weakened immune systems and elevated stress hormones. It altered body size, feeding and parenting, and it changed animals’ success at hunting or escaping hunters. Pooled across the experiments, noise raised mortality by 138%. If 10 in every 100 animals would die in a world without human noise, 24 would die in a world with it. That’s large enough, the authors say, to “threaten population viability.” The effects on how species interact may matter just as much. Animals tended to steer clear of noisy areas, so their numbers there were 37% lower. The prey that remained were on high alert. So predators in noisy places caught 25% less prey, even though they worked harder to find it. But noise doesn’t necessarily help prey either. A loud sound might send a prey animal into a burrow or other enclosed space to hide. Those close quarters can amplify the noise, and that can flush the animal back into the open, where a predator is waiting. The fix, the researchers suggest, starts with treating sound as part of habitat. Kunc points to “measures such as low-noise zones that give animals a genuine acoustic refuge.” In an epoch defined by human influence, quiet may be one of the habitats most worth saving. items.descriptionOriginal: At 7 am in Delhi, the morning commute could become a visibility test over the next couple of weeks. In Lucknow and Patna, similar scenes play out as winter fog settles over roads, neighbourhoods and railway tracks, sometimes remaining until late morning. Now picture a winter morning in Bengaluru or Hyderabad . The temperature may have dropped overnight, and residents may step out wearing jackets, but the city is unlikely to wake up under the same blanket of persistent fog. So, if both regions experience winter, why does one see frequent spells of dense fog while the other experiences it far less often? The answer lies in more than temperature. Geography, moisture in the air, wind speed, overnight cooling and atmospheric conditions determine whether fog forms, how thick it becomes and how long it stays. Research by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and other climate scientists offers a closer look at why winter fog varies across India. Why the northern plains wake up under fog The Indo-Gangetic Plains, stretching across Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal, are among India's most fog-prone regions during winter. 🚨 Anti smog gun is now being used to spray water to mitigate air pollution. Visuals from Delhi, Ring Road near AIIMS. https://t.co/AWXJMn9NQC — Mumbai Rains (@rushikesh_agre_) November 9, 2026 An IMD research paper, Study of Winter Fog Over Indian Subcontinent: Climatological Perspectives , published in the journal MAUSAM in January 2014, examined winter visibility patterns across the country using meteorological observations. The researchers, G K Sawaisarje and colleagues, found that the Indo-Gangetic Plains experienced an average of seven to 10 foggy days in December and more than eight days in January. The region also had conditions particularly favourable for fog formation. Between December and February, average wind speeds were around 0.6 metres per second, temperatures ranged from 9 C to 15 C, and relative humidity stayed between 72% and 84% during the observations. But what makes these conditions important? Much of the fog across northern India is radiation fog. It forms when the ground loses heat overnight, cooling the air immediately above it. When this air reaches its dew point, the moisture present in it condenses into tiny water droplets, creating fog. Clear skies, sufficient moisture, and light winds allow this process to continue. When winds are too strong, the air mixes with warmer layers above, making it harder for fog to develop and remain close to the ground. Delhi, Lucknow and Patna: What the numbers reveal A 2023 study published in the International Journal of Climatology, titled Fog Trends in India: Relationships to Fog Type and Western Disturbances, examined three-hourly meteorological observations from 69 locations across India between 2000 and 2020. Researchers Daniel K E Smith and colleagues identified 10,262 fog events and found that radiation fog accounted for 68.1% of all events and 70% of dense fog events. The study also recorded an average of 54 fog events annually in Delhi, 45 in Patna and 39 in Lucknow. It identified statistically significant increasing trends in fog frequency in all three cities over the periods examined. Another factor influencing these conditions is the movement of western disturbances — weather systems originating around the Mediterranean region and travelling eastwards towards India. These systems can bring moisture and alter atmospheric conditions over northern India. In Delhi, 46.9% of radiation fog events beginning in December and January coincided with an active western disturbance. Kolkata's fog follows a different clock Move eastwards towards Kolkata, and the pattern begins to change. A September 2023 study published in Urban Climate, titled Event-Based Fog Climatology and Typology for Cities in Indo-Gangetic Plains , examined half-hourly visibility observations from seven cities between 1991 and 2020. The researchers, Prasad Deshpande and colleagues, found that fog onset followed an east-to-west pattern, with western cities experiencing delayed onset. Fog intensity, meanwhile, followed a north-to-south pattern, with northern cities recording more intense events. Kolkata, located near the mouth of the Ganga and influenced by its coastal setting, experienced relatively shorter fog events. Unlike the other cities studied, fog in Kolkata generally dissipated earlier, between 8 am and 11 am. The city also recorded a smaller proportion of very thick fog events. The Deccan's elevated terrain, varying moisture availability, and different patterns of atmospheric circulation create conditions that are generally less favourable for widespread, prolonged winter fog Photograph: (Indian Express) Across the seven cities, January recorded the highest proportion of fog events. Around 61% began between 8 pm and 5 am, while approximately 70% dissipated between 9 am and 1 pm. Why the Deccan experiences less persistent fog The Deccan Plateau is not entirely free from fog. The 2014 IMD study documented significant fog occurrences in South Interior Karnataka. Coastal Karnataka also recorded an average of approximately 6.5 foggy days during the winter season. The Deccan's elevated terrain, varying moisture availability , and different patterns of atmospheric circulation create conditions that are generally less favourable for widespread, prolonged winter fog than those across the northern plains. Fog Vs Smog However, fog and smog are not the same. Pollution can reduce visibility even without the atmospheric conditions required for meteorological fog. When pollutants mix with fog droplets, they can also contribute to persistent winter haze. Urban heat-island effects, changing aerosol concentrations, and atmospheric circulation can interact in complex ways, making it difficult to attribute changing fog frequency to a single cause. Ultimately, India's winter fog is not one uniform weather phenomenon. Delhi's frequent radiation fog, Kolkata's shorter morning spells and the relatively rare fog events across much of the Deccan reflect how local geography and atmospheric conditions shape each city's winter. Understanding these differences matters beyond predicting the morning commute. Fog affects road safety, railway and aviation operations, while the interaction between fog and pollutants has implications for air quality and public health. Sources: 'Fog Trends In India: Relationships To Fog Type And Western Disturbances' : By Daniel K. E. Smith, Stephen R. Dorling, Ian A. Renfrew, Andrew N. items.descriptionOriginal: Ο Ελληνικός Ερυθρός Σταυρός (Ε.Ε.Σ.) συνεχίζει να πρωτοστατεί στην προώθηση της εθελοντικής αιμοδοσίας στην Ελλάδα, διοργανώνοντας, σε καθημερινή βάση, αιμοδοσίες σε όλη την επικράτεια, προκειμένου να ενισχύσει τους συνανθρώπους μας που το έχουν ανάγκη. Μέσα από τη συστηματική υλοποίηση δράσεων αιμοδοσίας, ο Ε.Ε.Σ. συμβάλλει στην κάλυψη των αυξημένων αναγκών της χώρας σε αίμα, ευαισθητοποιώντας παράλληλα τους πολίτες για τη σημασία της εθελοντικής προσφοράς. Στο πλαίσιο αυτό, η Υπηρεσία Αιμοδοσίας του Ε.Ε.Σ. πραγματοποιεί τον Νοέμβριο του 2026 σειρά εθελοντικών αιμοδοσιών σε διάφορες περιοχές της Αττικής, σε συνεργασία με σχολεία, επιχειρήσεις και τοπικούς φορείς. items.descriptionOriginal: Χωρίς συμβεβλημένα με τον Εθνικό Οργανισμό Παροχής Υπηρεσιών Υγείας (ΕΟΠΥΥ) ιδιωτικά διαγνωστικά εργαστήρια βρίσκεται η Χίος, μετά την απόφαση των ακτινοδιαγνωστικών εργαστηρίων του νησιού να διακόψουν τη συνεργασία τους με τον Οργανισμό, αναδεικνύοντας με τον πιο ηχηρό τρόπο το πρόβλημα της πρόσβασης των νησιωτών σε βασικές υπηρεσίες υγείας. Το θέμα αναδεικνύει η Πανελλήνια Ομοσπονδία Εργαστηριακών Γιατρών (ΠΟΕΡΓΙ), η οποία, μάλιστα, απαντά σε δηλώσεις του Υπουργού Υγείας, Άδωνι Γεωργιάδη, ο οποίος έκανε λόγο για «καρτέλ» των διαγνωστικών στο νησί. Η παραπάνω εξέλιξη έχει άμεσο αντίκτυπο στους κατοίκους Χίου, οι οποίοι καλούνται να πληρώνουν ιδιωτικά όποιες διαγνωστικές εξετάσεις χρειάζονται, καθώς χάνουν τη δυνατότητα εξυπηρέτησης μέσω των συμβεβλημένων εργαστηρίων του ΕΟΠΥΥ, να πάνε δηλαδή στα διαγνωστικά με παραπεμπτικό και να πληρώνουν συμμετοχή. Για τους ασθενείς, ιδιαίτερα όσους χρειάζονται συχνές εξετάσεις, το κόστος μπορεί να μετατραπεί σε σοβαρό εμπόδιο στην έγκαιρη παρακολούθηση της υγείας τους. Η ΠΟΕΡΓΙ με σημερινή ανακοίνωσή της παρεμβαίνει στην αντιπαράθεση που έχει ξεσπάσει μετά τις δηλώσεις του υπουργού Υγείας Άδωνι Γεωργιάδη στη Βουλή, καταγγέλλοντας τη δημόσια στοχοποίηση των εργαστηρίων, τον χαρακτηρισμό τους ως «καρτέλ» και τις απειλές περί ανάκλησης των αδειών λειτουργίας τους. Η Ομοσπονδία αποδίδει την αποχώρηση των εργαστηρίων από τον ΕΟΠΥΥ στους ασφυκτικούς οικονομικούς όρους που επιβάλλουν οι μηχανισμοί rebate και clawback, υποστηρίζοντας ότι οι υποχρεωτικές επιστροφές έχουν καταστήσει τη λειτουργία πολλών εργαστηρίων οικονομικά μη βιώσιμη. «Η σύμβαση με τον ΕΟΠΥΥ δεν αποτελεί υποχρέωση ισόβιας και άνευ όρων συνεργασίας. Κάθε πάροχος υπηρεσιών υγείας οφείλει να τηρεί τις νόμιμες υποχρεώσεις του, έχει όμως και το δικαίωμα να αξιολογεί κατά πόσο οι οικονομικοί όροι μιας σύμβασης επιτρέπουν τη συνέχιση της λειτουργίας του» , σημειώνει, μεταξύ άλλων, η Ομοσπονδία των εργαστηριακών γιατρών. Η ΠΟΕΡΓΙ ζητά την οριστική κατάργηση του clawback και καλεί την κυβέρνηση να αναλάβει την ευθύνη χρηματοδότησης της Πρωτοβάθμιας Φροντίδας Υγείας. «Η ευθύνη για την επάρκεια και τη χρηματοδότηση των υπηρεσιών υγείας ανήκει στην Πολιτεία και δεν μπορεί να μεταφέρεται στους ιδιώτες παρόχους, με την απαίτηση να συνεχίζουν να παρέχουν υπηρεσίες υπό οποιουσδήποτε οικονομικούς όρους» , σημειώνει. Ειδήσεις σήμερα Η έλλειψη ύπνου δυσκολεύει τη λήψη αποφάσεων και μας καθιστά ευκολότερα θύματα διαδικτυακής απάτης Καρκίνος νεφρού: Ανησυχητική αύξηση στους κάτω των 50 ετών – Τα 4 ύποπτα συμπτώματα Παπανδρέου: Η Ευρώπη πρέπει να νικήσει τον διαβήτη μια για πάντα

items.descriptionOriginal: Every day, vegetable peels, leftover food and other kitchen scraps find their way into garbage bins across Indian homes. Once collected, much of this biodegradable waste ends up in landfills, adding to the country's growing waste management problem. But what if this waste could be turned into manure within 24 to 48 hours, right where it is collected? Kitchen scraps are sorted and prepared before being broken down into manure through a microbial process. That is what Nisargruna, a waste-processing technology developed by Dr Sharad P Kale, a scientist at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), aims to do. Already being used in Goa, the technology converts one tonne of kitchen waste into around 150 kg of nutrient-rich manure. Turning a tonne of kitchen waste into manure in two days The process begins with separating food waste, including vegetable peels and leftover food, from plastic and other dry waste. The biodegradable waste is then cut into tiny pieces before a special mixture containing microorganisms is added. These microorganisms break down the organic matter naturally, while air is supplied to speed up the process. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) Within 24 to 48 hours, the waste is converted into manure that can be used to n ourish plants and soil. Unlike conventional waste disposal systems that transport garbage to distant dumping grounds, Nisargruna allows the entire process to take place at the point where the waste is collected. This means kitchen waste can be treated locally instead of being mixed with other garbage and sent to landfills. Treating food waste close to home India generates around 78 million tonnes of food waste every year. When biodegradable waste is mixed with plastic and other discarded materials, managing and recovering useful resources becomes harder. Nisargruna offers a way to handle this problem at the source. Nisargruna enables communities to process their kitchen waste locally, reducing the amount of garbage that needs to be transported to landfills. By processing wet waste locally, the technology can reduce the amount of garbage that needs to be transported to landfills. It can also mean fewer garbage trucks on the road and cleaner dry waste, making it easier to recover and recycle materials such as plastic. The manure produced in the process can also find use in gardening and soil enrichment, giving discarded food scraps another purpose. Could more Goan villages turn their food waste into manure? The technology's journey in Goa began in Bicholim, where Nisargruna was first implemented. Now, plans are underway to set up these units across municipalities and village panchayats in the state, taking decentralised waste processing to more communities. First implemented in Goa, the technology is now being considered for wider adoption across the state's municipalities and village panchayats. Photograph: (X/@ The Logical India ) For cities and villages dealing with mounting piles of mixed garbage, the idea offers a practical alternative: instead of transporting every bit of waste elsewhere, process what can be reused where it is generated. A vegetable peel need not end its journey in a landfill. With the right process, it could return to the soil as manure within just two days.

items.descriptionOriginal: As Delhi wakes up to another morning of polluted air, a layer of dust settles on cars, windows, and balcony railings. However, amid the haze, money plants continue to trail down walls , marigolds bloom in pots, and hibiscus plants put out fresh leaves. Their survival raises a question for anyone who tends a balcony garden. How do plants continue to grow when the air around them is so polluted? Are some plants better equipped to withstand poor air quality, and what can gardeners do to help them cope? The question has become particularly relevant after Diwali. On the night of 8 November, Delhi's AQI reportedly climbed to 2,283, according to real-time readings cited by The Times of India . The official Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) average for Diwali day stood at 376. By 11 November, the city's AQI was around 301, in the 'very poor' category, according to Business Standard. Plants face the same polluted conditions, but their ability to survive depends on the species, duration of exposure, and growing conditions. How does polluted air affect plants? Plants need sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to grow. Their leaves absorb light and exchange gases through tiny openings called stomata. Dust and particulate matter settling on leaves can interfere with these processes, affecting the light reaching leaf surfaces and the functioning of stomata. As Delhi wakes up to another morning of polluted air, a layer of dust settles on cars, windows, and balcony railings. Photograph: (Invest India) Prolonged exposure can also affect photosynthesis and plant growth, as research on particulate matter and plant physiology explains. A high AQI reading does not mean every plant will immediately wilt. Some plants may continue to put out new leaves and flowers even as dust accumulates on their foliage, making regular care important. Which plants can tolerate polluted conditions? Researchers use the Air Pollution Tolerance Index (APTI) to assess how plants respond to pollution. It considers factors such as leaf pH, chlorophyll content, relative water content, and ascorbic acid levels. An Indian study of plant species in Delhi included Dracaena deremensis and Tagetes erecta, commonly known as marigold, among the plants examined. Both were classified as pollution-tolerant in the study. 1. Marigold Marigold is a practical option for a sunny balcony. It grows well in containers and produces bright flowers. Give it sufficient sunlight and well-draining soil, and avoid keeping its roots constantly wet. The Royal Horticultural Society's container-growing guide explains how to choose suitable conditions for potted plants. 2. Dracaena Dracaena is an option for an indoor or semi-shaded spot. Grown for its foliage, it can adapt to indoor conditions when it receives suitable light and is not overwatered. 3. Neem, peepal, and Pongamia For larger terraces or open spaces, neem, peepal, and Pongamia are worth considering. A research paper by The Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences examines pollution tolerance in tree species, including peepal and Pongamia. These trees are not practical for most small balconies, but may suit larger outdoor spaces. Pollution-tolerant does not mean pollution-proof. Severe or prolonged exposure can still affect plant health. Why balcony plants may struggle even without pollution Polluted air is only one possible reason a balcony garden may deteriorate. Seasonal changes and everyday care also matter. Winter temperatures and shorter days As winter sets in, shorter days bring less sunlight, while lower temperatures can slow plant growth. Cold drafts and sudden temperature changes may damage sensitive plants. With growth slowing, plants usually need less water. The Royal Horticultural Society's winter-care advice recommends moving plants to brighter spots, keeping them away from cold drafts and avoiding overwatering. Plants face the same polluted conditions, but their ability to survive depends on the species, duration of exposure, and growing conditions. Photograph: (Image generated by AI) Too much or too little water Overwatering can leave roots sitting in water and lead to root rot. But letting soil dry out completely for long periods can also damage a plant. Check the soil before watering instead of following a fixed schedule. The University of Maryland Extension explains how excess water damages roots and causes leaves to yellow or wilt. Poor drainage and cramped pots Pots without drainage holes can trap excess water. Small containers can also restrict root growth, while compacted potting mix makes it harder for water and air to reach roots. Choose pots with drainage holes and repot plants when they outgrow their containers. Insufficient sunlight A flowering plant that needs direct sunlight may struggle to grow or produce flowers in a shaded corner. Without adequate light, plants may develop weak, elongated stems, pale or yellowing leaves, and fewer blooms. Before choosing a spot, check whether the plant needs full sun (at least six hours of direct sunlight), partial shade (around three to six hours of sunlight), or indirect light. Also, observe how sunlight moves across your balcony or garden during the day. A spot that receives morning sunlight may suit some plants better than one exposed to harsh afternoon sun. A little care can help plants cope During periods of heavy pollution, dust can build up on leaves, especially on balconies facing busy roads. Gently wipe broad leaves with a damp cloth or rinse suitable outdoor plants with clean water. Research on how leaves capture airborne particulate matter examines how particles collect on leaf surfaces. A flowering plant that needs direct sunlight may struggle to grow or produce flowers in a shaded corner. Photograph: (Greenway Biotech) Check plants for yellowing leaves , dry edges, and drooping stems. These symptoms do not always indicate pollution damage; they can also point to watering problems, inadequate light, or temperature stress. Balcony gardens cannot protect residents from Delhi's polluted air or make outdoor air safe to breathe. But choosing plants suited to the balcony and adjusting care as the seasons change can help them remain healthy, even when conditions outside are difficult.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News FireSat Satellites Begin Delivering Twice-Daily Wildfire Data Worldwide Reading Time: 3 minutes FireSat, a satellite constellation built for wildfire detection, launched its first operational satellites in July 2026 and began delivering twice-daily fire data worldwide. FireSat, a satellite constellation built specifically to spot wildfires, reached orbit for the first time as an operational system in July 2026. SpaceX launched three satellites from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California aboard a SpaceX rocket. Within two hours, all three had established contact with ground teams, marking the system’s shift from demonstration to active service. The constellation comes from Earth Fire Alliance , a nonprofit coalition built around a single goal: catching wildfires earlier than existing satellites can. Most space-based fire detection today relies on instruments designed for weather or general Earth observation. FireSat was engineered from the ground up for one job, drawing on interviews with more than 200 firefighters, incident commanders, and scientists worldwide. That focus shows up in the hardware. FireSat’s sensors can detect a fire as small as five meters by five meters, roughly the size of two parking spaces. Six imaging channels across five spectral bands work together to separate real fires from false alarms, keeping the error rate under five percent. A second midwave infrared channel addresses a specific technical problem. A single sensor can essentially overexpose when pointed at an extremely hot fire, much like a camera struggles with a bright light source. The extra channel is tuned to stay accurate even at the highest temperatures. These three satellites currently revisit the world’s most fire-prone regions at least twice daily. Earth Fire Alliance plans to shrink that gap to about one hour by 2029 as more satellites join the constellation. A full build-out of more than 50 satellites, targeted for 2030, would bring worldwide revisit times down to 20 minutes or less. Early results are already circulating. In September 2026, the team released its first active-fire images from the operational satellites, captured roughly three weeks after launch. Earlier tests with a single demonstration satellite had already caught a small roadside fire in Oregon that existing systems missed entirely. That demonstration satellite, launched in March 2025, spent more than a year in orbit proving the sensor technology before the operational constellation followed. During that period, it also captured thermal activity unrelated to wildfires, including a volcanic eruption and gas flares at an oil field, showing the instrument could distinguish between different types of heat sources. Those early tests gave engineers confidence to move from a single prototype to a working constellation. A wildfire burns through forested terrain at dusk, the kind of early-stage blaze FireSat is designed to catch before it spreads. Photo by Pixabay on Pexels. Beyond raw detection, FireSat tracks how a fire grows and moves once it starts. Data on a fire’s perimeter, spread direction, and radiative power feeds directly into incident commanders’ decisions. That kind of detail can shape evacuation orders and help responders decide where to send limited crews and equipment. Faster detection also offers a real cost benefit. Published research suggests that a one-hour revisit rate across the United States alone could help avoid more than a billion dollars in fire damage annually. Projections also point to roughly 3,500 homes protected and 21.9 million tons of carbon emissions prevented each year once the system reaches that pace. The project has been funded by a mix of philanthropic and corporate backers, including the Bezos Earth Fund, Google.org, and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation. Fire agencies such as CAL FIRE and research partners, including the Environmental Defense Fund, joined an early adopter program to help shape how the data is delivered. That early input helped earn the project a TIME Best Invention of 2025. Access to the data remains a central question as the system scales up. According to Earth Fire Alliance, the goal is to make FireSat data available to any fire agency, scientist, or community that needs it, not only wealthy nations with existing satellite programs. Whether that goal holds up as the constellation grows will shape how evenly its benefits reach fire-prone regions worldwide. For now, three satellites mark the start of what Earth Fire Alliance hopes becomes a global, persistent eye on wildfire . As more FireSat satellites join orbit over the coming years, the gap between a fire’s first spark and the moment responders learn about it should keep shrinking. The post FireSat Satellites Begin Delivering Twice-Daily Wildfire Data Worldwide appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Who Gets to Protect the Ocean? Coral Catch is Expanding the Circle of Marine Conservation Reading Time: 3 minutes In Indonesia, Coral Catch is helping women gain the skills, confidence, and opportunities to become divers, researchers, educators, and leaders in marine conservation. Marine conservation is often measured in numbers: corals planted, reef area restored, biodiversity returning. Those numbers matter, and Coral Catch tracks them closely. But as the Indonesian nonprofit’s work grew, so did a different question: who gets the opportunity to protect these ecosystems? Coral Catch began in Indonesia’s Gili Matra Marine Protected Area with a focus on coral restoration. Over time, the team saw that its impact was reaching beyond the restoration sites. Women were growing more confident underwater, pursuing roles in marine conservation and research that once felt out of reach, and finding opportunities to become educators, advocates, and mentors. As more women moved through the program, these individual experiences began to form something larger: a pathway into marine conservation that connects training and diving opportunities with research, restoration, community engagement, and professional development. Coral Catch began to see that its impact was not only about how much reef it could restore, but also about who had the opportunity to become an ocean protector and what could happen when that opportunity continued beyond the initial training. Tania’s experience is one example of what that pathway can make possible. She grew up in Tangerang, a city far from the ocean, and arrived on Gili Air in January 2025 determined to become a marine researcher. Over nine weeks, she trained as a diver and graduated as a scientific diver, gaining not only technical skills but also the confidence to pursue a place in marine conservation. Today, Tania leads shark research in the Gili Matra Marine Protected Area, studying how tourism affects white-tip reef sharks using underwater cameras and acoustic monitoring. She has secured her own research grant and now mentors new Coral Catch participants, becoming part of the same network that helped her move forward. Cenna’s experience reflects another side of the access challenge. Growing up in Surabaya, she saw diving as something women around her did not commonly pursue. At university, she joined a diving club and loved being underwater, but field positions often required experience she had not yet had the opportunity to gain. In 2022, an online talk by a Coral Catch alumna showed Cenna that marine conservation could be a path for her too. She joined Coral Catch’s second group of participants and later worked in sustainable fisheries and community development. Today, she is Coral Catch’s Project and Partnerships Manager, supporting the program and the women coming through it. A Coral Catch Superwoman shares marine conservation lessons with local schoolchildren, extending the program’s reach far beyond the reef. Photo courtesy of Coral Catch Their journeys are now part of a much larger network. Coral Catch has trained 44 Indonesian women, with around 50% progressing to professional-level diving qualifications, and the organization aims to reach 100 women by 2030. Many alumni continue working in marine conservation or sustainable tourism, sharing what they know with their communities, returning to Coral Catch as mentors or taking on new roles, and becoming examples for younger women who may not have previously seen themselves in conservation. This network is central to how Coral Catch approaches conservation. Through its Academy and other programs, participants can move from learning and hands-on training into research, restoration, community engagement, and professional opportunities. The goal is not simply to provide access to the ocean, but to create pathways that allow people to build skills and continue contributing long after their initial training. That approach matters because access to marine conservation is not equal. Through its work, Coral Catch has seen women face barriers to marine education, diving, field experience, and conservation careers. At the same time, coral reefs support livelihoods, food security, tourism, and coastal protection, making the health of these ecosystems closely connected to the communities around them. Coral Catch’s work therefore extends beyond its training programs. The Gili Dive Club gives local community members access to diving and marine conservation training every Sunday, creating another entry point for people who want to develop practical skills and become involved in protecting their local marine environment. Coral Catch also organizes conservation expeditions twice a year, giving participants opportunities to turn travel into meaningful, hands-on experiences in marine conservation. The same approach is now being explored beyond Indonesia. Through its collaboration with Universiti Malaysia Terengganu, Coral Catch is looking at how lessons and approaches developed through its work in Indonesia can be adapted to support women and coastal communities in a different regional context. That does not mean simply copying the Indonesian model. Malaysia has its own cultural, ecological, and institutional context, so Coral Catch is working with local partners and listening to what communities and women there need. What carries forward is the broader foundation of conservation, empowerment, local capacity building, and community ownership. For Coral Catch, restoring reefs remains essential. But conservation is also about creating the people and pathways needed to sustain that work. When women have access to training, field experience, research, mentorship, and professional opportunities, they can become not just participants in conservation, but divers, researchers, educators, mentors, and leaders shaping the future of the world’s oceans. The post Who Gets to Protect the Ocean? Coral Catch is Expanding the Circle of Marine Conservation appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: “It’s only my stomach. My arms and legs are thin.” But that ‘only’ may be exactly why we need to look more closely. Some fat sits just under the skin, the kind you can pinch. But some build up deeper inside the abdomen, around the organs. That is visceral fat, and it is more closely associated with insulin resistance and cardiometabolic risk. Thin arms and legs tell us what your limbs look like, not where your body is storing fat. And less muscle can matter too, because muscle is one of the main places the body uses glucose after a meal. So don’t rely only on the mirror or the weighing scale. Measure your waist. Does that number mean you definitely have a health problem? No. A tape measure cannot diagnose visceral fat. Your waist is a signal, not a verdict. If it keeps growing, keep up balanced meals, aerobic and strength activity and consistent sleep, and take the repeated trend to a qualified doctor to understand the bigger picture. That is legitimate medical guidance, not your body being judged. Talk to a qualified doctor about your metabolic health. This is general information, not a diagnosis or medical advice. #CountWhatMatters #VisceralFat #WaistSize #MetabolicHealth #KnowYourNumbers [normal weight growing waist, visceral fat explained, why waist size matters, thin limbs belly fat, cardiometabolic risk India]

items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. In the bag A low-cost, low-tech intervention is saving lives in maternity wards across Africa. As the New York Times reports in a story shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas, the maternal drape is a plastic pouch that can be used to easily measure blood loss. This allows health workers to act quickly in the case of postpartum hemorrhage, which is extremely dangerous. When combined with the necessary treatments, this intervention cut deaths by postpartum hemorrhage by about two-thirds. “The drape is not an A.I. thing — it’s the absolute opposite,” Dr. Hadiza Galadanci, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Bayero University in Kano, Nigeria, told the Times . “It’s a simple, simple, intervention that can solve our problems.” Michaela says: I had no idea a simple, low-cost plastic bag is saving so many mothers’ lives. Bird’s-eye view In a lighter (but just as surprising) story of lives being saved, googly-eyed buoys are helping prevent seabirds from getting caught in fishing nets. According to a Mongabay story that caught the attention of Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, these devices scare the birds away from the fishing gear. A study off Cornwall, England, found that nets fitted with kites shaped like birds of prey had 71 percent lower odds of catching seabirds, and nets with spinning “looming-eye” buoys had 59 percent lower odds. Becca says: I kinda love these “googly-eyed buoys,” despite their uncanny resemblance to Clippy the paperclip . What else we’re reading The fix for America’s terrible internet is hiding in Tennessee — shared by RTBC Founder David Byrne from Vox What If a Crisis Pregnancy Center Was Pro-Choice? — shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby from The Cut The planet’s vital signs are getting worse. One of the easiest fixes is your diet. — shared by Michaela Haas from Grist In other news… Just after last week’s historic midterm elections, we wrapped up The Depolarization Series , an exploration of the many ways people are defying division and really listening to those who disagree with them. You can check out the full series here — and don’t miss the many fantastic videos we shared on Instagram. The post What We’re Reading: An 80-Cent Plastic Bag Is Saving Mothers’ Lives appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.description: Στο Fargo της Βόρειας Ντακότα, ο Prakash Mathew και η σύζυγός του Jane είχαν έναν όμορφο κήπο που οι άνθρωποι συχνά σταματούσαν να θαυμάσουν. Σκέφτηκαν να γράψουν τα ονόματα των επισκεπτών τους και χαιρετούσαν τον καθένα ονομαστικά την επόμενη φορά. Με την πάροδο του χρόνου, παρείχαν επιπλέον καρέκλες και κάλεσαν τους ανθρώπους να καθίσουν και να συνομιλήσουν, και ένα διαφορετικό είδος κήπου εμφανίστηκε. «Όταν πήγαμε για το δικό μας…
items.descriptionOriginal: In Fargo, North Dakota, Prakash Mathew and his wife Jane had a beautiful garden people would often stop to admire. They made a point of writing down their visitors' names and would greet each by name the next time. Over time, they provided extra chairs and invited people to sit and chat, and a different kind of garden emerged. "When we went for our walks, we could hardly walk two blocks without stopping and talking to someone." Jane died suddenly in December of last year. When summer came, Prakash continued to go to the driveway, and people still joined him. He asked, "What if we did this — sat in my driveway, but intentionally, every other week, with a topic?" Everybody loved it. Driveway Dialogues was born. A neighborhood spirit had been planted, "with a garden, a few extra chairs in front of the house, and a curiosity to care for others."

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Electric School Buses are Cutting Charging Costs in New York City Reading Time: 3 minutes Electric school buses now serve New York City students, and a trenchless charging method cut construction costs by 13%. Electric school buses now carry students across Brooklyn and Queens. First Student and Con Edison, the local utility, finished the first phase of this project . It serves the New York City Department of Education. The charging setup is what sets this project apart. First Student built its First Charge system without traditional underground trenching. That choice cut infrastructure construction costs by 13%. Trenching means digging long ditches to bury cables. That work takes time and disrupts daily life in a crowded city. Skipping it simplifies construction and helps buses reach students sooner. Here is a simple way to picture it. For every $100 a traditional installation would cost, the project saved about $13. Those savings help a fleet that needs many chargers for its electric school buses. First Charge is an above-ground system designed by bus operators, for bus operators. It is modular, meaning its parts fit together, and it can grow with a fleet. Con Edison adds that crews did not need to bury the service line to the chargers. A service line is the cable that brings power to a site. The utility says other fleet owners can copy this idea to save money and finish projects faster. Vicki Kuo, a Con Edison senior vice president, says the utility wants electric vehicles to be affordable. Lower upfront costs help make that goal real. Outside funding also helped. Con Edison and the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) contributed money to the project. That included six bus vouchers and funding for four retrofit buses, which are existing buses converted to electric power. First Student also helps school districts find funding for electric school buses. Since 2023, it has secured millions of dollars in Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) funding for customers. The buses also charge on a schedule that saves money. Load management software sets charging for off-peak hours. Those are times when fewer people use power and energy costs less. The project also includes bi-directional charging technology. This allows electricity to flow both into and out of a battery. Partners are also exploring more ways to lower energy costs for fleets. Electric school buses in this project use bi-directional charging technology that lets electricity flow both into and out of a battery, while partners explore more ways to lower energy costs for fleets. Photo courtesy of First Student . Kevin Matthews, head of electrification at First Student, says scaling up electric school buses takes more than vehicles. Fleets also need the right chargers, technology, and a strong utility partner. Costs vary by district. First Student says Type C and Type D electric school buses cost around $375,000 each. Its analysis shows lifetime ownership costs matching diesel buses by 2029. Cold weather affects electric school bus range. First Student’s Quebec buses travel 80 to 90 miles per charge, or about 70 in deep cold. Newer, larger batteries reach 100 to 120 miles. Maintenance may get easier too. First Student sees fewer fluids to manage and far fewer brake problems. Fewer moving parts also cut repair time. Electric school buses offer a healthier, quieter ride. Con Edison notes the new buses produce no tailpipe emissions, which means no exhaust from the vehicle itself. They replace less efficient buses that burn fossil fuels. During the 2025-26 school year, First Student ran about 490 electric school buses. More than 550 more are on order. Its electric buses have driven over 11.2 million miles, about 450 trips around the Earth. First Student also runs a fleet of more than 48,000 vehicles across the U.S. and Canada. It carries millions of students each day. That reach means lessons from New York can travel far. Next up are 40 more electric school buses for the New York City Department of Education. First Student is also considering expanded solar use and a smart energy hub at its Brooklyn facilities. Transit agencies nationwide are also learning how electric buses can drive change. Cleaner buses can lower tailpipe pollution on every route. Could electric school buses roll out faster in other cities? First Student and Con Edison say the model can help other fleets overcome cost and construction hurdles. For students in Brooklyn and Queens, the payoff is a quieter ride on a cleaner bus. The post How Electric School Buses are Cutting Charging Costs in New York City appeared first on Happy Eco News .
