items.title: Διαγωνισμοί Μουστακιού, Διακοσμημένες Καμήλες & Παιχνίδια Χωριού: Τι Σας Περιμένει στο Pushkar Fair 2026
items.titleOriginal: Moustache Contests, Decorated Camels & Village Games: What Awaits You at Pushkar Fair 2026
items.description: Στην περσινή έκθεση Pushkar, δύο επισκέπτες από την Αργεντινή, ο Pablo και ο Costa, κατάφεραν να δέσουν μια παραδοσιακή σάφα του Rajasthani (τουρμπάνι) σε μόλις 15 δευτερόλεπτα. Η εντυπωσιακή τους ταχύτητα τους χάρισε την πρώτη θέση σε έναν διαγωνισμό που προσκάλεσε διεθνείς τουρίστες να δοκιμάσουν τις δυνάμεις τους σε μια τοπική παράδοση. Σε άλλα μέρη της έκθεσης, 33 άνδρες διαγωνίστηκαν για να επιδείξουν τη φροντίδα τους…
items.descriptionOriginal: At last year's Pushkar Fair, two visitors from Argentina, Pablo and Costa, managed to tie a traditional Rajasthani safa (turban) in just 15 seconds. Their impressive speed earned them first place in a competition that invited international tourists to try their hand at a local tradition. Elsewhere at the fair, 33 men competed to show off their carefully groomed moustaches. Some had curled them into elaborate shapes, while others proudly displayed the length they had spent years growing. Among them was Ram Singh, who spoke of the pride and care that went into maintaining his moustache. These cheerful competitions are part of what makes Rajasthan's famous Pushkar Fair so special. For a few days every year, traditions that have been passed down through generations become something everyone can watch, celebrate and even participate in. And this November, the celebrations are returning. Scheduled from 17 to 24 November 2026 , the cultural programme at Pushkar Fair promises eight days of folk performances, camel decoration competitions, traditional games, music, crafts and celebrations around the town's famous lake. Here's what makes this annual gathering worth experiencing. Where even a moustache can win you a prize At Pushkar, some of the most entertaining competitions celebrate things closely associated with everyday life in Rajasthan. Take the moustache competition, for instance. For many Rajasthani men, a well-maintained moustache has long been associated with pride, personal style and identity. At Pushkar, that tradition gets its own stage. Participants arrive in traditional attire, displaying moustaches that have often taken years to grow and maintain. Judges consider their length, appearance and styling, while visitors gather to watch. The competition is scheduled to return on 21 November 2026, alongside a turban-tying contest for international visitors. And the fun continues beyond the stage. On 22 November, women are scheduled to participate in a matka race, which involves balancing a clay pot while racing towards the finish line. A musical chairs competition is also planned. The initiative has also involved rural women and artisans in preparing camel wool and making handcrafted products. Photograph: (Shutterstock) These activities offer visitors an opportunity to experience a playful side of Rajasthan's cultural traditions. For local participants, they are a chance to share familiar customs with people who may be discovering them for the first time. When traditional village games become the main attraction Remember playing gilli-danda or satoliya as a child? At Pushkar Fair, these traditional games are getting their own place in the celebrations. On 18 November, local residents and international visitors are scheduled to compete in games such as langdi taang (hopping on one leg), satoliya (a game involving stacked stones and a ball) and gilli-danda (played using two wooden sticks). The following day will bring kabaddi matches, tug-of-war, volleyball and other rural sporting competitions. A football match between local players and international visitors is also planned for the opening day, while a cricket match inspired by the film Lagaan is scheduled for 23 November. The appeal lies in how easily these games bring people together. A visitor who may know little about Rajasthan's traditions can join a familiar game, learn something new and share the experience with local participants . For children growing up in a world of mobile phones and online games, it is also an opportunity to watch traditional outdoor games being played and celebrated. What makes a camel the star of the show? Of course, no visit to Pushkar Fair would feel complete without seeing the camels. For generations, these animals have been an important part of Rajasthan's desert life, helping people travel and transport goods across difficult terrain. Today, their place in the fair extends to some of its most recognisable cultural events. On 18 November, the fair is scheduled to host camel decoration and camel dance competitions. Camel owners traditionally prepare their animals with colourful cloth, ornaments, bells and decorative accessories. Some use carefully patterned trimming to create designs in the camel's coat. The result is a display that brings together animal care, local craftsmanship and traditions associated with Rajasthan's desert communities. Behind these decorated camels are people whose knowledge of raising and caring for the animals has been passed down over generations. Among them are the Raika, also known as Rebari, a pastoral community closely associated with camel herding in western Rajasthan. Camel owners traditionally prepare their animals with colourful cloth, ornaments, bells and decorative accessories. Photograph: (Shutterstock) Their expertise includes understanding camel behaviour, caring for animals and finding suitable grazing areas across changing seasons. That knowledge remains valuable, even as camel-rearing livelihoods face growing difficulties. The fair offers visitors a glimpse of this relationship between people and animals, and an opportunity to appreciate the communities who have helped preserve it. Meet the artists keeping Rajasthan's traditions alive There is another side to Pushkar that deserves equal attention: the musicians, dancers and craftspeople who bring the celebrations to life. This year's programme begins on 17 November with group dances by schoolgirls and a mandana competition. Mandana is a traditional form of decorative art in Rajasthan, created using geometric and nature-inspired patterns, often on floors and walls. Giving this art a place at the fair helps introduce visitors to a tradition they might otherwise encounter only in homes and villages. The evenings will bring performances by local artists, including the programme Voice of Pushkar , alongside Rajasthani folk music and dance. These performances give local talent an audience that extends beyond the region. For visitors, they offer an opportunity to experience Rajasthan's cultural heritage through the people who practise these art forms. And for the performers, every appearance is another chance to introduce their work to a new audience. From handmade crafts to camel-dung notebooks Some of the most interesting stories at Pushkar Fair can also be found among the people making and selling traditional products. On 20 November, the Food and Craft Festival is scheduled to open at Shilpgram, bringing another attraction to the celebrations. Such spaces offer visitors opportunities to explore local crafts, meet artisans and discover products that reflect Rajasthan's skills and traditions. One interesting example from previous editions is Camel Charisma, a social enterprise connected to Lokhit Pashu-Palak Sansthan (LPPS), based in Sadri in Pali district. The organisation works with camel-herding communities to create new income opportunities using materials obtained from the animals. Its products have included camel-milk soaps, woollen rugs and even handmade paper produced from camel dung. At an earlier Pushkar Fair, LPPS introduced notebooks, diaries and greeting cards made using this unusual paper. The initiative has also involved rural women and artisans in preparing camel wool and making handcrafted products. What makes these efforts meaningful is the connection between traditional knowledge and present-day livelihoods. When visitors appreciate and buy locally made products, they can help create demand for the skills and materials behind them. For communities whose traditional occupations are changing, such opportunities can make a difference. A celebration that brings an entire town together While the fairgrounds host competitions and performances , the celebrations extend into the town of Pushkar itself. Around Pushkar Lake, the evenings bring gatherings, lamps, rangoli and traditional ceremonies. The fair takes place around Kartik Purnima, an important occasion for pilgrims who visit the town and its sacred lake. This year, Kartik Purnima falls on 24 November, the final day of the main cultural programme. For visitors, this offers another way to experience Pushkar: through its bustling streets, markets, cultural gatherings and the communities who return each year. The fair brings together people with different reasons for being there, from local performers and artisans to pilgrims and travellers exploring Rajasthan. And perhaps that is its greatest appeal. A visitor might arrive hoping to photograph decorated camels, then find themselves watching a traditional game, listening to a folk musician or admiring something made by a local craftsperson. Behind each experience is someone who has learnt, practised or passed down a tradition. As Pushkar Fair prepares to return this November, these are the people who make it memorable. And the most meaningful part of visiting may be the opportunity to appreciate their work, learn something from them and help ensure that Rajasthan's living traditions continue to find new audiences. Sources: 'Camels are vanishing from India's desert regions. Can a new policy push save them?' : By Sanjana Nair & Aniruddh Sheth, Published on 3 November 2025 'Explained: At Pushkar fair, renewed concern over Rajasthan's 2015 camel law' : By Deep Mukherjee, Published on 18 November 2021

items.titleOriginal: Why Do Jaipur’s Streets Run in Straight Lines? A King & a Scholar Planned It 300 Years Ago
items.description: Το Google Maps κυκλοφόρησε στις 8 Φεβρουαρίου 2005, αλλά ένας βασιλιάς Rajput είχε σχεδιάσει μια ολόκληρη πόλη γύρω από ένα πλέγμα 278 χρόνια νωρίτερα. Όταν ο Sawai Jai Singh II ίδρυσε την Jaipur το 1727, χάραξε ευθύγραμμους δρόμους που διασταυρώνονταν σε ορθή γωνία, χώρισε την πόλη σε εννέα τομείς και έθεσε πρότυπα για το ύψος των κτιρίων και το πλάτος των δρόμων της. Αυτό το σχέδιο…
items.descriptionOriginal: Google Maps went live on 8 February, 2005, but a Rajput king had planned an entire city around a grid 278 years earlier. When Sawai Jai Singh II founded Jaipur in 1727, he laid out straight streets that crossed at right angles, divided the city into nine sectors and set standards for the height of its buildings and the width of its roads. That plan still shapes the walled city today, and it began as the answer to a practical problem. A hilltop capital running out of options Before 1727, the Kachwaha rulers governed from Amer, a hilltop capital about nine kilometres northeast of the site that became Jaipur. Droughts and famines had made Amer unsustainable, and the ICOMOS evaluation prepared for UNESCO adds that a growing population, a lack of water and concerns over security all demanded attention in a new capital. Jai Singh, who ruled from 1699 to 1744, chose a plain surrounded by mountains, an unusual decision in a region where cities typically grew organically on hills. A scholar king and a Bengali planner Jai Singh was a mathematician, architect and astronomer, and he consulted architectural books and architects while planning the city. UNESCO notes that he studied town plans sourced from across the globe . For the design itself, he turned to Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, a scholar from Bengal who worked as the king's chief auditor. The collaboration between Jai Singh II and Vidyadhar Bhattacharya brought together ideas from Indian architectural traditions and European mathematics, creating a distinctive approach to city planning. Photograph: ( Talk to Iconic ) Bhattacharya referred to ancient Indian texts on astronomy as well as books by Ptolemy and Euclid, and the city's grid draws inspiration from the Prastara plan of Vastu Shastra, a traditional Hindu system of architecture. ICOMOS records that the plan reflects an interchange of ancient Hindu, Mughal and contemporary Western ideas, with a grid-iron layout familiar in the West and zoning drawn from Hindu concepts. Nine sectors, three squares and uniform bazaars The plan divides the city into nine sectors called chowkris, each measuring about 800 by 800 metres. Two sectors hold the palaces and state buildings, while the remaining seven serve the public. Straight main streets cross at three public squares called chaupars, and colonnaded shops line the bazaars. The state itself built the main markets, shops, residences and temples along these streets, which gave the facades a uniform look, and the plan set specific standards for building heights and road widths. Underground canals and tanks supplied water to the new city, a priority for a court that had left Amer partly because of water shortages. Jai Singh wanted Jaipur to thrive as a centre of commerce, and UNESCO records that he wrote personal letters to bankers and merchants, inviting them to settle with tax concessions and gifts of land for elegant courtyard houses. Jaipur's nine-sector layout was designed to do more than organise buildings. It brought administration, trade, public spaces and residential areas into a carefully coordinated urban system. Photograph: ( Jaipur Beat ) Construction began in 1727, and the major palaces, roads and square took about four years to finish. Around 400 temples rose within the city, and local traditions of trade, craftsmanship and guilds have continued. The city's famous colour arrived later, when the lemon-coloured lime wash of its bazaars gave way in the 19th century to a wash the colour of red sandstone, which earned Jaipur the title of Pink City. Jai Singh's scientific interests also left a lasting mark, since the Jantar Mantar observatory, which UNESCO inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2010, sits within the area nominated for World Heritage status. 300 years on, Jaipur still follows the same plan In July 2019, the UNESCO World Heritage Committee inscribed Jaipur City, Rajasthan, on the World Heritage List, describing it as an exceptional example of indigenous city planning in South Asia. The committee found that the walled city's spatial organisation still reflects its 18th-century grid-iron plan, and that its gates, bazaars and public squares convey the city as it developed between the 18th and early 20th centuries. The Pink City's UNESCO recognition in 2019 acknowledged more than its architectural beauty. It celebrated an 18th-century approach to urban planning that continues to shape a living, evolving city. Photograph: ( ResearchGate ) The modern city has grown well beyond the boundaries set in 1727, and ICOMOS warned in its 2019 evaluation that population pressure, unauthorised new construction and widespread encroachments on the surviving city wall threaten the historic fabric. The grid itself remains mostly intact, and a plan drawn to solve a hilltop capital's problems of crowding, water and security still anchors a working city of bazaars and crafts. Jaipur looks like a grid, then, because several needs were met on one flat site. A king needed water, security and room for a growing population; a Bengali scholar consulted ancient Indian astronomy texts and the books of Ptolemy and Euclid; and a plain gave their straight lines space to run. Nearly three centuries later, that combination still gives the Pink City its shape. items.title: Η τσίχλα για την καταπολέμηση του καρκίνου μειώνει τα επίπεδα του HPV έως και 93%
items.titleOriginal: Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%
items.description: Ένα εκπληκτικό νέο όπλο κατά των μικροβίων που συνδέονται με τον καρκίνο της κεφαλής και του λαιμού θα μπορούσε να είναι τόσο απλό όσο το μάσημα τσίχλας. Οι επιστήμονες ανέπτυξαν ένα βιομηχανικό κόμμι που μείωσε τα επίπεδα του HPV έως και 93% σε δείγματα από το στόμα από ασθενείς με καρκίνο και σχεδόν εξάλειψε δύο επιβλαβή βακτηριακά είδη μετά από μία δόση του εκχυλίσματος του. Ακόμη πιο πολλά υποσχόμενο, η ανταλλακτική θεραπεία…
items.descriptionOriginal: A surprising new weapon against microbes linked to head and neck cancer could be as simple as chewing gum. Scientists developed a bioengineered gum that reduced HPV levels by up to 93% in oral samples from cancer patients and nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species after a single dose of its extract. Even more promising, the treatment spared beneficial bacteria in the mouth.

items.title: Οι επιστήμονες ανακαλύπτουν ένα γιγάντιο τρωκτικό 66 λιβρών που έζησε πριν από 34 εκατομμύρια χρόνια
items.titleOriginal: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago
items.description: Οι επιστήμονες ανακάλυψαν απολιθώματα ενός γιγαντιαίου τρωκτικού που έζησε στην Ταϊλάνδη πριν από 34 εκατομμύρια χρόνια, αποκαλύπτοντας ότι τεράστια τρωκτικά εξελίχθηκαν πολύ νωρίτερα από ό,τι πιστεύαμε. Ονομάστηκε Yakamys sirindhornae, το αρχαίο ζώο μπορεί να ζύγιζε περίπου 66 κιλά, περίπου δύο φορές περισσότερο από άλλα γνωστά τρωκτικά της εποχής του.
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have uncovered fossils of a giant rodent that lived in Thailand 34 million years ago, revealing that enormous rodents evolved much earlier than previously thought. Named Yakamys sirindhornae, the ancient animal may have weighed around 66 pounds, roughly twice as much as other known rodents of its time.

items.descriptionOriginal: The year I turned 30, I moved to a peaceful neighborhood on Los Angeles’ Westside. I was 10 minutes from Venice Beach and had an apartment all to myself. The only catch (besides street parking)? It was 450 square feet. A couple of friends helped me optimize the place: We assembled a custom Murphy bed, installed a wall-mounted folding table, and chose decor that made it feel joyful and airy. Though I lamented not having more space at times, I discovered that my scaled-down quarters came with some perks. Styling the studio so intentionally felt empowering, and because it was so small, I often enjoyed my meals out in the courtyard under the sun. Years later, despite having married and moved into a comfortable condo, I still occasionally yearn for more square footage, particularly during dinner parties or when family visits for the holidays. To refresh my perspective, I spoke to interior design experts and therapists who helped illuminate some of the unexpected benefits of having a smaller home — and offered tips for making the most of yours. Benefits domin_domin—iStock/Getty Images Plus Cost and Cleaning We’ll start with perhaps the most obvious but still occasionally overlooked perks: “Less square footage means less time cleaning and organizing. Owning less means spending less time managing and maintaining your belongings,” Phoenix-based interior designer Mackenzie Collier explained in an email to Nice News. “That frees up more time for hobbies, socializing, and anything else you’d rather be doing!” She added that smaller spaces force us to be more thoughtful about what we buy and why (a welcome mindset shift for many), and that the money we save on quantity can be used to invest in quality — e.g., well-built furniture, bespoke decor, art. And it’s not just our shopping carts that feel the difference, Sierra Troitsky , an interior designer in Indianapolis, pointed out. “Smaller spaces are often more economical and environmentally friendly as they cost less to heat and cool,” she said. Mental Well-Being Less square footage can contribute to a greater sense of well-being because it can encourage us to be neat and organized, “which is calming for the brain,” said Sipora Weissman , a licensed therapist in Ventura, California. In a tiny room, a pile of unfolded laundry is a lot more noticeable than in a large one, for example, so we may be more inclined to actually, you know, put it away . “As a therapist who works with adults who get overstimulated easily, living in a small space can be overwhelming or it can actually be very supportive to someone’s nervous system,” Weissman explained. “If you fill that small space with tchotchkes and clutter, that will be a recipe for an unsettled brain. There are many scientific studies that show the negative impacts of clutter on the brain. But if you take this small space living situation as an opportunity, it can be very conducive to your mental health.” More Intentional Decor Just as I experienced when decorating my tiny quarters, less to work with can have a focusing effect. “A small living room lends itself to intentional decorating because you’re forced to narrow in on fewer, impactful pieces that set the tone for the space — say, a beautiful sofa, a well-sized rug, task and accent lighting, and some meaningful artwork,” said Elena Navarro, an interior designer and professional organizer at Sparkly Maid Austin . View this post on Instagram She added: “I love that limited square footage forces you to really think through everything that you bring in the door, from new dishes to cozy throw blankets to holiday decor. Where is the item going to live? Do you use it enough to warrant giving it a permanent home?” Better for Gathering and Bonding The reason celebrity chef Ina Garten considers six people the ideal number for a dinner party is the same reason your modest home might lend itself to more meaningful gatherings: intimacy. “Small group events tend to produce an environment that allows for more personalized conversation,” explained Whitney Willborn , a Texas-based licensed clinical social worker, adding that it’s easier to not only include everyone in the conversation but also to spot when others appear to be excluded. If guests are spread out in different rooms or fragmented into groups, it’s trickier to notice when a new friend is standing awkwardly by themself, for example. Your own family might benefit from a smaller floor plan, too. Collier recently moved out of a 900-square-foot home, and her household has experienced some nostalgia for the cozier living situation. “There was nowhere to escape to, so we’d sit together, watch a movie, or play games,” she said. “Those shared moments became some of our favorite memories.” Spend More Time in Community My al fresco dining habit of yore highlights how the wide world can beckon when your indoors isn’t vast. Collier had the same experience. “I’ve found that living in a small space encourages me to spend more time outdoors and in my community,” she shared. “Whether it was tending to my garden, or heading to a local coffee shop to work, living small naturally pushed me to get out into the community more.” Tips Double Duty Interior designer Preeti Shah made her name in New York, where minuscule apartments are no big deal (one of the tiniest is an infinitesimal 55 square feet !). When she moved to an area of Houston filled with massive homes, she was bemused. At around 3,000 square feet, her house is among the smallest — yet she said it’s where her neighborhood pals prefer to hang out. Courtesy of Preeti Shah Shah’s lounge area with convertible coffee-to-dining room table A design principle Shah prioritizes, in any sized space, is double duty. “Anything I purchase, I would like for my client to be able to use it in more than just one way,” she shared. Ottomans are great for seating and storage, twin beds can become kings when guests stay over, and dining chairs should be comfy enough to be used as additional living room seating. In her own house, rather than a dining room table that sits unused, she opted for a convertible coffee table that lifts and extends to seat 10. Size and Amount Matter Troitsky explained that getting furniture that’s sized correctly can help a lot with how large your home feels (e.g., an enormous couch in a tiny bedroom might make the space seem small). But that doesn’t mean you should automatically purchase miniature versions of everything you’d buy for a bigger area. “It’s best to take inventory of what you actually use, need, and love, and start there,” Navarro said. She added: “For holiday decor, instead of trying to deck out every inch of your small living space, pick one or two areas to really lean into — the Christmas tree, the mantel, the coffee table, etc.” Get Comfortable With Borrowing Why use up valuable storage space on extra glassware and guest seating for your one annual holiday get-together when you can call a friend and ask to borrow theirs? As a bonus, it gives you both an excuse for a visit. Another option is to rent what you need when you need it. Ultimately, do your best to remember that, as Navarro put it, “the goal is always to make your guests feel at home — not to impress them with how big your place is!” RELATED: Make Your Home Happier With These Dopamine-Inducing Decorating Tips

Το στρατόπεδο βρίσκεται κοντά στο t…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. In March 2020, COVID lockdowns shuttered schools around the world, including at Tongogara Refugee Camp in Zimbabwe, where Prince Bashangezi was completing his A-Level studies. The camp sits near the Mozambique border, home to more than 17,000 people displaced by conflict across central and eastern Africa. Formal schooling stopped. Prince and a group of fellow A-Level students at USAP Community School, a school serving refugee youth in the camp, decided not to wait for it to resume. They founded TWEENS : Together We Educationally Empower Non-privileged Students. The model was built around what they had: each other. Teaching from inside the camp TWEENS began as a service learning project, with refugee students tutoring younger students in the same camp. The premise was direct. These were students who understood exactly what it meant to study without resources, without stability , often without continuous access to teachers, and in many cases without families to support them. They knew the particular difficulty of trying to build a future from inside a displaced population. So they taught each other. The program was supported by Education Matters Africa , a Zimbabwe-based nonprofit, and launched at a moment when any alternative to organized education was better than none. What began during a global lockdown became something that outlasted it. Prince was also a Waterford Kamhlaba UWC of Southern Africa alumnus, a school known for selecting students across conflict zones and economic hardship who show unusual potential and commitment. That network eventually connected him to the Global Student Haven Initiative at Pomona College in California, where he now studies computer science and economics. Marianne Langridge, who nominated Prince for this series, wrote that he “has turned his personal tragedy of losing his family during war into loving service for others.” That framing, loss converted into something that benefits others, runs through how Prince has talked about his work and what TWEENS is for. Langridge described his commitment as rooted in wanting students in refugee camps to “gain access to education so they can have hope for a better future.” Why peer tutoring works here There is something specific about a peer model in a refugee context that a standard school or aid program can’t replicate. The tutors in TWEENS are not professionals, not volunteers flying in from outside, not people working from a comfortable distance. They are students who live where the students they’re teaching live. They went through the same disruptions. Their credibility comes from proximity, not credentials. This is similar in structure to the peer-learning model that makes other youth-run programs effective, but in a refugee camp the stakes of educational continuity are different. A child who falls significantly behind in a displacement context faces a compounding disadvantage. Keeping any educational thread alive, even an informal one built by A-Level students during a lockdown, matters more than it might in a setting with backup resources. TWEENS was built on that understanding. From Tongogara to Pomona Prince arrived at Pomona College through the Global Student Haven Initiative , which supports students from refugee and displaced communities. He is studying computer science and economics, a combination that maps directly to the problems TWEENS is trying to solve: how technology and resource allocation interact to either expand or cut off access to education. Pomona profiled him in 2024 as part of a piece on Global Haven students finding opportunity in higher education. A fundraising campaign on GlobalGiving continues to support TWEENS’ operations, keeping the peer tutoring program funded as he completes his degree. What Prince Bashangezi and his fellow students built during a lockdown in a refugee camp, with nothing but time and knowledge and the willingness to share both, is still running more than five years later. TWEENS now offers an A-level program, a girls’ book club, and ongoing homework support alongside its original peer tutoring. To support TWEENS, visit their GlobalGiving fundraising page . The post Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The question hanging over international climate talks for years has not really been whether the world would shift away from fossil fuels. It has been whether the countries most responsible for burning them would actually put that transition in writing, with a plan attached. On November 3, Brazil did exactly that, releasing what it calls the world’s first global roadmap for phasing out coal, oil and gas. The document doesn’t bind anyone. It’s voluntary, and it acknowledges upfront that countries will move at different speeds and need different kinds of support. It names the transition as “urgent, inevitable and yet possible” and lays out a three-phase agenda running from 2028 to 2033, during which countries are urged to start drawing up plans and transforming their energy systems. “Countries differ in how fast they can move and in the support they need,” it states, “but every country gains from immediately planning its transition away from fossil fuels.” Why COP30 ended without naming fossil fuels The COP30 climate summit, held earlier this year in Belém, ended without final text that explicitly named fossil fuels. Saudi Arabia, Russia, and other major oil producers pushed back against direct language. Fortunately, the Brazilian presidency didn’t treat that as a dead end. Instead, it spent the remaining months of its COP30 term putting together a voluntary framework that any country can use to plan its own phaseout, entirely separate from whatever gets negotiated at a formal summit. COP30 chief executive Ana Toni framed the roadmap in terms of self-interest as much as obligation. “The transition is inevitable, so start planning now and as soon as possible, because this will be good for your country, for your society, for your economy,” she said. Brazil also released a companion roadmap on halting deforestation by 2030. A three-phase transition plan, tailored by country The roadmap doesn’t tell anyone exactly what to do. It says outright that “there is no unique solution for this complex puzzle” and pushes countries to tailor their approach to their own circumstances and starting points. The framing throughout is that the transition is a logistics problem, something to start working on with tools and knowledge that already exist, not a debate to be settled at some future summit. COP30 president André Corrêa do Lago was blunt about it: “Everyone can start to act now. The agreements already exist. What’s important is to implement them.” The document also points out that current policies still leave the world short of the commitments made at COP28 in Dubai in 2023, when nearly 200 nations agreed to language about “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems.” Three years later, that language hasn’t moved much. The roadmap is an attempt to change that without waiting on another round of negotiations to get there. The roadmap’s role at COP31 in Antalya The COP31 conference opened in Antalya, Turkey, on November 9 with the roadmap on the agenda, though Brazil has been clear it’s not there for renegotiation. “We are not suggesting negotiations,” Corrêa do Lago said. It’s a standing offer. Turkey and Australia, which are co-steering this year’s talks, have put electrification at the center of COP31’s agenda as a path to cutting emissions. The concern critics have raised is a practical one: the draft text doesn’t specify clean sources, which leaves open the possibility that “electrification” gets used to describe fossil fuel expansion rather than a genuine move to renewables. How that plays out over the two weeks in Antalya will shape what the summit actually delivers. Climate advocates are pushing for specificity. “The roadmap must not end up as just another report gathering dust on a shelf,” said Fanny Petitbon, a policy analyst at 350.org. “COP31 must be the moment when governments take this work forward, with clear commitments, timelines and the resources to deliver a fair and orderly exit from coal, oil and gas.” The framing shift that may outlast any summit The roadmap has no legal teeth. However, what it does have is a particular assumption baked in, namely that the question isn’t whether the fossil fuel transition happens, but how. That’s a different starting point than the one that has dominated climate negotiations for most of the past decade, where the fight was still about whether countries would formally commit to leaving fossil fuels behind at all. Brazil’s document takes that commitment as a given and asks what planning for it looks like. Whether the summits that follow treat it that way remains to be seen, but the document is in the world now, and that changes what any country can point to when it decides to start. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Brazil releases the world’s first fossil fuel phaseout roadmap first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: The best photography makes you slow down and notice something that might otherwise go overlooked — and the finalists for the eighth edition of Close-Up Photographer of the Year do just that. The shortlisted images were just revealed out of a record 15,388 submissions across 11 categories. The above shot, titled “Golden dust,” is one of the contenders in the animals category and features a Eurasian hoopoe taking a dust bath outside of Aurangabad, India. The dust helps remove excess oil from the bird’s feathers so they don’t stick together, but according to photographer Sarthak Agrawal, the swirling particles also make a good shot “especially difficult” (and thus especially impressive). “This year’s shortlist is a fabulous showcase of imagination, technical expertise, and natural curiosity,” competition co-founder Tracy Calder said in a press release shared with Nice News. The top 100 pics and the winning photographers will be announced in January, but submissions aren’t closed just yet. The competition holds an adjacent challenge that follows a specific theme, and this year’s is “Close to Home.” Hopeful shutterbugs of any age and skill level have until Nov. 30 to enter and Dec. 7 to upload their pics to the website. “Proving you don’t have to travel far to find something extraordinary,” the website states about the theme choice, which was voted on by the public. “We’re looking for close-up, macro, and micro photographs taken in a home and its immediate surroundings: the home’s rooms, outbuildings (such as sheds, garages, and greenhouses), garden, balcony, doorstep, or the street directly outside. This may be your own home or the home of family or friends.” Scroll to view a selection of the shortlisted images. Studio Art: “Rose Thorns” by Donald Bolak © Donald Bolak/CUPOTY “Fairly high level of magnification for a macro shot of a single rose thorn. The larger thorn is about 3/8 inch high. This is one of the things I enjoy most about macro — discovering sights unseen and unimagined. In this case a slightly surreal and alien landscape where rose thorns can be mountain peaks.” Young: “A Little Punky” by Oliver Lacey © Oliver Lacey/CUPOTY “I photographed this male Green Jumping Spider (Mopsus mormon) with its characteristic (and rather impressive) mohawk hairstyle in my suburban backyard in Brisbane, Australia.” Invertebrate Portrait: “Isopod portrait” by Adam Ferry © Adam Ferry/CUPOTY “I found this woodlouse resting underneath a piece of bark in a local woodland in Surrey, England. As it was fairly cold the woodlouse remained perfectly still allowing me to capture this focus stack of 80 photos. I love the high level of detail I could due to the increased magnification as the portrait filled most of the frame.” Underwater: “Rockpool Sanctuary” by Lisa Skelton © Lisa Skelton/CUPOTY “Young elephant seal pups or ‘weaners’ gather around natural rock pools on the Falkland Islands, using the protected waters to practice swimming and diving until they are ready to venture out to sea.” Intimate Landscape: “Where Worlds Collide” by Johannes Kowalewski © Johannes Kowalewski/CUPOTY “High above the Baltic Sea, an ancient beech forest glows in autumn colorrs atop the dramatic white chalk cliffs of Jasmund National Park on the island of Rügen, Germany.” Animals: “Nosepick” by Steffen Foerster © Steffen Foerster/CUPOTY “A blackish cinclodes or tussock-bird (Cinclodes antarcticus) picks at the nose of a resting southern elephant seal (Mirounga leonina) on Sea Lion Island, in the Falkland Islands.” Insects: “Spoonwing” by Lucien Harris © Lucien Harris/CUPOTY “I followed this spoonwing for over 10 minutes as it clumsily flew along the border of an overgrown field in the Peloponnese region of Greece, waiting for the perfect backdrop to compose a photo of this beautiful creature.” Underwater: “Fish Out of Context” by Marco Domenicucci © Marco Domenicucci/CUPOTY “A shoal of goldfish swim in an urban pond inside a metropolitan business district. Two worlds divided by a thin waterline: glass and concrete above and an aquatic ecosystem below.” Young: “Fight for the Perfect Fishing Spot” by Sasha Jumanca © Sasha Jumanca/CUPOTY “I managed to photograph these two blue kingfishers in December while they were defending their fishing territory in Schlosspark Nymphenburger, Munich. They faced each other directly and even tried to push one another under the water, showing how they compete for the best spots. This kind of behavior is quite rare, as kingfishers usually defend their territory by calling or chasing each other, rather than through physical contact.” Intimate Landscape: “Untitled 14” by Lukas Furlan © Lukas Furlan/CUPOTY “I was already fascinated by this scene, but rotating the image later revealed an entirely different world, almost like looking through a portal. It’s a reminder of the magic of experimentation and unexpected discoveries in photography.” Animals: “Suspended” by Joao Pontes © Joao Pontes/CUPOTY “In Portugal, there is no reptile quite as remarkable as the chameleon. Every year, towards the end of summer, the Algarve fills with juvenile chameleons. Naturally discreet, they become more active as the sun climbs higher in the sky, setting off to explore the world around them. Here, at the edge of the ocean, they inhabit the coastal dunes. At their scale, the slender stems of sea pinks become towering lianas, suspended pathways through this sandy jungle. To capture this image, I used a fisheye lens, aiming for a composition that would reveal not only the chameleon itself, but also the perhaps unexpected habitat it calls home.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Going digital is often assumed to be a modern, efficient strategy that will save energy and resources: picture smart cities and industries humming along, with everything needed to run them stored cleanly in the cloud. The reality is just the opposite, according to a new study. Across 20 of the world’s largest economies, the growth of information technology has increased environmental burdens—largely because of the energy required to build and run digital infrastructure . In the new study, researchers gathered World Bank data on the G20 economies from 1990 through 2023. This group of large economies accounts for 80% of global GDP and 70% of carbon emissions. The researchers looked at three indicators of digitalization: internet usage, landline telephone subscriptions, and cellular subscriptions. They used a variety of statistical techniques to probe the direct and indirect associations between these indicators and carbon emissions. Past studies have established that information and communications technologies have yielded huge social and economic benefits for nations around the world, but the environmental consequences of these technologies have been less clear. All three indicators of digitalization are associated with higher carbon emissions, the researchers found. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {height: auto;position: relative;}.IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby:hover , .IRPP_ruby:visited , .IRPP_ruby:active {border:0!important;}.IRPP_ruby .clearfix:after {content: "";display: table;clear: both;}.IRPP_ruby {display: block;transition: background-color 250ms;webkit-transition: background-color 250ms;width: 100%;opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: #eaeaea;}.IRPP_ruby:active , .IRPP_ruby:hover {opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: inherit;}.IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl {background-position: center;background-size: cover;float: left;margin: 0;padding: 0;width: 31.59%;position: absolute;top: 0;bottom: 0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {float: right;width: 65.65%;padding:0;margin:0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text {display: table;height: 130px;left: 0;top: 0;padding:0;margin:0;padding-top: 20px;padding-bottom: 20px;}.IRPP_ruby .IRPP_ruby-content {display: table-cell;margin: 0;padding: 0 74px 0 0px;position: relative;vertical-align: middle;width: 100%;}.IRPP_ruby .ctaText {border-bottom: 0 solid #fff;color: #0099cc;font-size: 14px;font-weight: bold;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .postTitle {color: #000000;font-size: 16px;font-weight: 600;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .ctaButton {background: url(https://www.anthropocenemagazine.org/wp-content/plugins/intelly-related-posts-pro/assets/images/next-arrow.png)no-repeat;background-color: #afb4b6;background-position: center;display: inline-block;height: 100%;width: 54px;margin-left: 10px;position: absolute;bottom:0;right: 0;top: 0;}.IRPP_ruby:after {content: "";display: block;clear: both;} Recommended Reading: The average Internet user spends 3,230 hours online every year. Here's the carbon footprint of that. Strikingly, this pattern was almost entirely due to direct effects—that is, the energy needed to build and power digital infrastructure. “Data centers, device connectivity, and communication networks consume significant amounts of energy, which is largely sourced from carbon-intensive electricity,” the researchers write. The results suggest that the environmental benefits of digitalization depend on green electricity to power it—and at a global scale, that shift largely hasn’t happened yet. Clean energy is well known to be a key factor in determining the environmental benefits of electric cars . That relationship might not be as obvious in the case of digital technologies—it’s easy to overlook the energy required to make bits and bytes go bopping around the planet—but it’s no less crucial, the new work shows. The researchers expected that the early stages of digitalization, such as land line phone use, would be associated with increasing environmental burden but later stages, represented by internet and cellular adoption, with reduced carbon emissions—a pattern known as an environmental Kuznets curve. “In fact, economic and digital expansion continue to increase emissions rather than reduce them in the G20, revealing that these economies prioritize higher production and income over the cleaner environmental trajectory they often claim to pursue,” the researchers write. The upshot is that a push for digitalization needs to be accompanied by an effort to decarbonize the electricity that powers digital technologies, the researchers argue. Going forward, they say, governments should evaluate digitalization efforts not just in terms of technology access but also in terms of their climate impacts. Source: Alabdulwahab S. et al. “ ICT and CO2 Emissions in the G20: A Channel-Based Mediation Analysis .” Sustainability 2026. Image: ©Anthropocene Magazine

Stretching 202 metres, this eight-coach train can carry 557 passengers and reach 280 kmph during testing. Inside, passengers can expect ergonomic seats, charging points, wide windows, LED lighting and dedicated executive-class seating. But there’s more! Wheelchair-friendly doors, accessible toilets, Braille signage and dedicated spaces for passengers with reduced mobility make inclusivity a priority. Emergency talk-back units, multilingual announcements and Wi-Fi-based entertainment will add to the experience. Two B28 sets can join to form a 16-coach train. With seven more high-speed rail corridors announced in Budget 2026–27, India’s bullet train journey is only getting started! items.descriptionOriginal: Handmade paper can be made from cotton rags, recycled newspapers, bamboo and even agricultural waste . But have you ever imagined that elephant and rhinoceros dung could become paper too? In Assam, retired mining engineer Mahesh Chandra Bora and his daughter, Nisha Bora, are turning this unlikely idea into a business. Through their venture, Elrhino, they transform wildlife waste into handcrafted paper and stationery, creating livelihoods for rural communities while encouraging people to see the value of protecting these animals. The idea began with a question that came to Mahesh while he was on a flight. He read about paper being made from elephant dung in Rajasthan and wondered: if it could work in a state with relatively few elephants, why not in Assam, where elephants and one-horned rhinoceroses are part of the landscape? From a kitchen blender to a paper-making venture After retiring, Mahesh decided to explore the idea himself. He understood that elephants and rhinos eat large quantities of grass and other vegetation that their digestive systems cannot break down completely. Their dung, therefore, contains plenty of plant fibres that can be used to make paper. What began with experiments at home grew into Elrhino, a venture founded in 2014. Photograph: ( TBI team ) He began experimenting at home, using his wife's kitchen blender and window screens to work out how the fibres could be turned into sheets. It took repeated trials to get the process right, but the experiments eventually yielded handmade paper. What started as a personal project began taking the shape of a business, with Mahesh determined to make conservation and local employment part of its purpose. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Anuj Mohanty (@anujmohanty_) His daughter, Nisha, soon joined him. After spending 17 years in the corporate world, she left her career to help develop the venture, bringing her experience in market research and business to the table. Together, they established Elrhino in 2014, officially known as Elrhino Eco Industries Pvt Ltd, to turn their idea into a sustainable enterprise. How dung becomes paper The process relies on the fibres left behind after elephants and rhinos digest their food. The collected dung is cleaned, washed and boiled before being processed into pulp. This is combined with other materials , including recycled paper, cotton waste and plant fibres, to create sheets. The resulting paper is then pressed and dried before being used to make finished products. Elrhino's range includes notebooks, journals, paper bags, lampshades, playing cards and other stationery and decorative items. Some products also incorporate natural fibres from plants such as banana stems, which are readily available in Assam. The dung is cleaned, boiled and processed into pulp before being pressed into sheets of paper. Photograph: (Instagram/ @ anujmohanty_ ) The paper's visible flecks and distinctive texture offer a glimpse of its unusual raw material. More importantly, using these alternative fibres reduces reliance on wood pulp and offers another way to make use of resources that would otherwise go to waste. Giving villagers a reason to protect wildlife For Mahesh and Nisha, the idea was never just about making paper. It was also about changing the relationship between local communities and the wildlife around them. Elephants and rhinos can sometimes stray into agricultural areas, damaging crops and creating difficulties for farmers living near their habitats. At the same time, poaching and habitat loss threaten these animals. By sourcing dung from local villagers, the venture creates additional livelihood opportunities for rural communities. Photograph: (Instagram/ @seuj_sandhan ) Elrhino works with local villagers who collect dung, particularly from areas around wildlife habitats, and contribute to the paper-making process. By purchasing this material and creating work around its processing, the venture provides communities with an additional source of income. This creates a different kind of connection with wildlife. When dung has economic value, the presence of elephants and rhinos can bring opportunities alongside the challenges of living near them. The approach gives communities a tangible stake in conservation, although it works alongside, rather than replaces, the need to protect habitats and prevent poaching. The business also provides opportunities for rural artisans to develop skills in handmade paper production and craftwork. Good for villagers, good for wildlife Elrhino shows how an unconventional idea can bring together environmental responsibility, entrepreneurship and rural livelihoods. For Mahesh, the journey began with a question on a flight and a series of experiments at home. With Nisha helping turn the idea into a business, those early trials have grown into a venture that makes everyday products from an unexpected material. Through Elrhino, Mahesh and Nisha are giving wildlife waste a new purpose while encouraging communities to value conservation. Photograph: (Instagram/ @seuj_sandhan ) The stronger possibility is just as interesting: if wildlife waste can become a valuable resource, it can support both the people living alongside these animals and the conservation efforts needed to protect them. Sometimes, an idea that sounds unlikely at first can open up a completely different way of looking at the world. In Assam, this father-daughter duo is showing that even a notebook can begin with something found along a forest path. Sources: 'ELRHINO' by Your Network of Opportunities To Scale. items.titleOriginal: 10 Million Hectares of Sal Forests: 7 Ways One Tree Supports India’s Rural Economy
items.description: Ένα γεύμα που σερβίρεται σε ένα πιάτο με φύλλα, ένα μεταξωτό σάρι υφαντό από άγριο μετάξι και το θυμίαμα κατά τη διάρκεια μιας προσευχής μπορεί να μοιάζουν με τρία άσχετα μέρη της καθημερινής ζωής. Αλλά μοιράζονται μια ενδιαφέρουσα σχέση. Το καθένα, με τον δικό του τρόπο, μπορεί να εντοπιστεί στα δάση και σε ένα δέντρο που έχει υποστηρίξει κοινότητες για γενιές. Αυτό είναι το δέντρο σαλ, επιστημονικό…
items.descriptionOriginal: A meal served on a leaf plate, a silk saree woven from wild silk , and incense burning during a prayer may appear like three unrelated parts of everyday life. But they share an interesting connection. Each, in its own way, can be traced back to the forests and a tree that has supported communities for generations. This is the sal tree, scientifically known as Shorea robusta. Found across the forests of eastern and central India, particularly in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal, Bihar, and Madhya Pradesh, it has been an important part of rural livelihoods and traditional practices. According to a 2024 research review , Sal forests cover an estimated 10 million hectares in India. For communities living around these forests, the tree is valued for much more than its timber. Its leaves, seeds, resin, flowers, and fruit have found different uses over the years, with some becoming everyday household products and others supplying local industries. According to the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) , its uses range from timber and resin to seed oil and animal feed. Here is a closer look at how this one tree finds a place in so many aspects of life. 1. Its leaves become plates and bowls One of the most familiar uses of sal leaves is something many Indians may have eaten from. Across several parts of the country, communities collect mature leaves and stitch them together to make disposable plates and bowls. One of the most familiar uses of sal leaves is something many Indians may have eaten from. Photograph: (Amazon.in) Commonly called pattal or khali , these plates are used for everyday meals, weddings, religious ceremonies, and community feasts. Smaller bowls, known as dona , are also made from the leaves. In Odisha, they are closely associated with local food traditions. A research paper published in the Bulletin of the National Research Centre documents how these leaves are used to make plates and bowls, both by hand and through machine-pressed processes. It also highlights leaf-plate making as an important source of income for tribal communities across several states. Unlike plastic alternatives, the plates are biodegradable and break down naturally after disposal. For many forest-dependent families, collecting and stitching leaves is more than a traditional practice. It is also a way to earn an income from resources available around them. 2. Its seeds yield oil used in soaps and confectionery The small seeds that fall from the tree have considerable commercial value. After collection, they are processed to separate their kernels, which contain a fat commonly known as sal fat or sal butter. This fat is used in the manufacture of soaps and confectionery. Once refined, it can also serve as a substitute for cocoa butter in certain food products. The Comptroller and Auditor General of India documents its importance as a raw material for soap and confectionery manufacturing. Even the material left behind after extracting the oil does not go to waste. Known as oilcake, it contains protein and starch and can be used as animal feed, according to ICAR. Collecting and processing these seeds have also supported forest-based livelihoods, particularly in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, and Madhya Pradesh. 3. Its resin becomes incense The tree produces a natural aromatic resin known as sal dammar, which has several traditional and commercial applications. Collected from its trunk, the resin is used to make incense and also finds applications in certain paints and varnishes. According to Indian Woods, a publication available through the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA) , the resin has several such applications. Historically, it was also used to seal gaps in boats and ships, helping prevent water from entering. This made it useful for waterproofing wooden vessels. For communities familiar with the forest, collecting resin provides another way to make use of a natural resource without cutting down the tree. 4. Its wood builds homes and railway tracks The wood is among the most valued hardwoods in India. Hard, heavy, and durable, it is particularly useful for construction and other applications that require strength. It is used for beams, posts, door and window frames, railway sleepers, and structural work. Smaller branches and shoots can also be fashioned into agricultural implements and household tools. This is the sal tree, scientifically known as Shorea robusta. Found across the forests of eastern and central India. Photograph: (Catch Foundation) The wood is also used as firewood in rural households. From large construction projects to everyday objects, it serves a range of practical needs. 5. Its leaves help produce tasar silk There is another interesting connection between this tree and India's traditional textile industry. The tropical tasar silkworm, scientifically known as Antheraea mylitta, feeds on the leaves of several host plants, including sal, arjun, and asna. After feeding, the caterpillars spin cocoons, which are later processed to produce tasar silk. Known for its natural texture and rich appearance, this variety of wild silk supports livelihoods in several forested regions of eastern and central India. Its role in silk production is particularly interesting because the tree does not need to be harvested. Its leaves provide nourishment for the silkworms, supporting an industry that many forest-dependent families rely on. 6. Its fruit and leaves feature in traditional medicine Different parts of the tree have also found a place in traditional Indian medicine. The ICAR inventory of Indigenous Technical Knowledge records the traditional use of its fruit paste for treating diarrhoea. Its leaves have also featured in Ayurveda and Unani preparations, particularly in traditional remedies for skin-related conditions and wound care. These applications reflect the knowledge that communities living close to forests have developed over generations. However, traditional uses should not be mistaken for clinically established treatments, and further research is needed to establish their safety and effectiveness. 7. It supports forest-based livelihoods Beyond the products themselves, the tree plays an important role in the lives of communities living around India's forests. Collecting leaves, stitching plates, gathering seeds, and processing resin provide opportunities to earn an income from non-timber forest produce. For households with limited access to agricultural land, these activities can provide an important additional source of livelihood. A study by the International Institute for Environment and Development examines the importance of seed-based enterprises and forest governance in India, highlighting the relationship between forest resources and local economies. The small seeds that fall from the tree have considerable commercial value. Photograph: (Asia Research News) The products connect villages to wider markets. Leaf plates reach shops and eateries, seeds are sold to processing units, and resin finds its way into different industries. For the people who depend on these forests, the tree is not limited to a source of raw material. It is part of their everyday economy. Beyond these uses, the forests it forms provide habitat for wildlife, support biodiversity, and play an important role in maintaining ecological balance. For generations, communities living alongside these trees have understood their value beyond timber. They have learnt to make use of what the forest provides , turning leaves, seeds and other natural materials into products that serve everyday needs. It is a way of life closely tied to an understanding of nature, and a reminder that sometimes the greatest value of a tree lies in everything it offers, not just the part that can be cut down.

items.descriptionOriginal: In December 2023, a tiger crossed the Makri River and entered a mangrove patch near a village in Kultali, in West Bengal's Sundarbans. For the people living nearby, its presence was a serious safety concern. The tiger, too, was in danger. Over the next three days, forest officials, wildlife experts and local volunteers worked together to guide the animal back to its natural habitat. They tracked its movements, put up nylon nets and carefully created a passage towards the forest. On 11 December, the tiger finally swam across the river and returned to the mangroves, without needing to be captured. The successful operation showed how much difference trained local volunteers can make when people and wild animals come face to face. Now, more residents of the Sundarbans are learning how to help in such situations. On 24 October 2026, the Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) trained 33 newly engaged local volunteers, including 10 women , from Kultali block in South 24 Parganas district to help manage encounters between people and tigers. Their responsibility is an important one: helping protect their neighbours while ensuring that a tiger finding its way into a village can return safely to the forest. Ultimately, coexistence in the Sundarbans cannot depend on keeping people and tigers apart at all times. It also depends on what happens when their paths cross. Photograph: (Wildlife Trust Of India) What happens when a tiger enters a village? For people living along the forests of the Sundarbans, encounters with tigers are a real concern. Many residents depend on fishing, crab collection and other forest-based activities for their livelihoods. At times, tigers also cross rivers and enter areas where people live. When that happens, frightened residents may gather around the animal or try to drive it away. Confusion and panic can make an already dangerous situation worse. This is where Primary Response Teams (PRTs) come in. These teams consist of trained local volunteers who act as the first point of contact when wildlife enters a settlement. Their job is to alert forest officials, share information about the animal's movements, help keep crowds away and explain safety precautions to residents. They work alongside the Forest Department and trained wildlife rescue teams, rather than attempting dangerous rescues themselves. And because they belong to these communities, they understand the local landscape and the concerns of the people living there. Teaching 33 villagers how to respond safely The latest training took place at Sundarban Prakritishala, an education centre at Ambikanagar Haripriya High School. Led by WTI's Dr Abhishek Ghoshal and Prosenjit Sheel, with technical support from biologist Samrat Paul, the workshop focused on understanding tiger behaviour and responding safely when an animal enters a village. Participants learnt how tigers move, how their presence can be monitored and why people's reactions can influence what happens during an encounter. The sessions also addressed misconceptions about tigers. Dr Ghoshal explained that some residents believe all Sundarbans tigers deliberately hunt humans or that their saliva is poisonous. Such fears can influence how people react when an animal approaches a settlement. Understanding a tiger's natural behaviour can help volunteers explain the situation to their neighbours and discourage actions that might put people or the animal at greater risk. There is research supporting the importance of these precautions. A 2022 study examining 118 tiger attacks on people around Uttar Pradesh's Dudhwa and Pilibhit reserves found that 88.1% were accidental or defensive, rather than deliberate attempts to hunt humans. Although the findings come from a different landscape, they show why preventing sudden encounters and understanding animal behaviour matter. For the Kultali volunteers, the training also included learning how to communicate with residents, manage difficult situations and rebuild trust following an encounter. Can technology help stop tigers from entering villages? Alongside learning how to respond, the volunteers were introduced to tools that could help warn communities about approaching wildlife. These included camera traps, drones and a device called the Animal Intrusion Detection and Repellent System (ANIDERS). Think of ANIDERS as a modern, sensor-powered scarecrow. When an animal approaches, its sensors can trigger bright lights and sounds intended to scare it away without injuring it. Cameras can also help identify animal movements and send alerts. In 2026, WTI and the local Forest Department began introducing these devices in tiger-prone areas of the Sundarbans as an experimental measure. But the technology has limitations. Each device can monitor only a restricted area, while the region's salty conditions can damage equipment over time. It therefore needs maintenance and cannot replace trained people on the ground. The idea is to give communities another way to detect danger early, alongside the knowledge needed to respond appropriately. 33 Primary Response Team members participated in a human-tiger conflict mitigation coexistence workshop in #Sundarbans. Hosted by WTI, @ForestDeptWB supported by @IUCN through the Integrated Tiger Habitat Conservation Program (ITHCP) Read more: https://t.co/AKIz3UQuOK https://t.co/pClO367iXO — Wildlife Trust of India (@wti_org_india) October 26, 2026 A growing network of neighbours looking out for one another The October workshop builds on several years of work in Kultali. Since 2018-19, WTI has established a network of 98 Primary Response Team members, including 18 women, through its human-tiger coexistence project. These volunteers help the Forest Department manage tiger-related emergencies and monitor approximately 24 km of protective nylon net fencing along Kultali's eastern coast. The fencing helps reduce the chances of tigers moving into settlements, while the volunteers help identify problems and support responses when an animal crosses into a village. The latest training group, which includes 10 women, also brings more women into these community-level efforts. The initiative is supported by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), through its Integrated Tiger Habitat Conservation Program, and the West Bengal Forest Department. For local residents, its value lies in having people nearby who understand the risks, know whom to contact and can help others respond safely. Veteran volunteer Ajay Kumar Das, known as a Bagh Bondhu , or Friend of the Tiger, describes his role as protecting the Sundarbans' tigers and mangrove forests while being "equally responsible for the safety of villagers when a tiger enters a village". That responsibility was visible in December 2023, when local volunteers helped guide a tiger back across the river. And it is the same responsibility that the 33 newly trained volunteers are preparing to take on. In the Sundarbans, where people's livelihoods and tigers' habitats overlap, a timely warning, a well-informed neighbour and the right response can make a difference to both human and animal lives. Sources: 'PRT members in Sundarbans receive training to manage human-tiger interactions' : By Wildlife Trust of India, Published on 25 October 2026 'Predicting negative human-tiger (Panthera tigris) interactions in mosaic landscapes around Dudhwa and Pilibhit tiger reserves in India' : By Mayukh Chatterjee,Nilanjan Chatterjee, Poonam Chandel, Tapajit Bhattacharya, Rahul Kaul, Published on 11 October 2022 'Use of an action-selection framework for human-carnivore conflict in the Bangladesh Sundarbans' : By Adam C D Barlow, Christina J Greenwood, Ishtiaq U Ahmad, James L D Smith, Published on 24 October 2010

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News New Wild Cat Species Discovered in Bolivia Marks First Feline Find in Over a Century Reading Time: 3 minutes A new wild cat species discovered in Bolivia began its scientific journey when a rescuer mistook it for a lost kitten and fed it noodles, rice, and eggs, only to realize the tiny spotted animal was wild. The Leopardus tilcayo , now known as the tilcayo tiger cat, represents the first new living feline species formally described anywhere in the world in more than 100 years. This new wild cat species discovered in Bolivia inhabits the Yungas, the lush cloud forest ecotone where the Andes Mountains descend into the humid Amazon basin near La Paz. The discovery began unceremoniously. A resident living near the forest found the small, spotted animal and assumed it was a lost domestic kitten in need of help. He fed the creature noodles, rice, and eggs, but it failed to thrive on human food and soon began showing distinctly wild behaviors, prompting its transfer to the Senda Verde wildlife refuge once it became clear this was no ordinary house cat. What happened next transformed a rescue story into a scientific milestone. Researchers initially believed the animal belonged to Leopardus tigrinus, one of several already-recognized tiger cat species found across South America. Genetic analysis told a different story entirely. The new wild cat species discovered in Bolivia proved genetically distinct enough from its relatives to warrant classification as an entirely separate species, resolving what scientists call the tiger cat complex, a long-standing taxonomic puzzle now understood to comprise not one or two species, but five distinct ones. Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, who co-authored the study published in Current Biology and leads the Bolivian Felid Research and Conservation Program, emphasized how rare a discovery of this scale is. Finding any new, relatively large mammal remains uncommon in modern science, since most newly identified animal species are small invertebrates or microorganisms rather than mammals occupying visible ecological niches. Her National Geographic-funded conservation work underscored how much remains unknown about wild cat populations even today. Physically, the tilcayo tiger cat is smaller than an average house cat, measuring roughly 18 inches from head to body and weighing between three and five pounds. Its light brown coat is patterned with dark rosettes, making it look like a leopard shrunk down to kitten size. The species possesses shorter fur than the clouded tiger cat, while its tail is longer and fuller than that of the northern tiger cat yet less bushy than its clouded relative’s, distinguishing features researchers used alongside genetic evidence to confirm its status as a separate species. Researchers discovered this new wild cat species in Bolivia through a genomic analysis of 38 Leopardus specimens, combining museum skulls and modern samples to build a phylogenetic tree that revealed Leopardus tilcayo as genetically distinct, along with a newly recognized subspecies and the elevation of two other lineages to full species status. Photo courtesy of Current Biology . Despite global scientific excitement over this new wild cat species discovered in Bolivia, local communities throughout the Bolivian Yungas have known about the animal for generations, calling it tilcayo long before researchers formally documented it. This disconnect between indigenous ecological knowledge and formal scientific classification echoes a pattern seen repeatedly across biodiversity research worldwide, where species considered newly discovered by international science have often been recognized and named by local communities for far longer. The implications extend well beyond taxonomic bookkeeping. Scientists currently know very little about the tilcayo tiger cat’s population size, behavior, diet, or broader ecological role within the Yungas ecosystem. Confirming it as a distinct species carries meaningful conservation consequences, since protections and population assessments applied broadly to tiger cats as a group may not adequately address the specific needs or vulnerabilities facing this particular Bolivian lineage. Conservation organizations reacted to the discovery with a mix of celebration and renewed urgency. Stephanie Allard, Chief Mission Officer of the Dallas Zoo, described the finding as an exciting reminder of how much remains unknown about the natural world, a sentiment echoed throughout the global conservation community following the announcement. The new wild cat species discovered in Bolivia also highlights the Bolivian Yungas as a biodiversity hotspot that deserves far greater scientific attention and protection. This transitional forest zone, squeezed between high Andean peaks and lowland Amazonian rainforest, harbors ecological communities adapted to its unique elevation gradient and climate, conditions that likely shaped the genetic isolation allowing Leopardus tilcayo to diverge from its relatives in the first place. As researchers continue studying this newly confirmed species , fundamental questions remain unanswered: how many tilcayo tiger cats persist in the wild, what threats they face from habitat loss or human encroachment, and whether formal conservation status should follow their scientific recognition. For now, the discovery proves that even in an era of satellite mapping and genomic sequencing, Earth’s forests still conceal mammals entirely unknown to formal science, waiting only for the right combination of curiosity, rescue, and careful genetic analysis to bring them into view. The post New Wild Cat Species Discovered in Bolivia Marks First Feline Find in Over a Century appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Ο Μαξ, ο οποίος δυσκολευόταν να βρει τη βάση του σε συμβατικές ρυθμίσεις περίθαλψης, μετακινείται στην κοινότητα Camphill Esk Valley με αυτό που ο φίλος του περιγράφει ως «μια σταθερή ευκολία που δεν είχα δει πριν…
items.descriptionOriginal: At Botton Village in North Yorkshire's moors, a philosophy researcher visits an old friend and finds something he didn't expect: a man transformed. Max, who had struggled to find his footing in conventional care arrangements, moves through the Esk Valley Camphill Community with what his friend describes as "a settled ease I hadn't seen in him before." His explanation is simple and quietly devastating: "It's been the best two years of my life. Much better than anything before." What the researcher gradually comes to understand - through months of shared meals, garden work, and community forums - is that Max hadn't just found better support. He had found a place where his presence mattered, where contribution and belonging were woven into the daily fabric of life rather than delivered on a schedule. The article raises a question that conventional social care policy rarely pauses long enough to ask: if what people most need is genuine community, what does it mean that we have built a system structurally designed to provide everything but that?
