items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Okanagan Nation Alliance Restores Salmon Access to Okanagan Lake Reading Time: 3 minutes The Okanagan Nation Alliance is restoring salmon access to Okanagan Lake for the first time in nearly 100 years through a newly completed dam fish passage. The Okanagan Nation Alliance has reconnected sockeye salmon to Okanagan Lake for the first time in nearly a century. A new fish passage now lets fish bypass a dam that has blocked the route since 1953. The milestone caps decades of restoration work led by Syilx Okanagan communities in British Columbia. Dams and channel work built through the last century cut salmon off from more than 350 square kilometers of lake habitat. The Okanagan Lake Dam at Penticton became one of the last major barriers standing in the salmon’s path. Until now, fish had no permanent route to swim safely around it. The Okanagan Nation Alliance runs one of Canada’s most extensive Indigenous-led fisheries programs. It comprises eight member communities and manages hatcheries, habitat restoration, and dam modifications across the Okanagan Basin. Its fisheries team has spent more than two decades working to bring salmon back. For Syilx Okanagan communities, the reconnection means more than fish counts. Elders describe a longstanding relationship between their people and salmon, one rooted in responsibility rather than simple resource use. Opening ceremonies for the passage included songs and drumming, along with tributes to community leaders who pushed for its construction over many years. Engineers designed the completed passage as a nature-like channel rather than a traditional metal fish ladder. Grating along the top lets sunlight reach the water and allows visitors to watch fish pass underneath. The Okanagan Nation Alliance’s completed fish passage is designed as a natural-looking channel rather than a traditional metal fish ladder, with grating along the top that lets sunlight reach the water and lets visitors watch fish pass underneath. Photo courtesy of Okanagan Nation Alliance . The route gives steelhead, rainbow trout, sockeye, chinook, and kokanee access to the lake and 13 tributary streams. An adjustable barrier built into the design filters out invasive species trying to follow the same path. That balance lets native fish through while keeping unwanted species out. Salmon runs in the Okanagan once numbered in the hundreds of thousands before dam construction and river channelization fragmented their habitat. The Okanagan Lake Dam, built in 1953, included an earlier fishway that never worked well. Water levels made it unusable for salmon during much of the year. The passage builds on a broader restoration effort the Okanagan Nation Alliance has carried out since the 1990s. That work includes a 12-year sockeye reintroduction program in nearby Skaha Lake and roughly 50 habitat projects across the basin. Modifications to two other dams further downstream have also opened additional spawning grounds. A conservation hatchery run by the Alliance raises sockeye fry each spring for release into historical spawning areas. Students take part in some releases through a program that introduces them to salmon biology and Syilx culture. In 2026 alone, organizers released 330,000 sockeye fry across the territory. Recovering salmon runs have also revived a small commercial and community fishery on Osoyoos Lake. In recent years, the Okanagan Nation Alliance’s fishing crew has landed record numbers of returning sockeye there, with thousands of fish distributed to member communities for ceremonies, trade, and food. A stronger run into Okanagan Lake could extend that momentum further north. Okanagan sockeye form part of a larger population that migrates through the Columbia River Basin shared by Canada and the United States. According to the International Joint Commission, Okanagan-origin fish account for the largest share of sockeye returning to that binational system most years. That transboundary status makes the newly reopened habitat significant well beyond British Columbia. International reviewers have noted the project’s design. The passage was nominated for the International Fish Passage Project of Distinction and presented at a fish passage conference in California in 2026. Recognition like this signals growing interest in Indigenous-led approaches to river restoration. Returns to the reopened habitat are expected to stay modest at first, since warm river conditions have limited recent salmon numbers. Even so, the passage will remain open for every future migration season. For a Nation that has worked for generations to see salmon return, a permanent route into Okanagan Lake marks a turning point rather than an ending. The post The Okanagan Nation Alliance Restores Salmon Access to Okanagan Lake appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία είναι μέρος της σειράς "Parenting: What Google Won't Tell You" — The Better India's υπό την ηγεσία των ανθρώπων της σειράς γονέων που ξεπερνά τις συμβατικές συμβουλές για να τεκμηριώσει πώς οι πραγματικές οικογένειες μεγαλώνουν πραγματικά τα παιδιά τους. items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "Parenting: What Google Won't Tell You" — The Better India's people-led parenting series that goes beyond conventional advice to document how real families are actually raising their children. Through real parents, parenting coaches, influencers and experts, the series brings honest, diverse and relatable perspectives on the questions, choices, challenges and solutions that shape everyday parenting — the things Google can't always answer. When Kiara Powar was 13, she came home from a badminton match, hugged her mother, and cried for an entire day. After years of playing the sport she loved, she had to give it up because severe migraines were causing blackouts on the court. For Shweta Powar, watching her daughter navigate the loss was heartbreaking. Kiara had already faced a lifelong health condition, bullying, and rejection from people she had grown up with. Now, she was being forced to step away from something that had brought her happiness. "I told her, 'It's okay if people talk about you. This is exactly when we have to fight back and keep working harder to prove our point,'" Shweta recalls. Today, Kiara is a sports presenter and sportscaster, hosting digital shows such as Bat, Ball Aur Baatein and Sports & The City . Her journey from a young badminton player to a career in sports has been shaped by the challenges she faced growing up with Type 1 diabetes, and the support of her parents, who never wanted her condition to limit her ambitions. With the support of her parents, doctors and coaches, Kiara trained professionally in badminton from the age of nine. For Shweta and her husband, Kiran Powar, a former first-class cricketer, the journey began when Kiara was just two years old and was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes. The diagnosis meant learning to manage a condition they knew very little about. But as parents, they made one decision early on: they would help their daughter understand her condition without letting it dictate what she could aspire to. Learning to live with diabetes, one day at a time The signs began about a month before Kiara's diagnosis. She was urinating frequently and gradually losing her appetite. After initial consultations failed to identify the problem, her parents sought another medical opinion. Shweta encouraged Kiara to face setbacks with confidence rather than let other people's opinions hold her back. The doctor recognised the seriousness of her condition and asked them to rush her to a hospital. Kiara was admitted to the ICU, where she remained under observation for 48 hours before doctors confirmed that she had Type 1 diabetes. "We had heard the word diabetes, but we didn't know what Type 1 juvenile diabetes was or what had to be done," Shweta says. At the time, managing the condition meant four insulin injections a day. Shweta and Kiran had to learn how to administer the injections, monitor Kiara's sugar levels, and adjust insulin doses in consultation with her medical team. The first few months were especially difficult. Shweta remembers being afraid of giving her daughter the injections, while the family struggled with the social stigma surrounding the condition. Initially, they avoided family gatherings and social occasions, worried about people's reactions. But after six months, they realised that shielding Kiara from the world was not the answer. "We didn't want our child to grow up under fear. We wanted her to face it, challenge herself and fight against the odds," Shweta says. They began focusing on helping her live as normally as possible. Her school nurse helped with insulin injections during the day, while Shweta managed her morning routine and made sure she received her evening dose and meals on time. At home, the family followed the same food habits as Kiara, with homemade, sugar-free alternatives to sweets. The aim was not to make her feel different, but to help her understand what her body needed. When badminton became her refuge Growing up in a sporting family, Kiara developed an interest in tennis at seven and began playing badminton professionally at nine. She wanted to build a future connected to sports. Her parents supported her ambitions while working with her doctors, coaches, nutritionist and trainer to manage her health alongside training. She followed a disciplined routine, carried meals to practice, and had support available in case her sugar levels dropped. But adolescence brought challenges beyond diabetes. At 13, Kiara experienced severe emotional distress after relatives and cousins stopped communicating with her. The stress affected her health , and she began experiencing confusional migraines that caused blackouts while playing badminton. Her parents focused on helping her become independent and confident while learning to manage Type 1 diabetes. After medical tests and repeated episodes on the court, her family had to confront a difficult decision: continuing the sport was no longer a risk they could ignore. Giving up badminton was painful, especially after the sacrifices she had made to pursue it. Yet her parents encouraged her to keep moving forward, even when others doubted what she could achieve. Making room for independence Kiran and Shweta also made practical adjustments to help Kiara balance her studies and sporting ambitions. When the demands of school and intensive training became difficult to manage together, they decided to homeschool her in Grade 6. Her days included badminton practice, strength training and lessons with tutors, allowing her to continue her education without abandoning the sport she loved. Throughout these years, her doctor, Dr Atish Laddhad, remained an important source of guidance, helping the family navigate frightening episodes of low blood sugar. Her coaches and trainers also helped them understand when to push forward and when to step back. As Kiara grew older, she gradually took responsibility for managing her condition. Today, even when travelling alone, she makes sure she carries extra medical supplies, needles and syringes. With her parents' unwavering support, Kiara has built a career in sports, proving that a health condition need not define a child's dreams or future. For Shweta, that independence is part of what parenting has always meant: being present without making a child feel incapable. "I feel you should treat the child as a normal child and allow them to do normal activities, especially what they want to do," she says. Today, as a sports presenter, Kiara remains connected to the world she has loved since childhood. Her path may have changed from competing on the badminton court to talking about sport on screen, but her parents' belief in her has remained constant. Kiara's journey has not been without difficult choices or setbacks. But her parents have tried to ensure that diabetes remains something she manages, rather than something that decides her future. Today, Kiara is a sports presenter, hosting digital shows such as Bat, Ball Aur Baatein and Sports & The City. Their approach has been simple: understand the challenges, build a dependable support system, and give a child the confidence to discover what she can do. All images courtesy of Kiara Powar

items.titleOriginal: Generous Paternal Leave Policies Improve Maternal and Newborn Health, Family Finances, and Workplace Equality
items.description: Αυτό το άρθρο γράφτηκε από τη Megan Kuykendoll, καθηγήτρια οικογενειακής επιστήμης και κοινωνικής εργασίας στο Πανεπιστήμιο του Μαϊάμι, για το The Conversation — έναν μη κερδοσκοπικό ειδησεογραφικό οργανισμό αφιερωμένο στην ανταλλαγή γνώσεων ερευνητών και επιστημόνων, με άδεια Creative Commons. Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Όταν γεννήθηκε το δεύτερο παιδί μας, ο σύζυγός μου είχε s…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Megan Kuykendoll , an instructor of family science and social work at Miami University, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . When our second child was born, my spouse had several weeks of paternity leave under his parental leave policy at work. I’m a certified family life educator , and parental leave comes up regularly in my teaching and community work. So I was aware of the benefits his leave could have for our family — in theory. Still, I could not have imagined how significantly his leave would end up affecting our family and our connections with community. During his leave time, my spouse took our oldest child to playdates and birthday parties. He quickly became connected with our small-town network of families with kids close in age. I witnessed my spouse becoming more comfortable being the “main” parent in public, going to kid-centered community events, and connecting with other parents. Our family is still seeing the benefits of those few weeks 10 years later. Leave for supporting parents after the birth of a child isn’t standardized or required by law in most places in the U.S. Even countries with generous paid time off for the birthing parent don’t always offer similarly generous time for the non-birthing parent. This diversity in leave policies can make it hard to assess the impact of leave for the non-birthing parent. But existing research suggests that extended leave for birthing parents and moderate leave for non-birthing partners positively impact infant well-being and reduce postpartum mental health challenges. Maternal and Newborn Health Leave for both parents with the birth of a child can significantly benefit parental mental health overall and maternal mental health specifically . Paternity leave assists in the mother’s recovery and contributes to less of an increase in stress and depression than for mothers whose partners didn’t take leave. One Swedish study showed that flexibility within paternal leave policies, such as allowing new dads to take intermittent time off after the birth of a child, helped reduce the incidence of maternal postpartum health complications . Children also benefit from paternity leave. When a father takes significant leave — meaning at least two weeks — children report experiencing more father-child closeness and better communication in the relationship up to nine years later. And overall child health tends to improve when fathers take paternity leave. When paid leave policies are available for both mothers and fathers , breastfeeding is more likely to last longer. Longer breastfeeding is strongly linked to overall infant health and decreased infant mortality . SolStock—E+/Getty Images Paternity leave is an opportunity for fathers to become comfortable in their parenting role and connect with other parents. Family Balance Allowing both parents to have sufficient time off to bond and adjust to their new roles can also have longer-term benefits within the family unit and contribute toward more equity in child rearing. Even in 2026, mothers are often considered the “default” parent, with fathers taking a more secondary role . While fathers are more involved now than in previous generations, mothers are still more likely to be the first call from school. And even with an involved father, mothers continue to carry the invisible mental load of the family , an unseen burden of data, obligations, and preemptive planning tasks. This overreliance on mothers comes with a price: Mothers report being more stressed and tired than fathers do. As I experienced in my own family, when fathers have ample time off, it sets up the dynamic to be more balanced between parents. This helps reduce the strain on recovering mothers and redistributes some of the care work that goes into raising children. Home Economics What’s more, paid leave policies have been shown to help families’ financial health . Pay rates during leave can vary widely depending on your company, organization, or country. Without full or close to full pay, many families cannot afford to take leave. In the U.S., for example, the Family and Medical Leave Act allows time off, but not in all circumstances , nor is that time required to be paid. Many families cannot afford to take the full allowable time off, using up sick or vacation time if available. Many parents in the U.S. end up going back to work sooner than seems healthy . New parents in the U.S. often find themselves in an economic bind — they can’t afford to take leave, nor can they afford to rely on a single income to have a parent stay home. But many also can’t afford the childcare rates for newborns, which tend to be particularly high. National averages for infant care at childcare centers are nearly $200 more per month than toddler care. While rates vary significantly depending on where you live and what type of care you choose, infant care remains the most expensive . Despite the lack of a paid U.S. federal leave policy for parents, both domestic and multinational companies have noticed that their workers care about parental leave policies. Some have begun to offer leave for supporting parents in order to recruit and retain workers . Outside the US U.S. leave policies consistently rank at or near the bottom when compared with other similarly developed countries, like the 38 members of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, or OECD. Some countries follow a “use-it-or-lose-it” model of parental leave, where fathers in particular are encouraged to take a more substantial role in childcare. Sweden and Norway, for example, earmark 90 days of leave for each parent, and it cannot be transferred to or split with the other parent. This encourages both parents to take time off. There are many options across countries with parental leave policies. Flexibility and defined expectations seem to be key contributors to getting the most out of the parental leave that is offered. Cultural Adoption When non-birthing parents are men, another barrier to taking leave is the perceived social acceptability within their communities. Even when paid paternity leave is available, many men struggle to take it because of how traditional gender roles and expectations of masculinity frame childcare as women’s work . To offset these kinds of social pressures, countries like Japan and Austria offer incentives such as bonus leave time for families when fathers actually take their available leave. Germany offers a similar bonus, and it has found improved couple relationship satisfaction when fathers take more of their leave time. Beyond improvements in maternal and infant health, both parents taking leave can create a more equitable workplace environment . Disparities and discrimination that come when only women take leave after birth can lessen when fathers and other supporting parents also take leave. Childbearing women are then less likely to be penalized, formally or informally, for taking parental leave. Paid parental leave policies that provide leave for all parents, regardless of gender, also can help reduce structural inequality in the workplace across race and class. In the U.S., Hispanic and Black workers often have less access to paid leave policies and may experience increased pressure to return to work earlier than their white counterparts. As more states, countries, and corporations adopt more flexible and inclusive leave policies, researchers will continue to learn how parental leave benefits both parents and children. What they’ve found so far leads me to believe that, just like we’ve seen with prenatal care and early education programs , parental leave will prove to be an early investment in healthy children and families that pays dividends in the long term. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s something about crisp fall air that makes you want to get outside, and if you have a dog, you’ve probably noticed they feel it too: the extra pull on the leash when the leaves start to turn, the way they pause longer than usual to investigate every scent the new season brings. Dog trainer Sassafras Patterdale says fall is one of the best times of year to take your dog somewhere new, partly because the cooler temperatures make longer outings more comfortable, and partly because places like farmers’ markets, pumpkin patches , and hiking trails offer something a backyard walk can’t: a real chance for your dog to build confidence around new people, places, and experiences, while you practice skills like loose-leash walking around genuine distractions. A little planning goes a long way Before heading out anywhere new, Patterdale recommends thinking through your dog’s comfort level with crowds. Younger puppies and newly adopted dogs who are still building confidence tend to do better at quieter times, like weekday visits or early weekend mornings, while dogs who are comfortable around people and other animals may be ready for busier gatherings. Neither is wrong; it just depends on where your dog is right now. Pack a few essentials: water and a portable bowl, treats for rewarding good behavior, and poop bags. A properly fitted harness or collar and a standard six-foot leash are good to have in any busy area, and depending on the weather and your dog’s coat, a sweater or jacket may be a smart call for smaller or short-haired dogs. Farmers market A farmers market is one of the more dog-friendly fall outings. The mix of people, other animals, food smells, and steady foot traffic gives your dog plenty of opportunities to practice calm, attentive behavior on leash, and plenty of reasons to earn a treat. Patterdale recommends offering praise and treats whenever your dog walks calmly at your side or glances back to check in with you. Those little check-ins are what you want to encourage. Keep your dog close and prevent them from sniffing or pawing at food displays, and be mindful of shoppers who may not be comfortable around dogs. Most farmers markets welcome well-behaved, leashed dogs, but policies vary by location, so confirm before you go. Pumpkin patch A pumpkin patch visit makes for good seasonal photos, and dogs tend to enjoy the outing for their own reasons entirely. The open space, interesting smells, and steady stream of new things to look at give them a lot to engage with, and it’s a naturally good setting to practice cues like “stay” somewhere unfamiliar and exciting. Patterdale recommends checking the farm’s pet policy before arriving, since some farms restrict dogs in certain areas, particularly active harvest fields, for food safety reasons. Farms that host seasonal activities often welcome leashed dogs in the public areas, so a quick call or website check usually settles it. Corn maze If the farm also runs a corn maze, it can be a fun extension of the visit. The winding paths give dogs a chance to sniff and explore at their own pace, which Patterdale says is some of the best mental stimulation you can offer on a walk. One thing to watch for: avoid letting your dog round corners ahead of you, since that can startle other visitors, particularly children, or lead to an unexpected run-in with another dog. Haunted corn mazes are generally better skipped, since the loud noises and sudden surprises tend to be overwhelming for most dogs, even confident ones. As always, confirm the pet policy before you go. Hiking trail For a quieter option that lets you and your dog set your own pace, a fall hike is hard to beat. Many state and local parks welcome leashed dogs, and autumn trails give dogs a lot to work with: the crunch of leaves underfoot, the smell of damp earth, the cool air that seems to make dogs want to cover more ground than usual. Patterdale recommends allowing extra time so your dog can stop to sniff and investigate along the way. Dogs experience a huge portion of the world through their noses, and giving them space to follow a scent or linger over a fallen log makes the whole outing more satisfying for both of you. Check park regulations before heading out, since rules about dogs on trails vary by location and trail type. Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Water has always been part of how many American cities move people, but for most of the country’s history it has been an afterthought compared to roads and rails. A new generation of electric ferries is beginning to change that, and some of them work in a way that is surprising: they handle the problem of water by getting out of it. The physics problem that held electric boats back Electrifying boats has always been harder than electrifying cars, and the reason comes down to drag. Water resists a moving vessel far more than air resists a moving vehicle, which means boats require substantially more energy per mile. That high energy demand, combined with the weight of batteries, has made it difficult to design an electric vessel that can carry enough passengers far enough to be useful as everyday transit. Hydrofoils get around this in a way that seems almost too obvious once you hear it. These vessels use underwater wings to lift the hull clear of the water as they accelerate, and once the hull is airborne, drag drops sharply. Vessev , a company that builds fully electric hydrofoil boats, says its design cuts drag by about 66 percent, which lets the boats carry smaller, lighter battery packs without sacrificing range. “We substantially reduce the drag that you feel, and that’s really what makes electrification viable,” said Eric Laakmann , Vessev’s chief executive and co-founder. What the ride is like The transition happens fast. As a Vessev boat accelerates through New York Harbor, the hydrofoils push the hull about a foot and a half above the surface, and the sensation of a boat working against waves gives way almost immediately to something smoother and quieter, closer to gliding than crossing water. “We’re picking up speed. We’re going for a takeoff,” Laakmann said during a recent demonstration, drawing curious looks from passengers on a nearby sightseeing ferry. His company is still a novelty to most people on the water, and he knows it. From demonstration to daily commute Vessev operates passenger services in New Zealand, with Australia next and its first US route planned for Lake Tahoe. Laakmann’s ambition runs past tourism: he wants electric vessels to be as unremarkable as buses, something commuters use because it’s there. “More like subways, more like buses, more like Ubers, more like taxis but on the water,” he said. That idea has already taken root in parts of Europe. Stockholm commuters are riding electric hydrofoil ferries built by the Swedish company Candela, which says its design uses as much as 80 percent less energy than conventional vessels of a similar type. Norway has ordered 20 of the same boats for coastal service. The US is later to this shift, but several cities are starting to move. San Francisco prepares for a half-billion-dollar overhaul San Francisco carries about 3.5 million ferry passengers a year across a region shaped by its bay, and every one of the 18 vessels in the current fleet runs on diesel. Four battery-powered ferries are set to join the fleet over the next two years as part of an electric overhaul worth roughly half a billion dollars, including new charging infrastructure at its docks. Converting a ferry network is more complicated than swapping out a car fleet. Ferries run on fixed schedules and cannot stop mid-route to recharge, so operators have to design the entire system around the relationship between battery range, trip time, and how much power the shoreside chargers can deliver in the minutes a vessel sits at the terminal. Seamus Murphy, who runs the agency, put it plainly: “We have a lot of waterfront.” San Francisco’s new vessels won’t use hydrofoil technology , but the agency says they’ll make it the first ferry operator in the country to run high-speed, all-electric service. The economics of a fleet switch For a long time, the financial math and the environmental math didn’t add up at the same time. Battery-powered ferries cost more upfront, but electric motors tend to be more efficient than diesel engines, and the savings on fuel and maintenance accumulate. Rising diesel costs have shifted the balance, as has continued progress in battery technology. “You make the upfront investment at the beginning and then you save over time, and at the end of the day you’re going to have lower costs in the long term,” Murphy said. How well that holds up depends on the route: long distances, tight turnaround windows, and limited charging opportunities can all make the switch impractical. Not every waterway is suited to a fully electric vessel. For shorter commuter routes in cities with the right geography, though, the numbers are starting to work. For San Francisco’s expansion, both the boats and their batteries are being manufactured in the US. Murphy sees this as a window that won’t stay open indefinitely. “These jobs are going to get created in other countries and we have an ability to create them here if we manage this in the right way,” he said. “We don’t want to be left behind.” Water as working transit Transportation is the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the US, and watercraft burning diesel contribute their share, particularly around busy ports and waterfront neighborhoods. Electric ferries could cut both emissions and the localized air pollution that diesel docks generate, while also opening up routes that weren’t previously viable and connecting communities by water without the cost of new roads or rail. It won’t happen all at once. Some cities will move fast; others will take years to follow. But the direction looks clear. “I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Laakmann said, standing on a boat that had just crossed a harbor without burning a drop of fuel. items.description: Οι επιστήμονες ανακάλυψαν μια κρυφή οδό ντοπαμίνης από το έντερο στον εγκέφαλο που εξηγεί γιατί ο πικρός καφές και άλλες αρχικά δυσάρεστες γεύσεις μπορούν να γίνουν αγαπημένες με την πάροδο του χρόνου. Η ανακάλυψη αποκαλύπτει πώς ο εγκέφαλος μαθαίνει να λαχταράει συγκεκριμένα τρόφιμα και θα μπορούσε τελικά να οδηγήσει σε νέους τρόπους αναμόρφωσης των διατροφικών συνηθειών και των διατροφικών προτιμήσεων.
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have uncovered a hidden gut-to-brain dopamine pathway that helps explain why bitter coffee and other initially unpleasant flavors can become favorites over time. The discovery reveals how the brain learns to crave certain foods and could eventually lead to new ways of reshaping eating habits and food preferences.

items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία δημοσιεύτηκε αρχικά από το Open Campus. Περνώντας από το συμβουλευτικό γραφείο του New River μια μέρα, η Stephanie Addikis παρατήρησε ότι τα βιβλία ζωγραφικής και τα Lego που είχε βοηθήσει να αποθηκεύσουν σε ένα κοντινό κουτί ήταν… «πολύ αγαπημένα». items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by Open Campus . W alking by New River’s advising office one day, Stephanie Addikis noticed that the coloring books and Legos that she had helped stock in a nearby box were … “well-loved.” This was just what she was hoping would happen. The “busy box” stuffed with toys is part of a new effort at New River to support parenting students. When students are filling out the FAFSA or visiting with their adviser, they can bring their children and know they will have toys nearby to entertain them. “I don’t think we realized how many kids were coming on campus until we put these out, and now they’re really being utilized,” said Addikis, who is the adult career coach and community outreach specialist at New River. New River Community College is working to integrate more support for parenting students throughout campus. Courtesy of New River Community College A report released a couple weeks ago from The Institute for College Access & Success, or TICAS, showed that about a quarter of students attending rural-serving institutions are parents. But those colleges are also less likely to have childcare on campus than their non-rural counterparts. A lack of data on the number of parenting students is one of the biggest challenges for colleges trying to support them, according to one of the authors of that report, Erika Roberson. There’s a reason that Addikis was so excited to see used toys on campus: She does not know exactly how many parent students go to New River. While at least five states have now required public colleges to ask students if they have children, and Virginia just passed similar legislation this spring , the lack of standardized data collection makes serving these students even more difficult. And supporting them matters because student parents are more likely to be students of color, low-income and the first in their families to go to college. Those challenges combined make them less likely to graduate than their non-parenting peers. But, like rural places do, these colleges are getting creative in expanding support even with limited data and funding. To collect more thorough data, Roane State Community College in eastern Tennessee is partnering with Achieving the Dream . Others are collaborating with local churches, women shelters, groups like United Way and other nonprofits to connect student parents with resources. Our reporter at partner newsroom The Fort Worth Report, Dang Le, recently reported on new childcare centers that opened at Tarrant County College with the support of the college, county and a childcare nonprofit. “Not all these schools are receiving robust grants to do this work,” Roberson said. “Maybe there are existing partnerships that schools have that they might be able to tap into to more explicitly support their student parents, or maybe there are ways in which they can modify syllabi to include family-friendly policies that don’t have dollar signs on it.” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Rather than one new program, it’s a cultural shift that student parents are looking for, according to another recent report focused on six public rural-serving colleges and universities in California . In other words, student parents want to feel seen — by their counselors, advisers, professors and other staff members or peers. While parents make up a large portion of students at rural-serving schools, it’s common for these students to still feel isolated . That’s why several colleges featured in the TICAS report are starting peer parenting groups and hosting events. New River, for example, has a dedicated family study room with child-sized furniture in their library (which also serves as a public library) and consistently hosts events or dinners for students and faculty with children. New River provides care packages for new and expecting parents, including diapers, wipes, a Walmart gift card and t-shirts. Courtesy of New River Community College Addikis said she felt this cultural shift even more prominently at New River when funding to parent-support programs decreased. New River was one of the first five colleges to receive the College Attainment for Parent Students grants from the Virginia Foundation for Community College Education. In those first couple of years, the college created cohorts of 20 student parents, and each parent was eligible for $2,000 stipends per semester, including summer semesters. Now, the foundation associated with the community college system gives each of the 23 schools some funding, so the grant amounts have decreased. New River adjusted by starting an application process, and they granted 17 students $500 each this year. Addikis said more than half of the students who applied said they rely on friends and family for childcare, so this stipend will likely help reimburse things like gas or food. But with fewer financial resources, Addikis started to look at what she could do to grow relationships with these student parents and remind them that they are not on their own. For example, she has a work-study student who is also a parent this semester, and that student is planning to start a student parent club on campus. The challenge, she said, still remains in increasing awareness about the resources on campus. One thing that she said helped was creating a section of their first-year orientation course specifically for adult learners and highlighting resources available for parents. “I see it now as a warm hug, and a lot of love and support and just a building of awareness,” she said, talking about how the parent support has changed with less funding. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Still, researchers like those at TICAS still advocate for increased data and funding for student parent support, especially on rural campuses. Two federal grant programs in particular focus on this area: Childcare Access Means Parents in Schools and Basic Needs for Postsecondary Students. “I don’t want policymakers to forget rural parenting students,” Roberson said. “And if policymakers are really interested in strengthening rural economies, I think it’s important that they also invest in rural parenting students.” The post Colleges Are Getting Creative to Help Students With Kids appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: They left Sydney, Australia, to raise their children in India. And their twins helped them embrace their new home. Olivia and Andre had always imagined moving to India. Olivia is a teacher, while Andre runs a small business. They planned their move in 2022, but life had a surprise in store: twins! Born extremely prematurely, the children needed extra care. The couple decided to delay their move until the twins completed their health checks at the age of two. Once they were ready, the family finally made the move to India. Their biggest surprise? The children adapted to the heat, language and everyday way of life faster than their parents. Instead of comparing everything with Australia, Olivia and Andre followed their twins’ lead and embraced the experience with an open mind. Today, the family is proud to call India home. What they value most is the beautiful sense of community and the chance to give their children a different way of growing up. Sometimes, a new country doesn't just change where you live. items.descriptionOriginal: Every October, something extraordinary happens in the Maldives. Millions of dragonflies begin appearing across the islands, even though there is hardly any freshwater for them to breed in. Where are they coming from? Scientists believe many of these tiny travellers arrive from India, crossing hundreds of kilometres of open sea. Some may even continue their journey towards Africa. And here's what makes this so fascinating. The globe skimmer dragonfly ( Pantala flavescens ), also called the wandering glider, measures barely five centimetres and weighs around 300 milligrams. That's less than a gram! Yet this tiny insect may undertake one of the most remarkable journeys in the animal world, travelling thousands of kilometres with help from something familiar to all of us in India: the monsoon. But how does an insect so small cross an ocean without stopping? And why would it attempt such a journey in the first place? Scientists have spent years trying to answer these questions. The mystery of millions of dragonflies arriving in the Maldives In 2009, researcher R Charles Anderson published a study about something that had puzzled observers in the Maldives for years. Every October, enormous numbers of dragonflies appeared on the islands. But the Maldives has very little surface freshwater, making it an unlikely place for dragonflies to complete their life cycle. By studying when the insects appeared in India and the Maldives, Anderson found evidence suggesting they were travelling from southern India, covering approximately 500 to 1,000 kilometres. His findings, published in the Journal of Tropical Ecology , raised an even bigger possibility. What if the Maldives was simply one stop on a much longer journey towards East Africa? The answer appeared to be connected to the changing monsoon. It all begins with something as simple as a rain-filled puddle To understand why these dragonflies travel, we first need to understand where they raise their young. Many dragonflies lay their eggs in ponds and lakes. The globe skimmer has an unusual advantage: it can breed in temporary pools formed by rainfall. Think of the shallow puddles that appear in fields, open grounds and low-lying areas during India's monsoon. For this dragonfly, these pools can become nurseries. The female lays her eggs in the water, where the young dragonflies develop before emerging as adults. But these pools do not last forever. Once the rains stop, they begin drying up. So, as rainfall shifts from one region to another, the dragonflies move towards places where fresh water becomes available. India's southwest monsoon, which generally lasts from June to September, creates ideal breeding opportunities. And when the rains begin moving southwards, the dragonflies appear to follow. Measuring around five centimetres and weighing less than a gram, it is among the world's most widely distributed dragonflies. Photograph: (Bangalore Mirror) How can something weighing less than a gram fly across an ocean? Here's where the story becomes even more remarkable. If a dragonfly tried to cross the Indian Ocean by constantly beating its wings, it would soon run out of energy. So how does it manage? It may be doing something similar to what birds do: using favourable winds to help carry it forward. Anderson's research suggested that the insects travel with winds associated with a shifting band of clouds and rainfall near the equator. Scientists call this the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, or ITCZ. Simply put, it is a region where winds meet, creating changing weather patterns. As this region moves southwards after India's monsoon, it can bring winds that favour the dragonflies' journey. Anderson suggested that they may fly more than 1,000 metres above the ground, where helpful winds could carry them towards the Maldives. But there was still one important question. Could their tiny bodies survive such a long flight? In 2021, an international team of researchers led by Johanna S U Hedlund studied how much energy these dragonflies would need to cross the ocean. Using computer models, they found that the insects could save enormous amounts of energy by gliding through the air and flapping their wings only when necessary. According to their calculations, a dragonfly using a combination of gliding and wing-flapping could potentially remain airborne for around 230 hours under favourable assumptions. By comparison, continuously flapping its wings would exhaust its estimated energy reserves in roughly four hours. The research showed why the right winds could make such an extraordinary crossing possible. However, these figures come from computer models. Scientists have yet to directly track individual globe skimmers throughout the proposed ocean journey. From India to Africa, but the same dragonfly doesn't make the whole trip The Maldives may be only one part of the story. In 2023, researchers from IIT Kharagpur, including Sanat Ranjan Kumar, Amit A Pawar, Arnab Roy and Sandeep Saha, examined how winds and rainfall could connect the dragonflies' movements across the Indian Ocean. Their research suggested a possible migration route: October to December: Dragonflies leave India and travel towards the Maldives as seasonal winds change. January to March: Favourable winds and rainfall may help them move towards the Seychelles and mainland Africa. May to July: Strong winds over the western Indian Ocean, known as the Somali Jet, may help later generations travel from Africa towards India. Some dragonflies may breed in temporary rainwater pools along the way, including on islands where suitable conditions exist. And here is an important detail. The dragonfly that leaves India is not necessarily the one that returns. The journey is believed to unfold across several generations. One generation travels, reproduces where conditions allow, and its offspring continue the movement. Researchers estimate that four to five generations may be involved over a year, with young dragonflies emerging approximately 45 to 60 days after breeding. The Wandering Glider (#Pantala flavescens), or Globe Skimmer, is a #dragonfly species known as the world's longest distance #insect traveller, aptly named based on its migrating behaviour. #AareyForest #aareycolony #Aarey #SGNP #Odonata #saveaareyforest #Biodiversity #Mumbai https://t.co/Txu3Z7PdU0 — Rajesh Sanap (@RajeshVS87) August 24, 2022 A remarkable journey that still holds mysteries Scientists have pieced together this possible migration by studying dragonfly sightings, rainfall, wind patterns and the energy needed for flight. While the arrival of globe skimmers in the Maldives is well documented, much of the proposed journey between India and Africa remains a scientific hypothesis supported by modelling and observations. There is still plenty to discover about the exact routes they take, where they breed and how they choose the winds that carry them. But the research already gives us a fascinating way to look at something as familiar as the monsoon. The same seasonal rains that fill our ponds, fields and lakes may also help make an extraordinary journey possible for an insect small enough to rest on our fingertip. And the next time you spot a dragonfly after the rains, consider this: a creature that looks so delicate may be capable of travelling farther than we could ever imagine. Sources: 'High-flying dragons: how the globe skimmer migrates across the Indian Ocean' : By Neha Jain, Published on 10 November 2021 'Do dragonflies migrate across the western Indian Ocean?' : By R. Charles Anderson, Published on 10 July 2009 'Transoceanic migration network of dragonfly Pantala flavescens: origin, dispersal and timing' : By Kumar Sanat Ranjan, Amit A. Pawar, Arnab Roy, Sandeep Saha, Published on 21 June 2023

items.descriptionOriginal: Step off a busy Bengaluru road and into a tree-filled park, and the difference can be immediate. The harsh sun gives way to shade, and the air feels cooler. For a city once celebrated as India's Garden City, these green spaces have become especially valuable as concrete buildings and asphalt roads spread. But what if a park could help cool the streets around it, too? A 2026 study suggests that Bengaluru's parks are doing exactly that. Researchers found that their cooling influence can extend hundreds of metres beyond their boundaries. They also identified a surprising number that could help cities plan better parks: 2.49 hectares, or roughly six acres. How far can a park's cooling reach? Researchers Arpit Verma and Sonam Agrawal wanted to understand how Bengaluru's green spaces help reduce heat in the surrounding neighbourhoods. Their study, published in Advances in Space Research , examined 15 urban green spaces using satellite images collected during summer and winter. The findings were encouraging. Most parks showed a cooling effect of over 1 C in their immediate surroundings, even where buildings and roads covered more than 70% of the surrounding area. On average, this cooling extended approximately 186 to 246 metres beyond park boundaries, with stronger effects during summer. Think about what that could mean for a neighbourhood. A park's trees and vegetation may help reduce surface temperatures along nearby roads and built-up areas, benefiting spaces beyond those used by its visitors. Why trees make such a difference There is a simple reason parks tend to be cooler. Trees block sunlight from directly heating the ground. Plants also release moisture into the air, helping cool their surroundings. Concrete and asphalt behave differently. They absorb and retain heat, contributing to higher temperatures across heavily built-up neighbourhoods. This is part of what researchers call the urban heat island effect , where cities become hotter than their less-developed surroundings. Parks alone cannot resolve urban heat. Their effectiveness depends on vegetation, surrounding construction and the availability of space for green cover. Photograph: (News 18 Kannada) The Bengaluru study found that a park's ability to counter this heating depended on its size, shape and surrounding development. And that led researchers to an important question: How big should a park be to offer effective cooling? Why 2.49 hectares could be a useful benchmark The researchers discovered that bigger parks generally cooled a wider area. However, increasing their size did not always bring equally large improvements in cooling. Their calculations identified 2.49 hectares, approximately 6.15 acres, as an efficient size for cooling intensity, or how much a park reduces surrounding surface temperatures. For cooling a larger surrounding area, the suggested size was 5.29 hectares, or about 13 acres. These figures offer useful guidance for planners deciding how to use limited urban land. Bengaluru already has expansive green spaces such as Cubbon Park and Lalbagh. But residents across the city also need accessible greenery closer to their homes. The study suggests that thoughtfully planned neighbourhood parks could help, especially in areas crowded with buildings. What this means for Bengaluru's future There is one important distinction. The researchers measured land surface temperatures using satellites, rather than the air temperatures people experience. So, while the findings show how green spaces reduce surface heating, they cannot guarantee that every nearby street will feel a certain number of degrees cooler. The 2.49-hectare figure is also a planning benchmark, rather than a fixed rule for every park. BBMP is keen to reclaim Bengaluru's Garden City tag. Currently, 1408 parks gardens are being maintained by the civic body. While 1135 of them have been fully developed, work is on to beautify 273 #parks. #BBMP #Bengaluru https://t.co/LZuwUOEnXh — Maheshwar Rao.M, IAS (@GBAChiefComm) December 19, 2019 Still, the message for Bengaluru is valuable: protecting existing parks, planting trees and planning green spaces carefully can help tackle urban heat. For residents, a neighbourhood park is where children play, friends meet and people take their evening walks. The research shows that its benefits can travel beyond those familiar paths. And perhaps that is how Bengaluru can strengthen its Garden City identity: by ensuring that the greenery people enjoy inside a park can also help cool the neighbourhoods they call home. Sources: 'The interaction between urban heat island and urban parks: An in-situ measurement-based review' : By Semra Ogce, Huseyin Ogce, Siyu Yu, Robert D. Brown, Published on 31 May 2025 'Investigation of Urban Green Spaces as Potential Cooling Sources for Heat Mitigation in Bengaluru Metropolitan City, India' : By Arpit Verma and Sonam Agrawal, Published on 1 July 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Saiga Comeback Leads the Way in Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe Reading Time: 3 minutes Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe has helped saiga antelope rebound from about 20,000 to 4.6 million. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe has produced one of the largest wildlife recoveries on record. Saiga antelope numbers have climbed from roughly 20,000 in the early 2000s to about 4.6 million in 2026. The Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative has led this work since 2006. Altyn Dala means “golden steppe” in Kazakh. The initiative has helped protect 5 million hectares of grassland, an area larger than Denmark. It is also bringing back wild asses and wild horses that vanished from the region long ago. The saiga is a small antelope with a large, flexible nose that filters dust and warms cold air. Its herds migrate hundreds of miles across the steppe, a vast, dry grassland with few trees. By the early 2000s, those herds had nearly disappeared. After the Soviet Union collapsed, poaching surged across Central Asia. Hunters killed saigas for meat and for male horns, which sold for traditional medicine in Asia. Within about a decade, the population crashed by more than 95%. Five partners joined forces in 2006 to reverse that decline. Kazakhstan’s Committee for Forestry and Wildlife works with the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan. Fauna & Flora, the Frankfurt Zoological Society, and the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds bring international support. Their first priority was stopping the killing. Ranger teams and aerial patrols now cover the saiga’s range. Sniffer dogs and customs training help catch horn smugglers at the border. Next, the partners needed to know where the herds went. Since 2009, researchers have fitted saigas with satellite tags to map their migrations. That data shows which areas need protection and when. New reserves followed the herds. The most recent, Bokey Orda-Ashiozek in western Kazakhstan, covers about 657,000 hectares. Wildlife corridors also link reserves through private land, under joint plans with landowners. The strategy faced its hardest test in 2015. During the spring calving season, more than 200,000 saigas died within weeks, over 60% of the global population. A 2018 study in Science Advances linked the deaths to a bacterium that turned deadly in hot, humid weather. Because poaching was under control, the surviving herds could rebuild. Aerial surveys each spring tracked the comeback. The 2024 count found about 2.8 million saigas, and the 2026 count reached roughly 4.6 million. That is about 230 times the low point. In December 2023, the IUCN Red List moved the saiga from Critically Endangered to Near Threatened. The Kazakh association’s director, Vera Voronova, called it one of the most successful land mammal recoveries ever recorded. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe means rebuilding the full community of grazing animals, not just one species. Kulan, a wild ass native to Central Asia, disappeared from the Torgai steppe more than 100 years ago. Scientists consider them a keystone species, since their grazing and movement help shape the grassland. Reintroductions began in 2017, and partners aim to establish about 100 kulan in the region. A recent group traveled 2,139 kilometers by road from Altyn-Emel National Park. After a year in an acclimatization pen, the animals went free in August 2025. Przewalski’s horses are following the same path. Considered the last truly wild horse species, they vanished from the wild by 1969 and survived only in zoos. In Kazakhstan, they had been gone for about 200 years. Przewalski’s horses returning to the wild are part of restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe after about 200 years. Photo by Wijs (Wise) on Pexels. The first seven horses arrived at the Altyn Dala reserve in 2024. More followed in 2025 from Prague Zoo and Hungary’s Hortobágy National Park. In May 2026, five of them left their pens and began roaming free. Officials plan to bring 40 to 45 horses by 2029, enough to sustain the herd. A stallion named Galvan wears a GPS collar so rangers can follow his movements. Local support makes these gains last. The initiative runs education programs in rural schools and has published children’s books about steppe wildlife in Kazakh. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe depends on the next generation valuing these animals. Recovery has also created new tensions. Farmers in several regions report that saigas damage crops and compete with livestock for pasture. Authorities are now studying how to manage herd sizes without undoing two decades of conservation. Roads, railways, and fences still break up migration routes. Wildfires and farm expansion put pressure on ground-nesting birds. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe will require balancing people and wildlife for years to come. Twenty years ago, the saiga seemed headed for extinction. Today, millions roam the plains, joined by wild asses and horses returning after a century or more. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe shows what patient, well-coordinated protection can achieve. The post Saiga Comeback Leads the Way in Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: When Bridget Devaney's engagement ended after her fianc 's medical emergency, she was left holding plans for a trip to Northern Ireland and a wedding day that would never come. Rather than abandon it all, she posted an anonymous invitation on social media, and 11 women from the United States, Canada, and Wales said yes - to a stranger, a country, and an uncertain week. "When these women signed up for this trip, they didn't know my name. They didn't know what I looked like. They didn't know anything about me," Bridget told BBC News NI. On the day originally reserved for her wedding, the women dressed up and stood together against Northern Ireland's coastline for photographs that captured something the original plans never could have. What the trip quietly reveals is how much people are willing to show up for one another -- and how belonging can find us even in the ruins of what we thought our lives would look like.

items.descriptionOriginal: As winter approaches, the air across several Indian cities is likely to become harder to ignore. Smoggy mornings, hazy skies, and rising pollution levels often prompt families to rethink the air they breathe at home. Suddenly, an air purifier begins to look less like a luxury and more like a practical addition to the living room or bedroom. But walk into a store or browse online, and you will find air purifiers promising everything from cleaner air to near-total particle removal. One term appears repeatedly: HEPA. So, what does it actually mean? And how do you know whether the air purifier you are considering will do its job? Here are five things worth checking before you bring one home. 1. First, understand what HEPA means HEPA stands for High-Efficiency Particulate Air. In simple terms, it refers to a filter designed to trap tiny particles suspended in the air as it passes through the filter. According to the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), a HEPA filter can theoretically remove at least 99.97% of airborne particles measuring 0.3 microns. To put that into perspective, a micron is one-millionth of a metre. These particles can include fine dust, pollen, mould spores and smoke particles. This makes HEPA filtration particularly useful when outdoor pollution finds its way indoors or when household dust and allergens become a concern . Choosing an air purifier with the right Clean Air Delivery Rate (CADR) can make a difference to how effectively it cleans the air in a room. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times ) However, not every product that mentions HEPA necessarily meets the same standard. Terms such as "HEPA-type" and "HEPA-like" do not, by themselves, establish that a filter meets a recognised HEPA performance specification. What to check: Look for a clearly stated filter grade and supporting performance information, rather than relying on the word HEPA alone. 2. Choose a purifier that suits your room Imagine buying a powerful air purifier for your bedroom, only to find that it struggles to clean the air in your larger living room. The problem may not be the filter itself, but the amount of air the machine can process. This is where CADR, or Clean Air Delivery Rate, comes in. It tells you how much filtered air a purifier delivers over a given period. A higher CADR generally means the machine can clean the air faster , provided the room size and other conditions are comparable. A purifier with a highly efficient filter may still be less effective in a large room if its airflow is insufficient. What to check: Match the manufacturer's recommended room size and CADR to the space where you plan to use the purifier. A bedroom and an open-plan living area may need different capacities. 3. Remember that HEPA filters do not remove everything HEPA filters are designed to capture particles, not every type of air pollutant. They do not, on their own, remove most gases, volatile organic compounds (VOCs) or odours. For instance, cooking can release particles into the air, while certain paints, cleaning products and new furniture can release gaseous chemicals. An activated-carbon filter can help adsorb some gases and odours. This is why some air purifiers combine HEPA filtration with activated carbon to tackle different kinds of indoor pollutants. While HEPA filters capture airborne particles, activated-carbon filters help tackle certain gases, chemicals and household odours. Photograph: ( Livemint ) What to check: If odours or gaseous pollutants are a concern, look for a purifier with an activated-carbon stage in addition to its particle filter. Check the manufacturer's specifications for what it is designed to remove. 4. Check the cost and availability of replacement filters Buying the machine is only the first expense. Filters collect particles over time and eventually need maintenance or replacement to keep the purifier working effectively. Replacement intervals vary depending on the model, how often it runs and the pollution levels in your surroundings. A filter used through a heavily polluted winter may need attention sooner than one used in cleaner conditions. What to check: Before purchasing, find out the price of a compatible replacement filter, whether it is readily available and how often the manufacturer recomm ends replacing it. Also check which parts can be cleaned and which must be replaced. 5. Look beyond the filter when comparing models A good filter is important, but the machine around it matters, too. Noise levels can affect whether you are comfortable running it at night, while energy consumption can influence your electricity bill if you use it for several hours each day. It is also worth checking the manufacturer's safety information. Some air-cleaning technologies, particularly ozone-generating devices, can introduce pollutants rather than simply remove them. Understanding how different filters work can help families make informed choices about improving indoor air quality. Photograph: ( MarketWatch ) What to check: Compare noise levels , power consumption, warranty, service support and safety specifications. Choose a model you can comfortably run and maintain as recommended. Cleaner air starts with informed choices As pollution levels rise, wanting to make the air at home a little cleaner is understandable. For families, it could mean being more mindful of the air children play in, the bedrooms where everyone sleeps, and the spaces where they spend most of their day. An air purifier can be one part of that effort. Taking a little time to understand the filter, choose the right model and maintain it well can help you make a more informed choice for your home. After all, cleaner indoor air begins with knowing what you are bringing through the door. Sources: 'What Is a HEPA Filter — and Does Filter Grade Actually Matter?' by Karban, Published on 11 April 2026. 'What is a HEPA filter?' by EPA. 'The HEPA Air Purifier: What You Need to Know!' by IQ Air, Published on 30 March 2017.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News American Red Wolf Pups Fostered into the Wild in North Carolina Reading Time: 3 minutes American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild bring fresh genes to a critically endangered species. American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild mark a first in Saint Louis Zoo history. Three critically endangered, zoo-born pups now live with a wild Red Wolf family in North Carolina. Fewer than 40 American Red Wolves remain in the wild. They live only in northeastern North Carolina. That group would not even fill a single school bus. The wolves are critically endangered, which means they face a very high risk of extinction. Hunters nearly wiped them out in the 1800s and 1900s. They once roamed the southeastern United States and are native nowhere else. In the 1960s, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) teamed up with North American zoos. Together, they started a breeding and reintroduction program for the species. The three pups were born at the zoo’s Sears Lehmann, Jr. Wildlife Reserve. Staff collected them on April 20, when they were seven days old. They underwent a health exam before the trip. Zoo staff traveled with the pups to the Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge in northeast North Carolina. They cared for the pups hour by hour along the way. FWS biologists then placed them in a wild den, a shelter where a mother raises her young. Biologists watched the den to see whether the wild mother returned. She did, and she accepted the newcomers into her litter. Several months later, the pups began exploring outside the den, and trail cameras showed all three alive and thriving. This process is called fostering. A wild mother raises pups born elsewhere as part of her own litter. American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild add new genes to a very small population. Genetic diversity helps a population stay healthy. It improves disease resistance and reduces the harm of inbreeding, which happens when close relatives breed. Timing is the biggest challenge. A foster must happen within the first 14 days of a pup’s life. That is when wolf mothers bond with their young and are most likely to accept new pups. Two groups share the work behind American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild. FWS monitors breeding among wild wolves. The Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) Saving Animals from Extinction (SAFE) Program guides breeding among wolves in zoos. When a wild litter is born, SAFE looks for zoo-born pups within that narrow window. In 2026, the Saint Louis Zoo’s litter was the only one born in professional care. Partnerships between zoos and wildlife biologists make American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild possible and bring new genes to a very small population. Photo courtesy of Saint Louis Zoo . Professional care means wolves living in zoos and similar facilities. These American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild were the only eligible pups in North America. Regina Mossotti leads the SAFE American Red Wolf Program and serves as the zoo’s vice president of animal care. She says every pup counts when fewer than 40 wolves remain. She sees fostering as a key way to give these pups a chance to support the species’ future. Emily Weller coordinates the FWS Red Wolf Recovery Program. She says several recovery actions rely on close teamwork with SAFE. The American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild show how zoo partnerships directly help wild wolves. The wild mother had a large litter. The zoo cross-fostered a few of her pups into its litter at the reserve. This swap helps ensure she can care well for each pup. The exchange also moves genes between wild wolves and zoo wolves. Experts call that a rare and valuable chance for species recovery. The reserve covers 355 acres, roughly 270 football fields, and is closed to visitors. Wolves there learn survival skills with minimal human contact, preparing them for a possible life in the wild. In 2021, the zoo announced plans to develop about 20 acres for wolf conservation. Today, the reserve holds seven habitats for breeding and conservation. The zoo will share photo and video updates on its social media pages and website. Federal biologists continue to support the wild population through the national red wolf recovery effort. Each of the American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild strengthens a population found in only one region. Other reintroduction projects show similar promise, such as efforts to return gray wolves in Colorado . Careful releases and strong partnerships can help wildlife recover. American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild show what shared effort can achieve. Zoo staff, federal biologists, and a wild mother each played a role. The post American Red Wolf Pups Fostered into the Wild in North Carolina appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST DAILY Εάν η σελίδα σας For You ήταν γεμάτη από άτομα που ακυρώνουν ραντεβού για μπότοξ επειδή άρχισαν να τρώνε περισσότερο σολομό, έχετε βρει την τάση "eat your skincare". Η υπόθεση είναι ότι η σωστή διατροφή μπορεί να κάνει αυτό που υπόσχεται ένα ντουλάπι φαρμάκων γεμάτο ορούς. Είναι, ειλικρινά, ελκυστικό… αλλά είναι επίσης μόνο εν μέρει tr…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If your For You Page has been full of people canceling Botox appointments because they started eating more salmon, you’ve found the “eat your skincare” trend. The premise is that the right diet can do what a medicine cabinet full of serums promises. It is, honestly, an appealing one… but it’s also only partly true. The route food takes to your skin When you eat, nutrients get absorbed in the GI tract and travel through the bloodstream to wherever your body decides to send them. There’s no targeting involved, so your skin gets what’s available once everything else takes its share. Topical skincare works on a different logic entirely, putting concentrated ingredients directly on one spot without the detour. “Wrinkles and collagen loss are multifactorial,” says Dr. Kseniya Kobets , Director of Cosmetic Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care. “No single food or supplement is going to make a huge difference if the rest of your diet is poor, you are unhealthy or dealing with inflammation, excessive sun exposure or you don’t have a good skincare regimen.” Food can correct deficiencies that slow things down. Vitamin C and amino acids matter for collagen formation; fatty acids support the skin barrier. But more doesn’t mean more. “I think of it as filling the tank,” Dr. Kobets says. “You need the nutrients and building blocks, but overfilling it doesn’t make the collagen-making machinery work faster.” Too much vitamin C, she notes, can cause GI problems and, in some people, raise the risk of kidney stones. Can food protect you from the sun? Some of the content goes further: eat your sunscreen . That sounds ridiculous, but there’s real science underneath it. “There is interesting evidence around oral photoprotection ,” Dr. Kobets says. “Certain carotenoids, polyphenols and Polypodium leucotomos extract have been studied for increasing the skin’s resistance to UV-induced damage.” That’s not a reason to put the SPF away, though. “I sometimes think of these as an extra layer of defense, but definitely not an oral sunscreen,” she says. “No amount of blueberries, green tea or antioxidant supplements is going to replace properly applied and reapplied sunscreen, protective clothing and smart sun behavior.” What to eat for skin health If you want your diet to pull some weight here, the list is manageable. Dr. Sapna Palep , a dermatologist at Journelle Skin, recommends eggs, avocado, flaxseeds, walnuts, salmon, and dark chocolate, which between them cover protein, healthy fats, omega-3 fatty acids , and antioxidants. “Nutrition can influence inflammation, oxidative stress, the microbiome and skin-barrier function,” says Dr. Kobets. “What is good for your overall metabolic health tends to be good for your skin as well.” That’s the version of this trend that holds up: eating well really does support your skin, and the foods involved are things most of us would benefit from eating more of anyway. What food can’t do is replace sunscreen or stand in for a routine that’s doing something. Think of it as filling a role, not playing every position. Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM History was made in governors’ races across the country on November 3. In ten states, voters chose candidates who had never held that office before as a matter of historical record, not just political preference: a Black woman elected to the governorship for the first time anywhere in the United States, the first Native American woman to lead any state, the first Latina governor of Texas, the first elected Latino governor of California, the first Black governors of Florida, Nevada, and Wisconsin, and the first women ever to win governor’s races in Tennessee, Minnesota, and Ohio. The wins came from both parties and from states that historically appeared to share very little common ground politically, which is part of what made the night so hard to categorize. Georgia elects the first Black woman governor in U.S. history The result that will end up in history books is from Georgia, where Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor’s race to become the first Black woman ever elected governor of any U.S. state. The country had never crossed this threshold before, not in 250 years of gubernatorial elections. Lance Bottoms is 56 and served as mayor of Atlanta from 2018 to 2022 before moving to Washington as an adviser to former President Joe Biden. Her defeat of Republican health care executive Rick Jackson also makes her the first Democrat to win a Georgia governor’s race in more than two decades, in a state that has been in political motion since it flipped in the 2020 presidential race. New Mexico’s Deb Haaland becomes the first Native American woman governor New Mexico voters sent Deb Haaland to the governor’s office, making her the first Native American woman to hold that position in any state. Haaland, who is of Pueblo Indian descent, has been making this kind of history for most of her public career. She was among the first Native American women elected to Congress, and later became the first Native American cabinet secretary when President Biden appointed her as Interior secretary. Her defeat of Republican Gregg Hull is one more memorable and significant accomplishment. Latino firsts in California and Texas California and Texas, the two most populous states in the country, will each have a Latino governor for the first time. In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra , who served as state attorney general before becoming Biden’s Health and Human Services secretary, defeated Republican Steve Hilton to succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom. It was not a close race, but it crossed a threshold the state had never crossed despite having one of the largest Latino populations in the country. Texas is the bigger surprise. Democrat Gina Hinojosa , a state representative, defeated incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, one of the country’s most prominent conservative governors and a close ally of President Trump. Hinojosa is now both the first Latina governor of Texas and the first Democrat to hold the office in more than 30 years. Texas has been changing as its Latino population grows, and Tuesday’s result suggested that shift is now showing up at the top of the ballot. Florida, Nevada, and Wisconsin each elect their first Black governors Three more states elected their first Black governor on Tuesday, and these wins came from both sides of the aisle. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds, backed by President Trump, defeated Democrat David Jolly to succeed outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis. Donalds has served in Congress since 2021 and spent two terms in the state legislature before that; he campaigned on affordability and pledged to continue Florida’s conservative direction. In Nevada, Democrat Aaron Ford , the state’s attorney general, defeated Republican incumbent Gov. Joe Lombardo to become the first Black governor of any state west of the Mississippi River. Ford had already been Nevada’s first Black Senate majority leader and its first Black attorney general; he first won a state legislature seat in 2012, after a career that included practicing law and teaching math. Wisconsin’s win went to Democrat David Crowley , a Milwaukee County executive who beat Republican Congressman Tom Tiffany despite being significantly outspent. His path to the general election is a saga in itself: Crowley suspended his primary campaign before rejoining the race, with the backing of outgoing Gov. Tony Evers, after the candidate he had been supporting dropped out. He ran as someone who can work across the aisle, and the result suggested Wisconsin voters believed him. Three more states elect their first women governors Three states that had never sent a woman to the governor’s office did so on Tuesday. In Tennessee, Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn won a race expected to favor her, though by a narrower margin than most anticipated. She focused on immigration, confronting China, and cutting spending, and will become the first woman ever to hold Tennessee’s governorship. In Minnesota, Democrat Amy Klobuchar defeated Republican Lisa Demuth, the speaker of the Minnesota House, and will become the state’s first woman governor when she takes office in January. Ohio produced the night’s biggest upset. Democrat Amy Acton , who served as the state’s chief public health officer during the pandemic, defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in a race that turned notably rough in its final weeks, with an attack ad against Acton drawing national attention and criticism. She is now Ohio’s first woman governor, its first Jewish governor, and the first Democrat to hold the office in 20 years. What ten firsts in one night adds up to These results don’t necessarily add up to a single story about where the country is heading. Rather, what each of them does share is that the voters who elected them have done something that hadn’t been done before. Whether that came from changing attitudes about representation, the particular strengths of individual candidates, or just the specific dynamics of this incredible moment in the history of the United States of America, an election night this concentrated in firsts is certainly one to be remembered.
