items.titleOriginal: UK’s Pop-Up “Flower Pharmacy” Prescribed Mood-Boosting Bouquets
items.description: Το πρώτο «Φαρμακείο λουλουδιών» του Ηνωμένου Βασιλείου άνοιξε τις πόρτες του τον περασμένο μήνα — συνταγογραφώντας ανθοδέσμες αντί για φάρμακα σε όσους χρειάζονται ενίσχυση της διάθεσης. Η μοναδική εμπειρία στο Λονδίνο σχεδιάστηκε για να ενθαρρύνει τους ανθρώπους να σκέφτονται διαφορετικά για τα λουλούδια, δείχνοντας πώς μπορούν να διαδραματίσουν ρόλο στην καθημερινή ευημερία και όχι απλώς να δεσμεύονται για γενέθλια, anniv…
items.descriptionOriginal: The U.K.’s first “Flower Pharmacy” opened its doors last month — prescribing bouquets instead of medicine to those in need of a mood boost. The one-off experience in London was designed to encourage people to think differently about flowers, showing how they can play a role in everyday well-being rather than just being reserved for birthdays, anniversaries, and other special occasions. It was created in partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland and chartered horticulturist, TV gardener, and author David Domoney. Guests were matched with blooms tailored to their mood before leaving with a bouquet recommended to lift, calm, or energize them. For example, yellow flowers, including sunflowers, roses, freesias, and snapdragons, were prescribed to boost happiness, while calming bouquets featured blue and green blooms like hydrangeas, delphiniums, and chrysanthemums. For those who needed a dose of energy, there were also vibrant orange, red, and pink flowers. Courtesy of SWNS The event came as a poll of 2,000 British adults found 37% struggle when daylight saving time ends, with 29% admitting the time change leaves them feeling glum. Discussing the partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, which commissioned the research and the pop-up, Domoney said: “There’s something incredibly uplifting about flowers, and research has shown that they can have a positive effect on our mood and emotional well-being. From the cheerful yellows of sunflowers and freesias to the calming tones of blues and greens, color can influence how we experience the spaces around us.” “We often associate flowers with special occasions, but there’s no reason we shouldn’t enjoy their beauty and the benefits of having them around us in everyday life,” he continued. “Sometimes, it’s the simplest connections with nature that can make a real difference to how we feel.” Courtesy of SWNS The survey also found that around a third of respondents spend more time indoors following the clock change, while 28% find the darker evenings difficult and 22% experience lower energy levels. The good news? There are plenty of ways to lift that low mood, like listening to music, reading a book, exercising, spending time in nature and, yes, buying flowers. While just 9% of people said they regularly treat themselves to blooms, the emotional response to receiving them is clear — half said they feel happy after being presented with a bouquet, 45% grateful, 34% joyful, and 24% comforted. Courtesy of SWNS Monique Kemperman, horticulture expert for Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, said: “As the days become shorter and darker, small acts of self-care can make a real difference, and flowers are a simple way to bring color, joy, and positivity into everyday life.” “Our research shows just how much of an emotional impact they can have, yet many people still reserve them for somebody else or a special occasion,” she added. “The Flower Pharmacy is about encouraging people to see flowers as an everyday well-being boost rather than a treat.” This article was originally written by Jasmine Lenthall for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.titleOriginal: The best places to volunteer this Thanksgiving: 17 options for every schedule
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Υπάρχει ένα συγκεκριμένο είδος κινήτρου που εμφανίζεται στις γιορτές. Σκέφτεσαι: φέτος, θα κάνω κάτι. Φαντάζεσαι τον εαυτό σου σε μια ποδιά σε μια σούπα και νιώθεις ωραία. Το πρόβλημα είναι ότι πολλοί άλλοι άνθρωποι απεικονίζουν το ίδιο πράγμα την ίδια στιγμή. Οι περισσότερες τράπεζες τροφίμων και κιτ σούπας…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a particular kind of motivation that kicks in around the holidays. You think: this year, I’m going to do something. You picture yourself in an apron at a soup kitchen, and it feels good. The problem is that a lot of other people are picturing the same thing at the same time. Most food banks and soup kitchens see volunteer demand spike around Thanksgiving , sometimes to the point where they have more help than they can use on that one day. If you want your time to count, a little strategy goes a long way. The good news: there are 17 solid options below, and several of them work whether you have four hours, four minutes, or no desire to leave your couch. National organizations with locations near you These programs operate across all 50 states, so wherever you are, there’s likely a chapter close enough to walk in. Feeding America Feeding America runs the largest hunger-relief network in the country. If you want to volunteer at a food bank on Thanksgiving, call ahead first. Holiday demand often fills slots fast, and some locations redirect walk-ins toward future dates when the need is more consistent. Meals on Wheels Meals on Wheels delivers hot meals to seniors who can’t get out on their own. The flexibility here is part of the appeal: you can sign up for a single delivery route or build it into a regular habit. The Salvation Army The Salvation Army works across a wide range of needs, from veterans to abuse survivors to people experiencing homelessness. There’s almost always something useful you can do, even on short notice. Operation Turkey Operation Turkey runs a tightly organized four-hour shift from 8 a.m. to noon, packing meals for homeless individuals. If you want a defined commitment with a clear end time, this is a good fit. Feed My Starving Children Feed My Starving Children packs meals at permanent sites in Arizona, Illinois, Minnesota, and Texas. It runs on a reservation system, so sign up before the week of. Toys for Tots Toys for Tots runs its drives through December, so Thanksgiving week is peak season. Volunteer slots exist for collection drives, not just drop-offs. Goodwill Goodwill often looks for people who can share a professional skill, not just sort donations. If you have a background in workforce development, finance, or career coaching, that’s where you’d fit in. United Way United Way sponsors a range of community initiatives, including garden planting, literacy programs, and neighborhood projects. What’s available depends on your city, so look up your local chapter. Local options that don’t require a national signup Soup kitchens and community meal programs often run on the same skeleton crew year after year. A call a week ahead is usually all it takes. Animal shelters are another option, especially if you’re better with dogs than crowds. Staff still work on Thanksgiving, and extra hands for walks or socialization are usually welcome. If you’re up for something more active, turkey trots are 5K races held in communities across the country on Thanksgiving morning, with proceeds going to local charities. You walk or run, and the entry fee does the work. The National Park Service also coordinates trail maintenance and cleanup projects throughout the fall. Check the volunteer page for your nearest park. If you can’t leave the house Gift-a-Family Gift-a-Family lets you sponsor a family through their holiday wishlist. The sign-up deadline is November 30, so there’s still time. Homefront America Homefront America directs donations toward grocery and turkey vouchers for military families. Support Our Troops Support Our Troops coordinates handwritten letters to deployed service members. It takes about ten minutes and goes a long way. One thing to know before you go Holiday volunteering is genuinely good, but the reality is that organizations often need year-round help. Of course, showing up once during the holidays could be the gateway to showing up regularly. If you get redirected on Thanksgiving Day because a food bank is at capacity, ask when they need people most. Often the answer is right after the holiday rush! Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post The best places to volunteer this Thanksgiving: 17 options for every schedule first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.title: Το ράντσο της Μοντάνα όπου οι αυτιστικοί άνθρωποι είναι καυγάδες και οδηγοί
items.titleOriginal: The Montana Ranch Where Autistic People Are Wranglers and Guides
items.description: Το προσωπικό στο Erik’s Ranch & Retreats λέει ένα ρητό: Σεντόνια, πετσέτες και ζωή άλλαζαν καθημερινά. Το Erik's Ranch είναι ένα καταφύγιο επισκεπτών, όπου τα αυτιστικά άτομα είναι θυρωροί, οδηγοί, τσακωτοί, μάγειρες και πολλά άλλα. Βρίσκεται σε 230 στρέμματα παρθένου βοσκοτόπου και άγριας φύσης κοντά στο Livingston της Μοντάνα, το ράντσο απέχει λιγότερο από μία ώρα από το Εθνικό Πάρκο Yellowstone. Προσφέρει…
items.descriptionOriginal: T he staff at Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has a saying: Sheets, towels and lives changed daily . Erik’s Ranch is a guest retreat where autistic people are concierges, guides, wranglers, cooks and more. Located on 230 acres of pristine pasture and wilderness near Livingston, Montana, the ranch is less than an hour from Yellowstone National Park. It offers horseback riding, fly fishing, nature hikes, history walks and experiences with ranch animals and wildlife — most led or assisted by paid neurodivergent “members,” most of whom also live on the property. The inspiration for Erik’s Ranch dates back to 2008, when founder Kathryn Nordberg was pondering how her son, Erik, whom she described as “a moderately functioning teenager with autism,” would live as an adult — and particularly what would happen when she was no longer around. Ranch manager Cameron Porter (in black hat) and member John Rekedal help a visitor from New Jersey mount her steed for a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen “As someone challenged with expressive language, there weren’t very many opportunities for kids like him,” she said, sitting in the well-appointed kitchen of the ranch’s six-bedroom lodge. So she established a nonprofit with a boutique-style hotel in Edina, Minnesota, where, even after she’s gone, Erik and others like him can live, work and thrive. There, adults on the autism spectrum work and live independently and are guided by life coaches toward achieving personal goals like interviewing, equine or cooking skills; or setting up an Etsy page to sell their artwork. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Using a similar model, in 2014 Nordberg opened the Montana ranch, where not only employees on the spectrum benefit: She designed most of the cabins specifically for neurodivergent guests. Though anyone can appreciate the soothing atmosphere, it’s particularly accommodating for those on the spectrum, who sometimes experience sensory overload. The calmingly simple cabins provide awe-inspiring vistas of the surrounding mountains with little to no sign of human activity. Hardware was selected to close drawers, cabinets and doors with hardly a sound. Walls, furnishings and bedding are muted earth tones and lights have dimmers. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch is run primarily by young autistic people, some of whom also live on the property. The ranch has unparalleled views of the Absaroka-Beartooth Mountains. Autistic and other neurodivergent people are often misunderstood and feel out-of-place, experiencing discrimination, social exclusion, bullying and other situations that can lead to low self-esteem. That — and an inexorable need to mask their differences — often results in depression and anxiety. Some studies indicate that people on the spectrum are four times more likely to experience major depression compared with the general population. “Depression, loneliness, lack of confidence, feeling isolated, rejected, and a lack of community and people who care is what Erik’s Ranch is working to minimize and eliminate,” Nordberg said. And it’s working. John Rekedal, 21, lives in Minnesota but just spent his first summer working at the Montana ranch. When he’s home, he works in a large production greenhouse. And though his coworkers there are understanding, he prefers the camaraderie of working with the ranch’s small staff amid the hush of the surrounding mountains. Jacob Thoresen fetches horses from a pasture in preparation for a trail ride. Thoresen has been working for Erik’s Ranch and Retreats for 10 years. Credit: Jodi Hausen “I’m a whole lot more inclined to work outside,” he said. “And I know everyone’s name. It’s more relaxed.” Cornell University autism researcher Leslie Shaw analyzed a national sample of autistic adults who could answer a survey unassisted and found that only about 53 percent were working in 2023. Furthermore, in 2024, people with cognitive disabilities (of which neurodivergence is a subset) were employed at less than half the rate of people without any disability, according to Cornell’s Northeast ADA Center . These low employment rates may be due to neurotypical employers’ lack of experience with and understanding of neurodivergent people leading to misaligned work assignments, confusion and a fraught or untenable work environment. On a recent late summer day in Montana, Jacob Thoresen, 33, was gearing up to lead a small group of guests on a trail ride. He has been working with the nonprofit for 10 years and splits his time between its two locations. In black cowboy hat and jeans, he walked back and forth across the dirt-floored indoor arena to a tack room, gathering saddles and bridles. He saddled horses while other members dutifully scooped and cleaned areas around the animals. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch & Retreats is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. Thoresen had other jobs before coming to Erik’s. He was a baggage handler at the Minneapolis-Saint Paul Airport and worked in retail and manufacturing. He even tried a desk job. “But,” he said with a smile, “that isn’t me.” Thoresen said he’s gained confidence working with Erik’s Ranch & Retreats. “If you would have met me 10 years ago, I would have been, like, I couldn’t be able to do anything independent and be trusted to actually get the work done,” he said. “This place is teaching me how to be independent. In this last year, I’ve grown more.” He still gets support, but staff, recognizing his achievements, have loosened the reins. “I’m having to rely more on myself to work on those independent skills,” he added. Hannah Jacobs (left) helps Zoe Markman put fresh linens on a bed in one of the guest cabins at Erik’s Ranch. Credit: Jodi Hausen When asked what he finds challenging about working at Erik’s Ranch, Thoresen said workdays can be inconsistent. At the Minnesota retreat, he completes the same tasks daily. On the ranch, daily schedules shift and sometimes he gets overwhelmed. “But I can move through it,” he said. “I attribute that to the staff that I work with and just practice. They do a good job of seeing [my overwhelm] and being like, okay. And that helps, you know. I’ve had too many employers in the past that have been like, ‘Oh, you’re not having a good day? Well, just go home.’” Over the years, Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has employed 27 autistic young adults — 19 in the last year. The goal, Nordberg said, is to serve 30 members regularly. The organization is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. John Rekedal helps clean around the horses in the indoor arena before a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen Not far from Erik’s Ranch, Special K Ranch in Columbus, Montana, provides living quarters and jobs in farming, ranching and gardening and contracts with area businesses to employ adults with developmental disabilities. Over in Jackson, Wyoming, Vertical Harvest integrates people with a wide array of disabilities into their operations growing lettuces, microgreens, tomatoes and basil. In a fully accessible greenhouse, Vertical Harvest operates on what’s known as the “Grow Well” model of employment : providing opportunities for workers to pursue passions by creating or placing them in positions that correspond to their strengths and aspirations, their likes and dislikes. In other words, adapting the workplace to the employee rather than the other way around. Although she hadn’t heard of Grow Well, Nordberg embraces its philosophy. It doesn’t always work out as planned, though. “Not everyone wants to learn hospitality,” she said. In fact, one autistic young man told her he wanted to be a “white hat hacker,” using his computer skills for good. But she didn’t have a role that fit his skills and aspirations. In other instances, however, a member’s passions can be integrated into ranch operations. Part-time member Zoe Markman shows off a colorful collection of eggs gathered from the hens in the coop behind her. Credit: Jodi Hausen Zoe Markman, a 21-year-old autistic woman from Bozeman, loves animals — particularly chickens. So when Markman started working part-time at the ranch, Nordberg built a chicken coop and populated it with more than a dozen hens whom Markman gave punny names: Chiquille O’Neal, Princess Layer and Hen Solo. On a recent workday, Markman gathered more than a dozen colorful eggs. Nordberg also helped Erik start a baking business making cookies, brownies, scones and banana bread. Erik is a visual learner and communicator, so Nordberg created a pictorial cookbook with step-by-step instructions. She marked bins of flour, sugar and other ingredients with pictures so Erik can do most of the work independently. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The ranch can currently house five members and has five cabins and the lodge for guests on its expansive property. So Nordberg has room to expand, and she’d like to. But finances and land-use regulations present barriers. It’s expensive running a guest ranch, though the costs are partly covered by guest fees and philanthropy. And area permitting will only allow for seven more cabins. “This will never be a huge operation,” Nordberg said. But she’s gratified knowing there are places for Erik and others like him to live, belong and find meaningful work. This story was supported in part by the Solutions Journalism Network’s HEAL Fellowship. items.descriptionOriginal: Sewage is full of organic matter that can be a source of energy. But it also carries harmful chemicals as well as leftover medicines that conventional treatment methods can’t remove easily. Researchers now report a technology that can solve three sewage-related problems at the same time. Their new device uses bacteria in wastewater to generate electricity while breaking down a hard-to-degrade antibiotic and producing a valuable industrial chemical. The team published their results in Journal of Power Sources . There have been plenty of research efforts to harness microbes for treating wastewater while producing renewable energy. The approach uses microbial fuel cells , which are battery-like devices with two electrodes. In microbial fuel cells, bacteria grow on an electrode and devour organic matter , converting chemical energy into electrons, which flow in an external circuit to produce electricity. Then those electrons meet oxygen at the other electrode to create water. Turns out that microbial fuel cells usually generate very small amounts of electricity. “So we asked a different question: What else could those electrons do when they arrive?,” writes the team from hydrogen peroxide instead of water. Hydrogen peroxide is a household chemical used for disinfection and bleaching. It is also used widely in chemical manufacturing. The chemical industry makes it today using an energy- and chemical-intensive process in large plants. To get the right reaction in the microbial fuel cell, the researchers designed a new electrode. They embedded iron and nickel oxides on a flexible carbon fiber cloth. When they heated the cloth in the presence of acetylene at 800°C, a forest of carbon nanofibers grew out of it. “The metal particles rode the growing fibers upward, so every fiber ended with a metal oxide tip,” the researchers say. So the electrode has conductive fibers with a catalytic tip. And bacteria cling to this rough conductive surface and form a thick film. The team used the same electrodes on both side of the fuel cell. When they ran sewage spiked with the antibiotic chloramphenicol through the cell, it removed 99.99% of the drug while producing hydrogen peroxide in two days. “Next, we plan to run it longer, test other drugs, check the toxicity of the breakdown products and link several cells in series to raise the power,” the team writes. “So can dirty water help pay for its own cleanup? Not completely yet. But in two days, our system turned sewage into cleaner water, a useful chemical and a little electricity.” Source : Yashmeen Budania et al. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Protecting Forests from Disturbance Outperforms Restoration for Amazon Biodiversity, Study Finds Reading Time: 3 minutes Across 3 million hectares of the Brazilian Amazon, protecting forests from disturbance delivered greater biodiversity benefits than restoring already-cleared land, according to new research comparing conservation strategies. Conservation policy has long debated where limited funding should go: preventing deforestation outright, protecting standing forests from degradation, or restoring land already cleared. A study published in Science this September provides the clearest answer yet, using counterfactual scenarios built from observed land-use changes across three million hectares of the Brazilian Amazon’s deforestation frontier. Led by Leonardo S. Miranda of Lancaster University alongside researchers including Joice Ferreira of Embrapa, the team compared three intervention types against what actually happened on the ground. Protecting forests from disturbance, meaning avoiding fire and selective logging within standing forest, reduced biodiversity loss by 68.5% and carbon loss by 46.8% compared with the baseline scenario. Avoiding deforestation entirely mitigated 60.8% of carbon loss and 28.0% of biodiversity loss. Restoration of already-cleared land delivered the smallest gains for both outcomes. These findings challenge a common assumption in conservation funding, where restoration often receives outsized attention and investment despite standing forests requiring protection first. Protecting forests from disturbance proved nearly as effective as preventing deforestation for carbon storage, while substantially outperforming it for biodiversity outcomes, a distinction with direct implications for how governments and conservation organizations allocate resources. Neither single intervention alone reversed losses across the landscape. Combining avoided deforestation with protection from disturbance was necessary to achieve net-positive outcomes, increasing biodiversity by 12% and carbon by 18% above 2010 baseline levels. This combined approach proved essential precisely because deforestation and forest degradation operate through different mechanisms, requiring complementary rather than substitutable responses. Restoration still carries genuine value, particularly in landscapes where deforestation has already progressed extensively. The research team found that restoration delivered meaningful benefits, particularly on properties where much of the original forest cover had already disappeared, suggesting it works best as a complement to protection rather than a replacement. Protecting forests from disturbance addresses threats that often receive less policy attention than outright deforestation. Selective logging removes valuable timber species while leaving forest canopy nominally intact, and wildfires increasingly penetrate forest edges weakened by fragmentation and drought. Both processes degrade forest structure, reduce habitat quality for forest-dependent species, and release stored carbon, yet they generate far less public attention than visible clear-cutting. Protecting forests from disturbance targets fire and selective logging, threats that degrade forest structure without clear-cutting, with researchers finding that combined deforestation and disturbance avoidance are necessary to achieve net-positive biodiversity and carbon outcomes above 2010 baseline levels. Photo by Bill Salazar on Pexels. The study’s timing is especially urgent as climate change intensifies. The research team noted that combined interventions become increasingly important as warming progresses, since forest restoration efforts prove particularly vulnerable to wildfire risk. Newly planted or naturally regenerating young forests lack the structural resilience of mature canopies, making restoration investments vulnerable to being undone by the same fire disturbances the study identifies as critical to prevent. This vulnerability creates a policy challenge extending well beyond Brazil. As governments and international organizations increasingly emphasize forest restoration within climate commitments and biodiversity frameworks, protecting forests from disturbance offers a complementary message: restoration investments achieve far less impact when the remaining standing forest around them continues degrading from fire and logging. Joice Ferreira, principal investigator of the Capoeira restoration research program at Embrapa, emphasized that restoration remains essential precisely where forests have been lost across large areas, reinforcing that the study’s findings don’t diminish restoration’s role but rather clarify where and when it delivers the strongest returns. Restoration works best as part of integrated strategies rather than as a primary tool used independently of forest protection efforts. The research methodology itself offers a template for conservation planning elsewhere. By using observed land-use changes to construct counterfactual scenarios, the team measured what would have happened under different intervention choices and quantified trade-offs that previous studies could only estimate qualitatively. This approach allows policymakers to weigh cost-effectiveness directly rather than relying on intuition about which conservation strategy delivers the greatest return per dollar invested. As tropical deforestation frontiers worldwide face similar pressures from fire, logging, and agricultural expansion, protecting forests from disturbance provides an evidence-based framework extending beyond the Brazilian Amazon alone. The findings suggest that conservation funding achieves maximum impact not through any single strategy in isolation, but through carefully sequenced combinations addressing deforestation, degradation, and restoration simultaneously, each targeting the specific threats most relevant to a given landscape’s current condition. The post Protecting Forests from Disturbance Outperforms Restoration for Amazon Biodiversity, Study Finds appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Αλλά όπως υποστηρίζει σιωπηλά αυτό το δοκίμιο, η σειρά αυτής της ιστορίας είναι λάθος: οι άνθρωποι προστάτευαν μια χούφτα συκιές και τα πουλιά έκαναν όλα τα άλλα. Το peepal, το banyan, το guular -- thre…
items.descriptionOriginal: For centuries, the sacred groves of Rajasthan were understood as human gifts to nature -- places where belief drew a boundary and the forest was allowed to breathe. But as this essay quietly argues, the order of that story is wrong: people protected a handful of fig trees, and the birds did everything else. The peepal, the banyan, the gular -- three figs that tradition placed beyond the reach of the axe - fed birds through every lean season, and those birds, carrying seeds from across the landscape, built the grove outward from that protected center, generation after generation. "What belief really preserved was a process," the author writes, "a place where the planting could go on undisturbed for centuries." There is something worth sitting with in that realization: that the deepest acts of protection are often for something we cannot fully see, and that what looks like a tree standing alone is, if the birds still come, a forest in the making.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Forest Landscape Restoration in Mozambique Launches in Nampula Province Reading Time: 3 minutes Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique has officially begun in Nampula Province, aiming to restore 500 hectares of Miombo woodland and build local livelihoods. Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique took a major step forward this August with the official launch of a new project in Nampula Province. The initiative pairs the Mozambican government with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), funded by Swiss Development Cooperation. Its goal is to turn national restoration pledges into work that communities can see on the ground. The launch unfolded over two days in Ribáuè District, starting with a briefing for provincial officials and continuing with a public ceremony. Government representatives, private companies, researchers, and local residents participated. Seedlings planted during the event were handed over to a nearby school, where students will track their growth. IUCN’s country representative in Mozambique described the project as reaching well beyond tree planting. The effort aims to improve land productivity and strengthen household livelihoods alongside ecological recovery. That framing positions forest landscape restoration in Mozambique as much an economic strategy as an environmental one. Over the next four years, the project will focus restoration work on 500 hectares within Ribáuè District. Of that total, 400 hectares will restore Miombo woodland, while the remaining 100 hectares will support agroforestry systems mixing crops with trees. The work contributes to Mozambique’s broader Five-Year Programme target of restoring 52,000 hectares nationwide. That national target also feeds into Mozambique’s international commitments under global restoration initiatives. Countries across Africa have pledged millions of hectares to these efforts over the past decade, though turning pledges into on-the-ground results has often proven difficult. A dedicated project with clear hectare targets and funding attached is meant to help close that gap. Miombo woodland stretches across a huge swath of south-central Africa, from Angola to Tanzania and across much of Mozambique. The ecosystem stores significant amounts of carbon and supports roughly half of Africa’s remaining elephant population. Millions of rural households also depend on it directly for firewood, food, and building materials. That dependence cuts both ways. Wood fuel accounts for a large share of household energy use across the Miombo region, which keeps pressure on the woodland high even where restoration work is underway. Providing communities with alternative income sources, rather than relying solely on wood and charcoal, is central to keeping any restored area intact over the long term. Alongside the restoration targets, the project will establish three plant nurseries to supply seedlings for ongoing work. Planners also intend to develop beekeeping and support sustainable value chains tied to cashew, bamboo, and legally harvested timber. Those activities aim to give residents income tied directly to keeping the landscape intact, a key piece of how forest landscape restoration in Mozambique is meant to work in practice. Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique ties livelihood directly to conservation, with three community nurseries, beekeeping, and sustainable value chains for cashew, bamboo, and timber giving Nampula residents concrete economic reasons to keep the landscape intact. Photo courtesy of IUCN . Mozambique’s project forms part of a larger global effort known as the FLR Hub, implemented by IUCN alongside other international partners. The hub originally supported restoration work across six countries in Africa and Latin America. A new contribution from Switzerland, announced in late 2025, extended that reach to Mozambique, bringing the total to seven participating countries. According to IUCN, the hub aims to shift restoration efforts from scattered, one-off projects to coordinated approaches that attract long-term investment. That shift matters for a landscape as large and fragmented as the Miombo, where piecemeal efforts have struggled to keep pace with ongoing degradation. Implementation in Ribáuè will rely on continued collaboration between government agencies, private businesses, universities, and civil society groups. Success will depend on whether restored land can deliver real income for residents, not just healthier soil and more trees. Four years is a short window to prove that the model works, but it gives the project a clear point at which results can be measured against the hectare targets set at launch. If it works, forest landscape restoration in Mozambique could offer a model other Miombo countries draw on as they pursue their own restoration commitments. The post Forest Landscape Restoration in Mozambique Launches in Nampula Province appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ ΑΙΣΙΟΔΟΞΟΥ Μια νέα θεραπεία που εγκρίθηκε από τον FDA για το PTSD ανέφερε ύφεση 68 τοις εκατό σε κλινικές δοκιμές. Τα εγκεκριμένα φάρμακα με την καλύτερη απόδοση για την πάθηση ξεπερνούν περίπου το 10,9%. Η θεραπεία, που ονομάζεται Μαγνητική e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), αναπτύχθηκε από την Wave Neuroscience με έδρα την Καλιφόρνια σε συνεργασία με…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A newly FDA-cleared treatment for PTSD reported 68 percent remission in clinical trials. The best-performing approved medications for the condition top out at around 10.9 percent. The treatment, called Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), was developed by California-based Wave Neuroscience in collaboration with researchers at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology. It pairs brain activity mapping with personalized magnetic stimulation. The clinical trial also reported a 52 percent reduction in PTSD symptoms overall. “Our FDA trial reported a 52 percent reduction in symptoms, so more than a four-fold increase in efficacy,” said Erik Won, D.O., Wave Neuroscience’s chief medical officer. “And more importantly, we saw 68 percent remission in our clinical trial. From a clinical care perspective, that’s really meaningful.” These results come from different studies, not a direct head-to-head comparison, but the gap is hard to ignore. How MeRT personalizes treatment The process starts with an electroencephalogram (EEG) that records each patient’s brain electrical activity. An AI-assisted algorithm uses that data to build a personalized stimulation plan. A coil placed against the scalp then delivers targeted magnetic pulses through transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a technique already FDA-cleared for treatment-resistant depression . Standard TMS follows a generalized protocol. MeRT adjusts based on what’s happening in each patient’s brain. Dr. Kenneth S. Ramos, a precision medicine researcher at Texas A&M Health who helped guide the study, put it this way: standard TMS covers the leak with a tarp; MeRT tries to find and replace the damaged shingles. Participants received five sessions per week over five to six weeks, but improvements appeared to persist after the sessions ended. The first FDA-cleared non-drug option for PTSD PTSD was formally recognized as a diagnosis in 1980 . Since then, treatment has relied on two FDA-approved medications, both SSRIs, and psychotherapy. A 2020 review found medication remission rates reached 10.9 percent at most. MeRT will be the first FDA-cleared non-medication treatment specifically for PTSD. Dr. Israel Liberzon, the study’s lead psychiatrist and a distinguished professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, explained what that means for patients. “Right now, the FDA has approved only two medications for PTSD,” he said. “This is the first time that in addition to the medication, we have a non-medication option. There is psychotherapy that people use for PTSD, but psychotherapies require a lot of effort. People must participate actively, and many drop out because it’s too anxiety-provoking. So now we have a unique alternative.” About six percent of Americans will experience PTSD during their lifetime, with higher rates among women and veterans . In the United States, approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day. “People living with PTSD have been left with trial-and-error treatment, medications and their side effects, and limited outcomes—even when treated by the most dedicated and experienced physicians,” Won said. “Wave’s FDA clearance signals a fundamentally different future: one in which PTSD can be objectively evaluated, precisely treated and meaningfully healed.” Wave Neuroscience and Texas A&M Health are working on insurance coverage to make the therapy more widely accessible. Won also believes MeRT could eventually be adapted for depression, anxiety, and other psychiatric conditions. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Personalized brain therapy hits 68 percent remission for PTSD first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

Ο όρος αργκό που είναι δημοφιλής μεταξύ των Gen Z και Gen Alpha ορίζεται ως η καλύτερη απόδοση ή η καλύτερη απόδοση σε κάποιον ή κάτι. Πίστεψε…
items.descriptionOriginal: “Vibe coding,” is so last year. If you want to (try) to get on the same wavelength as teens and tweens, here’s another expression to add to your repertoire: Collins Dictionary has selected “mogging” as its 2026 word of the year. The slang term popular among Gen Z and Gen Alpha is defined as outperforming or outshining someone or something. Believed to be a shortened version of AMOG (alpha male of the group), the word traces back to bodybuilding culture around the 2010s. But it’s soared in popularity over the past year, with younger generations using it in a more playful way. Collins noted that experts found a 210% increase in usage of the “fast-growing slang word” in 2026, meriting the “word of the year” crown. So how do you use it? If your friend looks amazing in the selfie you just took, but your eyes are closed and hair is out of place — they’re mogging you. Or, to offer a more meta example, mogging is mogging the other words in the dictionary. Other words on the British dictionary’s shortlist include: Bixie : a haircut that’s shorter than a bob but longer than a pixie cut Fricy : a blend of fruity and spicy Friendslop : a low-budget, independently made video game designed to be played casually with friends Carspreading : the tendency of manufacturers to build cars that are longer, wider, and heavier Hydration break : a pause in a sporting contest to allow the contestants to drink fluids, especially in high heat Ghost job : a role advertised by an employer who has no intention of actually hiring anyone On Oct. 25, Dictionary.com announced its own word of the year: “Maxxing,” a shortened version of “maximizing” that can be used on its own or tacked on to the end of another word to describe the act of optimizing something. Derived from gamer lingo and in use for over a decade, the slang term broke through on TikTok in the 2020s. Its most famous usage is perhaps “looksmaxxing,” which refers to taking a person’s appearance to its full potential, but “sleepmaxxing,” “cozymaxxing,” and “booksmaxxing” have all joined the zeitgeist as well. “Really, anything in your life can get the maxxing treatment, if you do it wholeheartedly enough,” the online dictionary wrote in a blog post.

items.descriptionOriginal: P undits are describing last night as a romp for Democrats, a rebuke of Republicans, a blue tsunami, a rout in the red states. But underneath these headlines is a quieter, parallel story about voters choosing to abandon tribal allegiance and make decisions for themselves. For months, we’ve been hearing about the possibility of a blue wave — and then, in the same breath, the caveat: Is a wave even possible in today’s hyper-polarized America? And yet, in Texas, Florida, Kansas and beyond, the electorate refused to let party loyalty make their choice for them. Young, Latino and red-state voters moved, sometimes dramatically, in just two years. The composition of the two sides turned out to be less fixed than we imagined, with a meaningful number of voters willing to cast ballots across party lines when a candidate, issue or circumstance spoke to them. In Texas, where Democrats had historic wins, people of all parties have recently united to fight against a border wall through Big Bend National Park. Credit: Sam Karas Part of the story was turnout, said New York Times Chief Political Analyst Nate Cohn on The Daily . But, he added, “Many people who are registered as Republicans and voted for Donald Trump voted for the Democratic candidate.” This feels like a fitting conclusion to The Depolarization Project , our special series about how political polarization works and what we can do about it. The premise of that series was that depolarization isn’t about meeting in the middle. It’s about choosing to remain open and curious, rather than blindly clinging to arbitrary affiliations. In the end, many voters showed that their party label doesn’t have the final say. Data center opposition is proving to be a bipartisan, or even nonpartisan, issue across the U.S. Credit: Here Now / Shutterstock Wednesdays are normally “What We’re Reading” day here at Reasons to be Cheerful, so in that spirit, here’s a post-Election Day list of stories from our own depolarization series and from elsewhere around the web.
